Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet, whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel - who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong and makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So they who have believed in him, honored him, supported him, and followed the light which has been sent down with him - it is those who will be the successful.﴾ (Surat al-A'raf)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 123:

﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾

This noble verse resembles verse 48 of Surah al-Baqarah, in which Allah, blessed and exalted is He, says:

﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾

We say that this resemblance is apparent, but each verse conveys an independent meaning. In verse 48 the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it.﴾ In the verse we are discussing He says: ﴿Nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it.﴾ Why? Because His saying ﴿no soul will avail another soul at all﴾ — if we intend the first soul, the context suits it in the first verse; and if we intend the second soul, the context suits it in the second verse, which we are discussing. It is as though there are two souls with us: one that repays (the "jāziyah," the soul that discharges on behalf of another), and the other that is repaid for (the "majzā ʿanhā," the soul on whose behalf payment is made). The repaying soul is the one that intercedes, so the first thing accepted from it is intercession. If its intercession is not accepted, it says, "I will bear the compensation," meaning taking the ransom or whatever corresponds to the sin. But the soul on whose behalf payment is made, the first thing put forward from it is compensation or ransom. If that is not accepted from it, it seeks an intercessor. We have discussed this in detail when we addressed verse 48 of Surah al-Baqarah.

The Exalted comes to the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to clear away the dispute and doubt that the Jews raised when the qibla (the direction of prayer) was changed, and when the Muslims turned toward the Sacred Ka'bah instead of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It also addresses the argument the Jews made, that they are God's chosen people and that no prophet would come except from among them. God, blessed and exalted, wants to show the connection of the Arabs to Ibrahim and their connection to the House.

So the Truth, majestic is His majesty, says: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them﴾. Its meaning is: remember when God tried Ibrahim.

"Wa-idh" here is an adverb of time, and there is a difference between it and "idha", the conditional, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿When the help of God comes, and victory, and you see the people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾ (Surat al-Nasr). Here "idha" is an adverb but it also indicates a condition. As for "idh", it is only an adverb. His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Ibrahim was tried by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them﴾ mean: remember the time when Ibrahim was tried with words.

What is the meaning of "ibtila'" (trial)? People think it is evil, but in reality it is not so, because trial is a test: if we pass it, it is good, and if we fail it, it is evil. So trial is not evil, but a measure to test good and evil. The One who tried is God, glorified is He. He is the Lord, and "rabb" means the one who nurtures, who takes the one he nurtures through methods that qualify him to the perfection required of him. And among the foundations of upbringing is that the nurturer tests the one he raises, to know whether he has succeeded in raising him or not. The trial here is "with words", and "kalimat" (words) is the plural of "kalimah" (word). "Kalimah" may be applied to a sentence, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And to warn those who say, "God has taken a son." They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie﴾ (Surat al-Kahf).

So "kalimah" may be applied to a sentence and may be applied to a single term, as if you say, for example, "Muhammad," and stop. In that case it is not a meaningful sentence. The word intended in this verse is the divine obligation (taklif) from God.

His words, glorified is He: "Do" and "do not do." It is as if the divine obligation from God is merely a word, and you either fulfil its requirement or you do not. The scholars have differed about the words that Ibrahim received from his Lord. We say to them that these words must suit the station of Ibrahim, father of the prophets: they are a trial that makes him fit to bear the message. That is, the trial must be great. The scholars have said that the trials were ten, and some said forty. Ten of them are in Surat al-Tawbah, which is His words: ﴿Those who repent, who worship, who praise, who travel, who bow, who prostrate, who enjoin what is right, who forbid what is wrong, and who guard the limits of God﴾ (from verse 112 of Surat al-Tawbah).

This is the narration of Abdullah ibn Abbas. Another ten are in Surat al-Mu'minun. In His words, glorified is He:

﴿The believers have certainly succeeded, who are during their prayer humbly submissive, and who turn away from ill speech, and who are establishing zakah, and who guard their private parts, except from their spouses or what their right hands possess, for indeed, they are not blamed, but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are transgressors. And those who are to their trusts and their promises attentive, and who maintain their prayers. Those are the inheritors﴾ (Surat al-Mu'minun).

After that He said: ﴿Those are the inheritors﴾.

In Surat al-Ahzab He mentions from them the words of the Majestic, the Exalted:

﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the devoutly obedient men and devoutly obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humbly submissive men and humbly submissive women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their private parts and the women who do so, and the men who remember God much and the women who do so, God has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ (Surat al-Ahzab, verse 35).

In Surat al-Ma'arij He says:

﴿Except those who pray, who are constant in their prayer, and those in whose wealth is a known right for the beggar and the deprived, and those who believe in the Day of Judgment, and those who are fearful of the punishment of their Lord, indeed the punishment of their Lord is not safe, and those who guard their private parts, except from their spouses or what their right hands possess, for indeed, they are not blamed, but whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are transgressors, and those who are to their trusts and their promises attentive, and those who stand by their testimonies, and those who maintain their prayers﴾ (Surat al-Ma'arij).

From this discussion we conclude that God tried Ibrahim with words of obligation: do this, and do not do that. He tried him by being thrown into the fire while alive, and he did not waver, did not turn back, and turned only to God. The peak of the trial was that he was commanded to slaughter his son. That Ibrahim fulfilled all the obligations with passion and love, and added to them of the same kind, and that when he was thrown into the fire he did not care, and Jibril came to him and said, "Do you have any need?" and Ibrahim replied, "As for you, no. As for God, His knowledge of my condition suffices me from my asking." And that when he was an old man he was tried by slaughtering his only son, and he obeyed with a tranquil soul and contentment with God's decree.

The Truth says:

﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Musa? And of Ibrahim who fulfilled﴾ (Surat al-Najm, verses 36–37).

That is, he fulfilled all that was asked of him and performed it with passion for the method and for God's trials. Ibrahim, peace be upon him, succeeded in everything he was tried with or tested with. God was dearer to him than his family, his self, and his offspring.

What did God reward him with? He said: ﴿He said, "Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people"﴾ (from verse 124 of Surat al-Baqarah).

That is, the Truth, blessed and exalted, entrusted him to be a leader of mankind. God, glorified is He, knew Ibrahim's fulfilment, but He tested him so that we human beings would know how God chooses His close servants, and how they become leaders who take charge of affairs. Ibrahim received this good news from God and said, as the Noble Qur'an narrates to us:

﴿He said, "And from my descendants"﴾ (from verse 124 of Surat al-Baqarah).

What is "dhurriyyah" (offspring)? It is the progeny that comes and the child that is born. Because he loves that goodness should flow to his children and grandchildren, and this is the nature of human beings: they give the fruit of their movement and work in life to their children and grandchildren, and they are glad. That is why Ibrahim wanted to transfer the imamate to his children and grandchildren, so that they would not be deprived of the faith-based values that guard their lives and lead them to a bliss that does not end. But God, glorified and exalted is He, answers Ibrahim with a matter of faith as well, a rebuke to the Jews who abandoned values and worshipped material things. So the Majestic, exalted is He, says:

﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ (from verse 124 of Surat al-Baqarah).

So it is as if Ibrahim, through his deeds, had attained the imamate, but this is not transmitted except to the righteous among His servants who worship and glorify Him.

The words of the Truth, glorified is He: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ are intended for the Jews, who sold their faith-based values for material gain. It is an extrapolation about the unseen: that from the descendants of Ibrahim there will come those who will transgress and do wrong.

Among the marvels is that Musa and Harun, peace be upon them, were both messengers. The original messenger was Musa, and Harun came to strengthen his support because he was eloquent of tongue. The will of God, glorified is He, decreed that the prophethood continue in the descendants of Harun and not in the descendants of Musa. Prophethood is not an inheritance.

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. It is as if the covenant of God is what draws its holder; that is, He is the agent. Next we come to the question of lineage, blood, and colour. The sonship of prophets is not the sonship of all people. The prophets are chosen for their values, and their sons are those who take these values from them, not those who take lineage, blood, or colour. If we return to the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, when his son drowned, he raised his hands to the sky and said:

﴿My Lord, indeed my son is of my family﴾ (from verse 45 of Surat Hud).

So the Truth, blessed and exalted, answered him and said:

﴿Indeed, he is not of your family; indeed, he is one whose deeds are unrighteous﴾ (from verse 46 of Surat Hud).

The people of prophethood are those who take values from the prophets. Had the Truth, glorified is He, not said to us, ﴿indeed, he is one whose deeds are unrighteous﴾, we would have believed that he may have come from another man or for some other reason.

But God wants us to know that the non-attribution of Nuh's son to his father is because of ﴿indeed, he is one whose deeds are unrighteous﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 126:

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this a secure city, and provide its people with fruits, such of them as believe in Allah and the Last Day." He said: "And as for him who disbelieves, I will let him enjoy himself for a little, then I will drive him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination."﴾ (126)

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a place of security﴾. Since Allah has already made it a place of security, what is the benefit of Abraham's supplication that Makkah be a secure city? We say: when you see a request for something that exists, know that the purpose of it is the continuation of that existing thing. Abraham was asking Allah, glorified and exalted, to perpetuate the blessing of security in the House. This is because when you read the words of the Truth, blessed and exalted is He:

﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah and His Messenger, and the Book which He has sent down to His Messenger, and the Book which He sent down before. And whoever disbelieves in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day, has certainly strayed far away﴾ (Surat an-Nisa', 136). He addressed them by the term "believe," then asked them to believe. How? We say: Allah, glorified is He, commands them to persist and continue in faith. Therefore every request for something that exists is a request for the continuation of that existing thing.

And Abraham's words: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure city﴾ mean: O Lord, if You have already made this House secure in the past, then keep it secure until the Hour arises, so that everyone who enters it will be secure, because it is situated in a valley without vegetation. In the past, people used to fear going to it because security was lacking on the road. Or "secure" means that Allah perpetuates for everyone who enters it the blessing of faith.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Make this a city, secure﴾ are repeated in another verse which says: ﴿Make this city secure﴾. Once it came indefinite and once definite. We say that when Abraham said: ﴿My Lord, make this city secure﴾, he asked Allah for two things: that He make this place a city (baladan), and that He make it secure.

What is the meaning of making it a city (baladan)? There are names taken from tangible things. The word ghasb (usurpation) means stripping the skin off a sheep, as if one who takes something from a person by force strips it from him while he is still clinging to it.

When you hear the word balad, it refers to a city. The balad is also the spot (buqah) that appears in the skin, distinguishing it from the rest of the skin, such as a white patch on the face or the forearms, so that the spot that appeared is distinguished by the whiteness of its colour. A place that has no dwellings or buildings is level with the ground, so you cannot easily distinguish it. But when you settle in it and build structures, you make a mark that distinguishes it from the surrounding land.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And provide its people with fruits﴾ are among the requirements of security, for as long as there is sustenance and fruits, the elements of life are present and people remain in this city. But Abraham said: ﴿and provide its people with fruits, such of them as believe﴾, as if he were asking for sustenance for the believers alone. Why? Because when Allah said to him:

﴿Indeed I will make you a leader for the people﴾ (part of verse 124, Surat al-Baqarah).

Abraham said:

﴿And from my offspring﴾ (part of verse 124, Surat al-Baqarah).

Allah, glorified is He, said:

﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ (part of verse 124, Surat al-Baqarah).

Abraham feared, while asking on behalf of those who would dwell in Makkah, that Allah's response might be like the earlier response, as if it would be said to him: the wrongdoers do not receive the provision of Allah. So Abraham corrected himself and said: ﴿and provide its people with fruits, such of them as believe﴾. But Allah, glorified is He, wanted to draw Abraham's attention to the fact that the gift of divinity (ulluhiyyah) is not like the gift of lordship (rububiyyah). Leadership of the people is a gift of divinity, which only the believer attains, whereas provision is a gift of lordship, which both the believer and the disbeliever attain, because Allah is the One who summoned us all into life and guaranteed our sustenance together. It is as though the Truth, glorified is He, when He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, was speaking of the values of the method, which are given only to the believer, but provision is given to both the believer and the disbeliever. Therefore Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿and whoever disbelieves﴾. In this there is a correction of concepts for Abraham, so that he would know that everyone whom Allah, exalted is He, has summoned to life has his provision, whether believer or disbeliever, and good in this world is widespread. So, since Allah has summoned you, He has guaranteed your provision.

Allah did not say to the sun, "Shine upon the land of the believer only," nor did He say to the air, "Let no wrongdoer breathe you." Rather, He gave the blessing of preserving and sustaining life to everyone He created, whether believer or disbeliever. But concerning the one who disbelieves, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, I will let him enjoy himself for a little﴾. Enjoyment (tamattu') is something a person loves and wishes to continue and recur.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿fa-umatti'uhu (then I will let him enjoy himself)﴾ are evidence of the continuation of his enjoyment, meaning that he has enjoyment in this world. Every blessing has its enjoyment: food has its enjoyment, drink has its enjoyment, and sexual relations have their enjoyment. So enjoyment in this world consists of many things. But Allah, blessed and exalted is He, described it as "a little," because enjoyment in this world, however great it is and however many its forms, is still little.

Consider His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then I will drive him (idtarruhu) to the punishment of the Fire﴾. The meaning of idtarruhu is that he has no choice in the Hereafter. A person has choice in the life of this world, taking this and leaving that, but in the Hereafter he has no choice. He, being one of the people of the Fire for example, cannot choose Paradise. Rather, his limbs that were subjected to serve him in the life of this world, and which he ordered to disobey and they obeyed, have no authority over them for him in the Hereafter. This is the meaning of His words, glorified is He:

﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them concerning what they used to do﴾ (Surat an-Nur, 24).

That is, the limbs that used to obey the disbeliever in sins in this world will not obey him on the Day of Resurrection. The tongue that used to utter disbelief, may Allah protect us, will come on the Day of Resurrection and testify against its owner. The foot that used to walk to places of wine, amusement and debauchery will testify against its owner, and the hand that used to kill and steal will testify against its owner. His words "idtarruhu" mean that a person loses his choice in the Hereafter, then ends up in the Fire and in severe punishment, in fulfilment of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then I will drive him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination﴾. That is, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, warns the disbelievers that for them is the Fire and punishment in the Hereafter, not by their own choice, but while they are subdued.

Allah the Exalted says to His Messenger (ﷺ): Remember when Ibrahim was raising the foundations of the House. The verb "yarfa'" (raising) is used here in the present tense to depict the event as if it were happening now.

But is Ibrahim now raising the foundations of the House? Or did he raise them and finish? Of course he raised them and finished. However, Allah wants to bring before the mind the state of Ibrahim and Isma'il as they raised the foundations of the House. Allah wants the believers to picture the act of raising. Ibrahim had no ladder to climb and stand upon, and he had no scaffolding ("siqalah"). But the absence of these means did not prevent Ibrahim from devising a way and bringing the stone.

Allah wants us not to forget this act. Ibrahim and his son Isma'il would go off to search for a stone, and the stone must have been light in weight so that they could carry it to the place of construction. Then Ibrahim would stand upon the stone while Isma'il handed him the other stones with which the foundations of the House would be raised. Despite the hardship the two of them bore, they were happy, and all they asked of Allah was that He accept it from them. Acceptance (al-qubul), meeting (al-muqabalah) and receiving (al-istiqbal) all come from the root "muwajahah" (facing). That is, they ask Allah, standing before Him, about their work; they want nothing but reward: "Accept it from us," meaning, give us reward for what we do for Your sake and in carrying out Your command.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Innaka anta al-Sami' al-'Alim﴾, meaning: You, O Lord, are the All-Hearing who hears our supplication and hears what we say. "Al-'Alim" means the All-Knowing of our intention and the extent of our sincerity toward You. We perform this work seeking Your countenance and intend no one other than You. For actions are by intentions, and two men may do one and the same deed: one of them is rewarded because he does it seeking the pleasure of Allah and drawing near to Him, while the other is not rewarded because he does it for the sake of worldly gain.

Allah the Exalted knows the intention. If the deed is sincerely for Allah, He accepts it; and if it is not sincerely for His sake, He does not accept it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended. Whoever's migration was to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's migration was for a worldly thing he would obtain, or a woman he would marry, his migration is to that for which he migrated." (1) So, if the deed is not sincerely for Allah, there is no reward for it.

1 Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah, and al-Daraqutni, with various wordings.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 128:

﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims [in submission] to You, and of our descendants a Muslim nation [in submission] to You. And show us our rites [of worship], and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

There is a difference between being assigned a task and doing it with love, and performing the outward form of the assignment, leaving your work like one who has lifted the burden of duty from his shoulders. In this noble verse is the supplication of Ibrahim and his son Isma'il, who were saying: "O Lord, You commanded us to raise the foundations of the House, and we have done what You commanded us." This does not mean that we are content with Your assignment to us, because we want to taste the sweetness of assignment from You again and again. ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You﴾: we submit all our affairs to You.

A person cannot finish one duty and then seek another unless he has come to love the sweetness of duty and found enjoyment in it. A person finds no enjoyment in duty unless he keeps the reward for it in mind. Whenever he does something, he calls to mind the bliss awaiting him for this deed, so he seeks more.

As soon as Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them, finished raising the foundations of the House, they said: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims to You﴾, and they were not satisfied with that alone, but wished the sweetness of duty to extend to their descendants after them. So they say: ﴿and of our descendants a Muslim nation﴾, so that the course of God's method on earth may continue and duty may persist from descendant to descendant until the Day of Resurrection. Then they say: ﴿And show us our rites﴾, that is: explain to us, O Lord, what You want from us. Show us how to worship You and how to draw near to You. The "manasik" (rites) are the matters by which God, glorified and exalted, wants us to worship Him. His saying ﴿And show us our rites﴾ shows us that Ibrahim desired to open the doors of duty for himself, because he sees in every duty nothing but purification of the soul, good for his descendants, and bliss in the Hereafter. That is why he says, as the Truth relates to us: ﴿and accept our repentance. Indeed, You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾. As for "and accept our repentance," it is not necessary to understand it as repentance from sin, as if Ibrahim and Isma'il had fallen into disobedience and wished to repent to God. Rather, because they knew that those who would come after them would fall into sin, they asked for repentance for their descendants. And how did they know? When God, glorified and exalted, said to Ibrahim: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little while, then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire, and wretched is the destination﴾.

They asked God, blessed and exalted, for repentance and mercy for their descendants. God loves repentance from His servants, and He, glorified is He, is more delighted at the repentance of His believing servant than one of you who finds his camel after having lost it in a desert. This is because sin, when it takes a person away from God's method in order to give him immediate benefit, the sweetness of faith, if he is a believer, will draw him back to faith, away from sins. That is why it has been said: if you benefit from repentance and regret what you did, God will not only forgive your sins but will also transform your evil deeds into good deeds. We have said that the legislation of repentance was a safeguard for the whole society against harm and great evil. For if a single sin made you eternally abiding in the Fire with no repentance after it, the disobedient would become defiant and would increase in evil, the whole society would be struck by their evils, and people would despair of their Hereafter. Because the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

"Every son of Adam sins, and the best of sinners are those who repent." (1)

Therefore, it is from God's mercy, glorified is He, that He legislated repentance for us to spare us from the harshness of harm and sin.

1 Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Darimi in his Sunan, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 129:

﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom and purify them. Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾

The supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): that Allah, glorified and exalted, complete His favour upon his descendants and increase His mercy upon His servants, by sending to them a messenger who conveys to them the method of the heavens, so that there is no period of darkness on earth in which disobedience, corruption and disbelief spread and people worship idols, as happened before Ibrahim.

The phrase ﴿a messenger from themselves﴾ is a response to the Jews, who were distressed that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was from the Arabs, and that prophethood ought to have been among them. We say to them: our grandfather and your grandfather is Ibrahim, and you are from the descendants of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq, while Muhammad (ﷺ) is from the descendants of Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, the brother of Ishaq. There is no proof in what you claim, that Allah preferred you and chose you over the other peoples. Rather, the Truth, glorified and exalted, willed to strip prophethood from you because you wronged on earth, and "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."

The Truth, blessed and exalted, wished to say to them that this Prophet is from the lineage of Ibrahim, and that he belongs to Isma'il ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon them both.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who will recite to them Your verses﴾: that is, the verses of the Noble Qur'an.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and teach them the Book and wisdom﴾: We must know that there is a difference between recitation (tilawa) and teaching (ta'lim). Recitation is that you read the Qur'an; teaching is that you know its meaning and what it came with, so that you apply it and know whence it came. If the Book is the Noble Qur'an, then wisdom is the sayings of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), about which the Truth, glorified and exalted, said in His address to the wives of the Prophet:

﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of Allah and the wisdom﴾ (part of verse 34, Surat al-Ahzab).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and purify them﴾: that is, cleanse them, and lead them to the path of goodness and the completion of faith.

His saying, majestic is His majesty: ﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾: that is, the Mighty who is not overcome because of His dominion, and whom no one questions. ﴿And the Wise﴾: who does nothing except with consummate wisdom.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 130:

﴿Who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We had chosen him in this world, and he is certainly in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾

What is the religion (millah) of Abraham? It is the worship of God alone, with no partner, and a love of the obligations (taklif). Abraham fulfilled everything God charged him with and went beyond it. He met trial with obedience and patience. When God tested him with the sacrifice of his only son, he did not hesitate; he performed his duties with love, and he sought to preserve the sound method (manhaj) in his descendants.

God's words ﴿Who would turn away﴾ mean: who would turn aside and reject. It is said "raghiba fi kadha" (رغب في كذا), meaning he loved it and desired it, and "raghiba 'an kadha" (رغب عن كذا), meaning he turned away from it and avoided it. Those who turn away from the religion of Abraham and reject it are the foolish and the ignorant, and so God, glorified and exalted, said of them: ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. This is evidence of weakness of judgment and of failure to distinguish between what benefits and what harms. When there are those who have inherited wealth while their minds are immature, their reason not matching their age, we call them "sufaha" (السفهاء, the foolish). The safih (السفيه, the foolish person) is one whose judgment has not matured, and for this reason his guardianship over his property passes to a guardian (wali) or an executor (wasi), because by his foolishness he is unable to spend money on what is beneficial. The Noble Qur'an treats this matter with precision, saying: ﴿And do not give the foolish your property which God has made a means of support for you, but provide for them from it and clothe them and speak to them with kindly words﴾ (Surah al-Nisa').

We observe that God, the Blessed and Exalted, called the property of the foolish "your property" (amwalukum) and did not regard it as the property of the foolish person, because he is not fit to be responsible for it. He placed this property under the supervision of another person, more mature and wise.

God's words ﴿your property﴾ are so that the guardian or executor is as keen to preserve it as he is for his own wealth, or more so, but he is only a trustee. When a person reaches the age of maturity (rushd), or the foolish person is cured of his foolishness, his property is returned to him so that he may dispose of it. We see a number of children bringing lawsuits against their fathers and mothers, accusing them of foolishness because they do not handle their property well, and then they take this property and squander it themselves. What everyone who carries out this process must know is that he has no right to spend the money or waste it for his own account. There are two cases: either the person is poor, in which case he may eat in a reasonable manner (bil-ma'ruf), or he is wealthy, in which case he makes his work in the guardianship for God's sake and takes nothing in return. But to take the money and squander it on himself, on his desires, on his wife and children, this is rejected and he will be held accountable for it. God, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿Whoever is wealthy, let him abstain; and whoever is poor, let him eat in a reasonable manner﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 4:6).

Thus, the one who turns away from the religion of Abraham is a fool who possesses no reason capable of distinguishing between the harmful and the beneficial.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿We had chosen him in this world, and he is certainly in the Hereafter among the righteous.﴾ He was chosen in this world through the method (manhaj), through making him an imam, and through trial. Many people think that the elevated status of some in worldly affairs is God's choosing them by giving them the adornments of worldly life, and they take this as justification for believing that they have a high station in the Hereafter. We say no: the stations of this world have no connection to the Hereafter. For this reason, the Blessed and Exalted God said: ﴿We had chosen him in this world﴾, and He added: ﴿and he is certainly in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, so that we know that Abraham, peace be upon him, has a high station in this world and bliss in the Hereafter, both together.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 131:

﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾

Allah, glorified and exalted, wants to draw our attention to the fact that He said to Ibrahim, "Submit," and he said, "I have submitted." So what Allah the Truthful requires of His servant is that he submit to Him. Allah did not say "submit to Me," because that is understood. And He did not say "submit to your Lord," because submission is only due to Allah, for He is the One entrusted to us (al-ma'mun 'alayna).

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said in his reply: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds.﴾

This means that he will not be alone in the universe, for when he submits to Allah, who has subjected to him whatever is in the heavens and the earth, he will have harmonised with the universe that Allah created for man. Whoever submits his face to Allah, the Glorious, the Wise, the Mighty who cannot be overcome, the Capable whose capacity has no end, the Victorious who is never defeated, the Provider from whom sustenance comes alone, is more mature in mind. He has, in effect, submitted his face to all good.

The religion with Allah, glorified and exalted, from the time of Adam until the Day of Resurrection, is the submission of the face to Allah. And why the face? Because the face is the most noble thing in a person, the thing he takes pride in and regards as a mark of his dignity and honour. Therefore, when we want to show the utmost submission to Allah in prayer, we place our foreheads and faces on the ground. This is the utmost humility and submission: to place the most noble part of you, your face, on the earth, as a declaration of your submission to Allah, glorified and exalted.

Allah, majestic in His majesty, wants man to surrender his leadership to Allah, by making his choices in this world conform to what Allah wants. So when he speaks, he does not lie, because Allah loves truthfulness. When he is charged with something, he does it, because the obligation is for our benefit and Allah gains nothing from it. And when Allah, exalted be He, says, "Give charity from your wealth," he hastens to give from his wealth, so that He may return to him manifold multiples in the Hereafter, by the power of Allah.

Thus we see that the good for man in its entirety lies in making his desires in the life of this world conform to what Allah has willed. In that case he has harmonised with the whole universe, and you find that the universe serves him and gives to him, and he is happy.

As for one who submits his face to other than Allah, he has relied on a strong one who may weaken, on a rich one who may become poor, and on an existent one who may die and cease to exist. Therefore, in this state, he is characterised by foolishness, because he has relied on what harms and abandoned what benefits.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 132:

﴿And Abraham charged his sons with it, and [so did] Jacob: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."﴾

When you read the word "wasiyya" (charging, bequeathing), know that a bequest comes to move a person toward something beneficial at the last time you have in this world, because the last hours of a person in this world, if he has lived in it, do not deceive people at all. At the hour of his dying, he does not deceive himself, nor does he deceive anyone among the people. Why? Because he senses that he is about to meet Allah, glorified is He, so he speaks the word of truth.

Advice or bequest is an admonition that you love to be held fast by the one you advise, and you say it to him sincerely at the last moment of his life. Therefore Allah, glorified and exalted is He, comes to show us this in His saying:

﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Jacob, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?"﴾ (part of verse 133, Surah al-Baqara).

Thus Allah, glorified is He, wants to show us that a bequest is always to one whom you love, and that a person's love for his children is certain, whether this person is a believer or a disbeliever. We do not wish that there be in this world anyone better than us except our children, and we work toward that so that all good may be theirs.

Abraham charged his sons, and Jacob charged his sons. And the charge would have been: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion." So the charge was not a matter from Abraham, nor a matter from Jacob, but it was a matter that Allah chose for mankind, so neither Abraham nor Jacob found it fitting to charge their children except with what Allah had chosen. It is as if Abraham entrusted Allah with himself, so he carried out the obligations, and He entrusted him with his children, so he wanted them to hold fast to what Allah had chosen for them.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Abraham charged his sons with it, and [so did] Jacob﴾. Abraham is the great father, and his son Isaac, and Isaac's son Jacob. Jacob is the direct father of the Jews. Jacob charged them, as the Noble Qur'an relates to us: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims.﴾

You do not forbid a person from a matter unless it is within his power to avoid it, and you do not command him to it unless it is within his power to carry it out. So do Jacob's sons possess the ability to die while they are Muslims? Death is not in anyone's control. It comes at any time, suddenly. But since Jacob charged his sons, "Do not die except while you are Muslims," the meaning is: do not part from Islam for a moment, so that death does not overtake you except while you are Muslims.

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, concealed the time of death, its place, and its cause, so that this would be a notice of it, and people expect it at any age, in any place, and at any time. Therefore we may seek well-being in things in which death occurs. The poet says: "If it sleeps for you, every remedy is beneficial; and if it does not sleep, medicine is among its causes."
That is, if the appointed term has not yet come, medicine benefits you and is among the causes of healing. But if the appointed term has come, medicine becomes a cause of death, as when you go for a surgical operation and it becomes the cause of your death. So a person must hold fast to Islam and to the method, and never be heedless of it, lest death come upon him in his heedlessness and he dies not a Muslim, and we seek refuge in Allah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 133:

﴿Were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub (Jacob), when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim (Abraham), Isma'il (Ishmael) and Ishaq (Isaac), one God, and to Him we are submitting."﴾

This is an address from Ya'qub that applies to and touches the Jews contemporary with the revelation of the Noble Qur'an. Ya'qub said to his sons, what do you worship after me? ﴿They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are submitting."﴾

This is an acknowledgment by the Asbat (the tribes), the sons of Ya'qub, that they are Muslims and that their fathers were Muslims. Consider the precision of the Qur'anic expression in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We will worship your God and the God of your fathers﴾. It is as if nothing changed after the death of Ibrahim; and when Ya'qub was dying, the object of worship did not change, and He is Allah, the One, glorified and exalted. Therefore they said, as the Noble Qur'an relates to us: ﴿one God﴾. We will take from this verse a snapshot that benefits us in many matters, because the Qur'an will address, in the story of Ibrahim, that he spoke with his father about matters of belief. So He said, as the Noble Qur'an relates to us:

﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods? Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error."﴾ (Surah al-An'am).

We know that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is from the lineage of Isma'il son of Ibrahim, and the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam."

So if Azar, the father of Ibrahim, was a disbeliever and worshipper of idols, how is the noble lineage valid? We say: if the Qur'an had said ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father﴾ and stopped, the meaning would be that the addressee was the father of Ibrahim. But the saying of Allah ﴿to his father Azar﴾ came for a wisdom. Because when the name of the father is mentioned, it may not be the father but the uncle. For you, if you enter a house and a child meets you, you say to him, "Is your father present?" and you do not say "Is your father so-and-so," because he is well known so the child will not err about him. But if you intend the uncle, you ask the child, "Is your father so-and-so present?" In this case you intend the uncle and not the father, because the uncle is in the position of a father, especially if the father has passed away.

Thus the saying of the Truth, glorified and exalted: ﴿to his father Azar﴾, by mentioning the name, means "to his uncle Azar." If someone says, "Is there evidence for this?" we say: yes, there is evidence in the Qur'an in this noble verse: ﴿Were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers"﴾. The "fathers" is the plural of "father," and then Allah, blessed and exalted, specified the fathers: Ibrahim, who is the grandfather and is also called "father"; Isma'il, who is the uncle and is also called "father"; and Ishaq, who is the father of Ya'qub. Isma'il came before Ishaq.

So in this verse, the plural of "father" covers three: Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq; and Ya'qub, to whom death came, is the son of Ishaq. But when Ya'qub's sons addressed their father, they said "your fathers," then they brought their names specifically: Ibrahim the grandfather, Isma'il the uncle, and Ishaq the father of Ya'qub, and they applied the title "father" to all of them. So Isma'il was called "father" though he was an uncle, Ibrahim was called "father" though he was a grandfather, and Ishaq was called "father" and he was (truly) a father.

Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am the most noble of people in lineage, and without boasting." (2)

Some people say: how is that, when the father of Ibrahim was not a Muslim? And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam." (3)

If someone says: how is this, when the father of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was a polytheist worshipper of idols? We say to him: Azar was not the father of Ibrahim but his uncle, and therefore the Qur'an said ﴿to his father Azar﴾; it brought the name intending a fatherhood that is not literal. The fatherhood of Ibrahim and the fatherhood of Ishaq were known to the sons of Ya'qub, but Isma'il was residing in Makkah far from them, so why did his name come between Ibrahim and Ishaq? We say: it came in chronological order, because Isma'il is older than Ishaq by fourteen years.

And that He described the three as "fathers" is a sign to us from Allah, exalted is He, that the word "father" is applied to the uncle.

Allah, blessed and exalted, wants us to take note of the meaning of the word Azar. He also wants to draw our attention to the fact that the multiplicity of messengers from Allah does not mean a multiplicity of gods. Therefore He, glorified is He, said: ﴿one God﴾.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 134:

﴿That was a community that has passed away. For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾

And His saying, exalted is He: "khalat" means "was alone" (infarada). One says "khala fulan bi-fulan," meaning he was alone with him, and "khala al-makan min nazīlihi," meaning the place became empty of its occupant, so that the place was alone and the occupant was alone, with no connection between one and the other. Allah, blessed and exalted, says:

﴿And when they are alone with their devils, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we are only mockers."﴾ (part of verse 14, surah al-Baqarah).

That is, they were alone, they and their devils, and there was no one left in the place besides them. We have already said that every event (hadath) must have an originator (muhdith), that no event exists by itself, and that every event needs a time and needs a place. So when the Truth, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿That was a community that has passed away﴾, its meaning is that its time has ended and it has become separated from your time. The intended meaning of His saying: ﴿That was a community that has passed away﴾ is that its time has come to an end.

"Tilka" (that) is a demonstrative for a feminine addressed noun, and "ummah" (community) is the thing indicated. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to the Muslims in general. When Allah, glorified is He, says: ﴿That community﴾, it is as if it were distinguished by the unity of its creed and the unity of its faith, until it became one thing. Therefore He must address it in the singular. Consider His saying:

﴿Indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.﴾ (surah al-Anbiya', 93).

Here "tilka" refers to the community of Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub. They are a large group who had one creed.

And His saying: ﴿For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned.﴾ That is: that group was upon one religion, and it will be held accountable for what it did, just as you will be held accountable for what you have done. But Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿Indeed, Ibrahim was an ummah﴾ (part of verse 120, surah al-Nahl).

Ibrahim was a single individual, not a group? We say: yes, Ibrahim was an individual, but there were gathered in him of the qualities of goodness and gifts of perfection what is gathered only in a community.

And His saying: "qad khalat" is intended to make the Jews understand that they should not attribute themselves to Ibrahim by a false lineage, because the lineage of the prophets is not a lineage of blood, race, or affiliation. Rather it is a lineage of method and following. It is as if the Truth were saying to the Jews: being descended from the line of Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub will not benefit you, because the lineage of prophethood is a lineage of faith, which involves following the method and the creed. This lineage will not intercede for you on the Day of Resurrection, because each one has his own deeds.

His saying: ﴿For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned.﴾ "Kasb" (earning) is used for good, and "iktisab" (acquiring) is used for evil, because evil involves effort (ifti'al).

We must pay attention and be mindful of the verses of the Noble Qur'an so that we can refute those who try to attack the Qur'an. There is no meaning in which one verse demolishes another verse; rather, there is only a failure of understanding.

Some orientalists come and say that there is a verse in the Qur'an confirming that Allah gives by lineages, namely His saying, majestic is His majesty:

﴿And those who believed and whose descendants followed them in faith, We will join their descendants with them, and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds.﴾ (part of verse 21, surah al-Tur).

The children are believers. His saying: ﴿We will join their descendants with them﴾: the word "alhaqna" (We join) is used when you join a deficient one to a complete one. So if both are believers, it is as if you raise the rank of the children in honor of their believing parents. We say that faith is one thing, and acting in accordance with the requirements of faith is another. The father and the descendants are believers, but the parents exerted themselves greatly in deeds, while the children perhaps fell short a little. But here there is a raising of rank for the believers; that is, the father and the descendants must both be believers. As for non-believers, they are excluded and have no connection with their parents; the bond between them has been severed by faith and disbelief. The parents have many good deeds, and the children have fewer good deeds. Allah causes the children to enter Paradise with their parents, because the faith is one.

His saying: ﴿and We will not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾ means: We will not diminish anything of their deeds for them. So the parents and the descendants are held to account by their faith, and Allah, by His grace, joins the children to the parents. His saying: ﴿For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned.﴾ This is the process of faith in creed. Some may say that Allah, blessed and exalted, says:

﴿Every person is held in pledge for what he has earned﴾ (part of verse 21, surah al-Tur).

And He, glorified is He, says:

﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ (verse 39, surah al-Najm).

So how do the children receive reward without striving? We say: understand the texts well. His saying: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ defines justice, but it does not define the bounty which Allah, glorified is He, gives to whomever He wills of His servants, and this gives without reckoning. Moreover, who said that this is not part of their striving? Joining the believing children to the high station of their parents is an honoring of the parents' deeds, not an increase in the children's deeds.

The scholars have related to us that there was a son who was a believer, obedient and devout, and his father was a sinner against himself. When the father died, his son grieved for him, but he saw that his father was sitting above his head, with one of the large-eyed companions (hur 'in) keeping him company. The son wondered how his father attained this reward when he had been a sinner against himself, so he asked: "How did you reach this rank?" The father said: "What rank?" The son said: "That one of the large-eyed companions is with you." The father said: "Did you understand that she is a bounty for me?" The son said: "Yes." The father said: "No, I am a punishment for her."

And Allah, glorified is He, says:

﴿Say: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy—in that let them rejoice; it is better than what they accumulate."﴾ (verse 58, surah Yunus).

So you, in the Hereafter, will rejoice in the grace and mercy of Allah more than you rejoice in your righteous deeds, in confirmation of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Be steadfast, aim for moderation, and rejoice, for none will enter Paradise by his deeds alone." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." (1)

Perhaps someone will come and ask: what is the legal purpose of the funeral prayer over the dead? If it benefits him, then the benefit is an addition to his deeds; and if it does not give him more than his deeds, then what is its benefit?

We say: since the Law has obligated us to it, it has a benefit. Do you think the funeral prayer is not part of his deeds? It is included in his deeds, because he was a believer, and his faith is what moved you to pray over him, and what you ask for him of goodness, mercy and forgiveness, which Allah accepts. Is it said that he took other than his deeds? No; you did not supplicate for him except after good had reached you from him. But you do not supplicate, for example, for a person who took your hand to a tavern, or to an immoral act, or to an evil. Rather you supplicate for one who gave you good; and if Allah answers you, then it is from his deeds.

Allah, glorified is He, says that what those who came before you of the nations used to do, you will not be asked about. And even if you claim that Ibrahim was a Jew or a Christian, then, behold, you will not be asked about what Ibrahim used to do; but you will be asked about yourselves. The question is about your deeds.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 135:

﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, [then] you will be guided." Say: "Nay, [we follow] the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith (ḥanīfan), and he was not of the polytheists."﴾

When it says "they said" (qālū), its meaning is that those who said it were a group. The ones who said it were the Jews and the Christians, but each of them said a different statement from the other. The Jews said "Be Jews," and the Christians said "Be Christians."

We have three elements: the Jews, the Christians, and the polytheists (al-mushrikūn). Facing all of these are the believers. "And they said, be" — who is the intended addressee? The believers? Or it may be that the meaning is: the Jews said to the believers, the polytheists and the Christians, "Be Jews," and the Christians said to the Jews, the polytheists and the believers, "Be Christians," because each of the two sees good only in itself. But Islam came and took from Judaism Moses and his authentic Torah, and took from Christianity Jesus and his authentic Gospel, and everything that Muhammad (ﷺ) brought.

That means that Islam took the unity of the covenant of faith (al-ṣafqa al-īmāniyya) concluded between God, glory be to Him, and every believer. That is why you find in the Noble Qur'an His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ (part of verse 285, Surat al-Baqara).

We note that the polytheists did not enter into the statement because they are not People of the Book (ahl al-kitāb). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, [we follow] the religion of Abraham, ḥanīfan﴾ — that is, a response to them, and the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): that I will be a follower of the religion of Abraham, which is the ḥanīfiyya. They cannot disagree about Abraham: the Jews regarded him as one of their prophets, and the Christians regarded him as one of their prophets, and they did not deny him prophethood, but each of them wanted to attribute him to himself.

What is the meaning of ḥanīfan? Verbal derivations must have a relation to the linguistic meaning. Al-ḥanf is an inclination in the feet, such that one foot leans toward the other. It is a curvature in the feet, so that the right foot inclines to the left or the left to the right; this is al-ḥanf. But how is a word that indicates crookedness used and made a symbol of the straight path?

We have said that the messengers come only when negligence overcomes the method of God, because as long as there are followers of the Messenger who call to His method and enjoin the good and forbid the evil, there is good.

The human soul has colours. There is the self-reproaching soul (al-nafs al-lawwāma), which commits evil once, and then from within the self comes what denounces that evil, and it returns to good. But there is the soul that commands to evil (al-nafs al-ammāra bi-l-sū'), which lives only in evil, commands it, and incites others to do it. When society becomes corrupt and souls become commanders of evil, the saying of the Truth, exalted is He, applies to them:

﴿They used not to forbid one another from any wrong they committed﴾ (part of verse 79, Surat al-Mā'ida).

Heaven intervenes with a messenger who treats the crookedness of society. But God, blessed and exalted, placed the element of goodness in the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Hour arrives.

He, exalted is He, said:

﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind: you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and you believe in God. And if the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them; among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾ (verse 110, Surat Āl ʿImrān).

Thus God, blessed and exalted, has entrusted the community of Muhammad with the method, and as long as there are among them those who enjoin the right and forbid the wrong, no messenger will come after Muhammad (ﷺ).

Returning to His saying, ḥanīfan: we said that al-ḥanf is crookedness, and we say that the deviation from the crooked is uprightness. The messengers come only after a complete crookedness in society, to turn people away from the existing crookedness so that they incline toward moderation (i'tidāl), because opposing crookedness is moderation.

His saying, ḥanīfan, reminds us of God's blessing upon all existence, because it corrects the negligence of mankind regarding the method of God and takes people from the existing crookedness to moderation. Guidance according to the Jews and Christians, and its concept, is the fulfilment of the desires of their souls, because a human guides a human. And God, glory be to Him, said:

﴿The Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾ (part of verse 120, Surat al-Baqara).

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) lived among the Jews in Medina, but they fought him and were not pleased with him. And Abraham (peace be upon him) was a true believer and was not a polytheist.

**Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 136:**

﴿Say: "We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses and Jesus, and in what was given to the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are submitting."﴾ (136)

This noble verse explains the Almighty's words: ﴿the religion (millah) of Abraham﴾. It is faith in God alone, with no partner. It is faith in what was sent down to us, which is the Qur'an, and in what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, and in what was given to Moses, which is the Torah, and in what was given to Jesus, which is the Gospel, and in what was given to the prophets in general. So the correct message from God since the time of Adam until now is the unity of creed (al-'aqidah, the belief system), that there is no god but God alone, with no partner, and the unity of the cosmos, that God is the Creator, the Governor, and that everything that departs from the divinity (al-uluhiyyah) of the One, the Unique, belongs to God. Whatever departs from this, and is a distortion (tahrif) of the earlier religions, is a fabrication against God, the Glorified, which we do not accept.

As for His words: ﴿We believe in God, and in what has been sent down to us﴾, this is the noble Qur'an. It is not possible for anything that conflicts with it to be attached to it. Therefore, what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes is this same religion of Abraham. This confirms for us that the religion of Abraham is a revelation from God to him. All the messages, as we have said, call to the worship of the One, the Unique, who has no partner.

As for His words: ﴿and to Him we are submitting﴾, this means that Abraham was a Muslim, and all the prophets were Muslims, and whatever contradicts that is the work of humans. The meaning of Islam (submission) is that there is one who submits and one to whom one submits, who is God, Mighty and Majestic. We submit to Him in servitude, Glorified is He, and in following His method. A person does not surrender his face except to one who is more capable than him, more knowledgeable than him, and stronger than him, and to one who has no desire of his own. If you doubt any of these elements, then your submission is not real but imaginary. You will not hand over your reins to God, Glorified and Exalted, unless you are certain that His capabilities are above the capabilities of all created beings, and that He is free of need from the worlds. Therefore He has no need of what is in your hand; rather He gives you of goodness and blessings, Majestic is His majesty, and there is no existence higher than Him to which you may turn your face in submission.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 137:

﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they are [rightly] guided. But if they turn away, they are only in dissension. So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ (2:137)

We say: the question that presents itself regarding this verse is: is there a "like" of what we believe in, such that they may believe in it? In order for you to believe, you must say: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." So if someone says it after you, has he said what you said, or the like of what you said? He has said the like of what you said. That is, when I declare my faith and take the testimony that you have taken, I have said its like, because what you uttered does not leave you alone. But if I do something and say to another, "Do the like of it," he will do something new and will not do exactly what I did.

The same applies when you say to me: "Give charity like what so-and-so gives." The charity will not be the very same money, but its like. We say to whoever repeats this statement: you have not understood the meaning. Their faith is that they say "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," and the faith of others is that they say a phrase like this, that is, that they declare their faith like ours in Allah and His Messenger. So the "like" here is tied to the testimony, and everyone who embraces Islam pronounces the two testimonies like those who preceded them in faith. The likeness, then, lies in the formula, and their faith is that they say what we said.

The Blessed and Exalted Lord says: ﴿So if they believe in the like of what you have believed, then they are [rightly] guided﴾, that is, they are guided to the truth. ﴿But if they turn away, they are only in dissension﴾. "Turn away" means they withdraw, and "shiqaq" means opposition with you and opposition among themselves; each of them holds a viewpoint he claims and a guidance he has invented. Even if they meet in disbelief, they will not meet in the causes of disbelief, since each one has adopted a cause, and therefore they differ. "Shiqaq" derives from "mashaqqah" (hardship), dispute, and quarrelling, and "shaqq" is the separation between two things.

As for His saying: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾, that is, do not turn your attention to their battles or to their disputes, for Allah suffices you by all means against whatever else He is. Read His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Is not Allah sufficient for His servant? Yet they threaten you with those other than Him. And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾ (39:36).

Allah, glorified and exalted, says to His Prophet ﷺ: if the Jews, the Christians and the hypocrites try to plot against you and harm you and the believers, then Allah, glorified and exalted, suffices you, for He is All-Hearing, All-Seeing, and nothing is hidden from Him. The Jews attempted to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ more than once, and they tried to harm him with sorcery; Allah nullified their scheme and exposed what was hidden of it and informed His Messenger of it. Whatever means they use, apparent or hidden, Allah will suffice you against their evil. Therefore He said: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. That is, He hears what is said and knows what they plot; indeed, He knows what is in their breasts before they utter it. So do not believe that anything escapes Allah, glorified is He, or eludes Him. Every movement before it happens is known to Him, and every plot before it is completed is defeated by Him. If Allah, glorified and exalted, is with you, then what do you fear? And of whom are you afraid? And who can reach you? You have with you the Creator of this universe and its Governor, from whom nothing is hidden in the heavens or on the earth, who knows everything that will happen until the Day of Resurrection and after the Day of Resurrection. As long as with you is the Mighty who never weakens, the Living who never dies, and the Knowing of everything, do not fear anyone, for you are under the protection of Allah, glorified is He.

The Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 138:

﴿The dye of Allah. And who is better than Allah in dye? And we are worshippers of Him.﴾ (2:138)

What is the ṣibgha (dye)? The ṣibgha is the introduction of a colour onto a thing so that it changes it to another colour. You dye the thing red, or blue, or any colour you choose. Dye penetrates the dyed object especially if the object has hair-like pores, such as cotton or wool. For this reason synthetic fibres cannot be dyed. Why? Because the hair of cotton or wool is, in its structure, like a tube.

If we bring a lamp of oil and place in it a wick of cotton, with the head of the wick in the oil, then light it from the top, we find that the oil flows through the tubes and ignites the wick. If we try this with synthetic fibres, the oil cannot flow through them; rather the fire consumes the fibres, because they have no capillary tubes like cotton and wool. For this reason you find synthetic fibres easy to wash, because sweat does not enter their pores, whereas cotton garments need great effort because their pores are saturated with sweat and dirt.

So the dye's substance must penetrate the pores of the cloth. As for paint (ṭilā'), it is different. It is an external layer that you can remove. For this reason, those who issue rulings about nail polish for women, and say it is like henna, we say to them: No. Henna is a dye that permeates the living matter and remains until the skin is shed with it; that is, you cannot remove it when you want. But nail polish you can remove at any time, even moments after applying it. So nail polish is not a dye.

His saying, glorified is He: "the dye of Allah." It is as if faith in Allah, the creed of Ibrahim, and what Allah sent down to His messengers is the divine dye that penetrates the human body. And why the word ṣibgha? So that we know that faith permeates your whole body. It is not a dye from outside your body, but a dye that Allah placed in the cells of the heart, present within it at the moment of creation. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

("Every child is born upon the fitra until his tongue speaks for him; then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian.")(1)

It is as if faith is a dye present by nature. It is the dye of Allah. If his parents are Muslims, he remains upon the fitra. If his parents are Jews or Christians, they make him Jewish or Christian, that is, they take him and place him in water, saying, "We have dyed him with the water of baptism." This is the meaning of the dye of Allah.

The Truth, glorified is He, wishes to show us this by making the difference of our colours one of the signs of His power. This difference in colour is from the dye of Allah. The difference of human colours is not paint but is in the very nature of creation. So this one is white, this one is dark, this one is yellow, this one is red; this is the dye of Allah. What they do of baptising the child does not give a dye, because faith and religion do not come from outside the human being but from within him. For this reason faith moves every organ of the human body. Read the saying of the Truth, glorified is He, the Exalted:

﴿Allah has sent down the best of speech, a Book consistent, paired (in its verses), at which shiver the skins of those who fear their Lord; then their skins and their hearts soften to the remembrance of Allah. That is the guidance of Allah; He guides thereby whom He wills, and whoever Allah sends astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ (39:23)

This is the effect that Allah places in hearts: an inner matter, not an external one. As for the faith of non-Muslims, it is an external paint and not a dye, because they have abandoned the dye of Allah. We say to them: No, this paint is from you yourselves, but our religion is the dye of Allah.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is better than Allah in dye?﴾ is a question they cannot deny, and the answer comes in accordance with what the questioner, glorified is He, intends: that there is none better than Allah in dye.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And we are worshippers of Him﴾ means: obedient to His commands. The worshipper is one who obeys the commands of Allah and avoids what He has forbidden.

Commands always come with something burdensome that asks you to do it, and prohibitions come concerning something beloved to your soul; there is hardship in leaving it. This is because man desires immediate benefit, superficial benefit, while Allah, glorified is He, directs us to true benefit. Immediate benefit gives you fleeting pleasure and deprives you of lasting bliss in the Hereafter and enjoyment of the bounties of Allah, glorified is He.

When you hear the muezzin and do not rise for prayer because it is heavy on your soul, you have given your soul a fleeting pleasure, such as occupying yourself with conversation with someone, or playing backgammon, or other things. You abandon that true benefit that leads you to Paradise. For this reason Allah, glorified is He, said:

﴿And indeed, it is difficult except for the humbly submissive, who expect that they will meet their Lord.﴾ (2:45–46)

So worship is command and prohibition: a command that is hard on your soul so you find it burdensome, and a prohibition concerning something beloved to your soul that gives you fleeting pleasure, so you want to do it.

Thus His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And we are worshippers of Him﴾ means: obedient to His commands, because we have believed in the Commander as God and Lord to be worshipped. When you believe, Allah makes the things you used to find burdensome beloved to you, and makes it easy for you to refrain from the things you love because they give you fleeting pleasure. This is the dye of Allah that gives us worship. Read His saying, blessed and exalted is He:

﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of Allah. If he obeyed you in much of the matter, you would be in distress. But Allah has endeared to you faith and has made it attractive in your hearts, and has made hateful to you disbelief, wickedness, and disobedience. Those are the rightly guided.﴾ (49:7)

Thus Allah, glorified is He, with the dye of faith, makes goodness beloved to us and makes us hate evil; not as hypocritical display outside the self like paint, but like a dye that permeates a thing and becomes one thing with it, the two never separating.

﴿Say: Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him.﴾ (2:139)

(1) Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan.

The determination of the command "Say" (qul) is an awakening to the task of responsibility (taklif) for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). God, glory be to Him, when He says to His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) "Say," it would have sufficed for Him to state what He desires. For when you tell your son, "Go to your brother and say to him, your father commands you to do such-and-such," the boy goes and says these words without saying the word "say" himself. But God's address to His Messenger (ﷺ) with the word "say" draws our attention to the fact that this command is not from him but from God, glory be to Him, and the Messenger's task is only to convey (al-balagh).

The repetition of the word "say" in the verses attributes the words spoken to the greatness of their first speaker, who is God, blessed and exalted. So the speech is not from the Messenger of God; its speaker is God, majestic in His majesty.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Say: Do you dispute with us concerning God, when He is our Lord and your Lord?﴾ The word muhajjah (disputation) means argument by proof: each of the two debaters brings the proof that supports his opinion or viewpoint. When you read His words, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered the one who disputed with Abraham concerning his Lord?﴾ (Qur'an 2:258), that is, each of them stated his proof. And there must be two opponents, each of whom holds his opinion against the other's opinion, and each tries to bring the proof that establishes the truth of his words, so his opponent answers him with a proof that demolishes this speech, and so on.

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿Do you dispute with us concerning God, when He is our Lord and your Lord?﴾ Since God is the Lord of all, it would be logical for us to meet, because He is my Lord and your Lord, and our share of Him is equal. But since proof has been established between us, one of us is upon falsehood. Read His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And those who dispute concerning God after He has been responded to, their argument is void with their Lord, and upon them is wrath, and for them is a severe punishment﴾ (Qur'an 42:16).

Disputation cannot take place between truth and truth; it takes place only between truth and falsehood, and between falsehood and falsehood, because there is one truth but there are a hundred paths to falsehood. So since disputation has taken place between us and you, and we are upon the truth, then you must be upon falsehood. And so that God, the Exalted, may settle this matter and prevent contention and quarrelling, He, glory be to Him, says: ﴿To us our deeds, and to you your deeds, and we are sincere to Him﴾. That is, we do not want a quarrel, because quarrelling will benefit nothing. We have our deeds and you have your deeds, and every deed will be recompensed to its doer according to the degree of his sincerity toward God. We have made our worship sincere to God alone, and you have directed your worship toward what your desires love.

God, the Exalted, who is our Lord and your Lord, does not prefer anyone over anyone except by righteous deeds sincere for the sake of God's face. Therefore we place sincerity first, and the deed may be one before people: this one takes thereby reward, and that one takes thereby sin and punishment. So what matters is that the deed be purely for God.

Someone may say that sincerity is in the deed, and the deed's place is the heart, and so as long as a person does not harm anyone and does not commit an evil, it is not necessary for him to pray, as long as his intention is sincere. We say that the matter is not intentions only, but deeds and intentions together. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Actions are only by intentions" (1).

So there must be a deed after the intention, because the intention benefits you alone, while the deed returns to people. If in your intention is to give charity and you give charity, the poor benefit from your wealth. But if in your intention there is no doing good, and you do it to gain a reputation or to please people, the poor benefit from your wealth and you will not benefit from the reward of this wealth. God, the Exalted, wants your deed to be joined with the intention of sincerity to God. The deed is movement in life, and the intention is what gives reward to its doer or withholds reward from him. Therefore God, majestic in majesty, says:

﴿If you disclose your charities, they are excellent; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds, and God is Aware of what you do﴾ (Qur'an 2:271).

God, the Exalted, wants us to give charity, and the poor man will benefit from the charity whether your intention is that you be called the benefactor who gives charity, or that you be called a man of righteousness and piety, or that you conceal your charity. The deed takes effect and people benefit from it, whether you intended it or did not.

If you decide to build a building, the intention here is ownership. But thousands of people benefit from this work, beginning with the one who sold you the piece of land, and the one who prepared the engineering drawing for you, and the excavation workers, and the one who laid the foundation, and the one who did the construction, and others and others. These have benefited from your work with a livelihood for them, whether God was in your mind or was not in your mind; they have benefited.

Thus every deed in which there is benefit for people, whether you intended it or not. But God does not reward deeds in their bare form; He rewards intentions by their sincerity. If your deed was sincere for God, God rewards you for it. But if your deed was for another aim, there is no reward for you with God, because He, glory be to Him, is the most self-sufficient of partners from partnership.

As for those who wonder that a disbelieving person presented an important discovery to humanity but was not a believer in God, and wonder: will he be punished in the Fire? We say yes, because he worked while God was not in his heart. Therefore he is recompensed in this worldly life: statues are erected for him, his name is given to squares, and his name is immortalized in the world for which he worked. But since God was not in his intention, there is no reward for him with God.

1 Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Daraqutni, with various wordings.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 140:
