Glory be to Him and exalted, He made for this instinct a fervour, because the life that will come through it has the consequences of children and hardships. Had Allah not connected it with this pleasure, many people would have turned away from it, but He, glory be to Him, connects it with pleasure so that the extension of life occurs with a violent and strong impulse from the human.

Therefore the Truth, glory be to Him, does not surprise the human with an obligation except after preparing him with complete preparation, because if He obligated him before he matured instinctively, before he had the capacity to preserve the species, the human would say: "Allah obligated me before this was in me." Then the covenant of faith would not be valid.

Therefore the Truth delays His obligation on His servants until the maturity of intellect and the maturity of instinct are both complete for them, and until the human enters into the obligation with all its constituents, and all its instincts and emotions; so that when he enters a covenant of faith, he must keep to his covenant.

Thus the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, wants to cultivate in the human his selfhood from the moment he becomes fit to preserve the species in another. And as long as he has come to possess a complete selfhood, the Truth wants to forbid him from submission to others. At that point, let no one say: "I will do as my father did." But there are those who said: "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon." Why do they follow their fathers in the false method, and not follow them in the rest of worldly matters, in clothing, in food, and in all aspects of life?

So nothing has made them follow what they found their fathers upon except that they found in it what agrees with their desire, as evidenced by the fact that they have broken away from following their fathers in things they saw in the conduct of the fathers and differed from them in; and as long as they have differed from them in many things, why do they follow them in the false religion?

Allah wants to free the human from the bondage of this following, and He alerts the servants: "Use your intellect, O you who have come to possess a selfhood, and let each of you know that with the maturity of intellect he must arrive at guidance to the one, unique Creator. If you were attached to your father at the outset because he sustains and supports you, this father is merely a cause that Allah willed for you, but Allah is your Creator, and He is the one who sent down the method to which you must attach yourself so that your life becomes growth and good." And He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿And fear a day when no parent will avail his child, nor will a child avail his parent at all﴾ (part of verse 33 of Surah Luqman).

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, explains this matter to us precisely. If the fathers do not understand, then what of the position of the sons? The sons must reform themselves by the method of the Truth. Another verse with the same meaning has come in Surah al-Ma'idah, but with a difference in wording. Here in Surah al-Baqarah the Truth says: "And when it is said to them, 'Follow what Allah has sent down.'" And in the verse of Surah al-Ma'idah the Truth says:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 104).

Between the two verses there is agreement and difference. His saying here, "Follow what Allah has sent down," means that we should reflect deeply and apply the method of Allah. The verse of Surah al-Ma'idah, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," is the first difference.

The second difference between the two verses lies in their answer to the words of the Truth. In this surah, Surah al-Baqarah, they said: "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon," and this statement contains a reproach to them. But in Surah al-Ma'idah they said: "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon," and this means they were content with what they had, and denied following the method of heaven. This position is stronger and more emphatic in negation. Therefore we find that the Truth did not address them in that verse with "Follow," but said to them "Come," meaning: rise from the lowland of what you have to faith in the method of heaven. And since you have...

The Almighty says next:

﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is that of one who shouts to what hears nothing but a call and a cry: deaf, dumb and blind, so they do not understand.﴾ (2:171)

The one who *yan'iq* (ينعق, "shouts to") is the one who makes a sound and calls out loudly to livestock, and he is the shepherd. So the word *yan'iq* gives us the picture of a shepherd tending animals. This shouting from the shepherd is meant to attract the herd so that they follow him. He does not tell them what he wants them to do. Instead, he signals to them with his voice what he wants, and he walks ahead of them so that they follow him to the pasture or to the water source. The call is only an attention-getter and an invitation, but what is wanted from the call becomes a physical movement that the animals see. It is as if the herd understands from the shepherd only the call and the cry. Yet they call and cry for what purpose? The animals do not know the goal of it, except that the shepherd walks ahead of them and guides them. Thus we understand that there is a (shepherd), (livestock), and (a voice from the shepherd), which is merely a call and a cry.

In our matter, the counterpart of these three is the Messenger when he calls. He is the (shepherd), and whom does he call? He calls the (flock), who are the people. And with what does he call the flock? Does he call them only so that they come to him, or does he call them so that they come to him and command them to do things? He commands them to follow the method of heaven.

This is the difference between the shepherd of livestock and the shepherd of human beings.

When the Messenger comes and says: (O my people, I am a messenger to you, and a warner to you), this is the call, and the content of that call is (worship God). (Look into the heavens and the earth), (do such-and-such of the commands, and refrain from those prohibitions). This is what the Messenger wants.

So the Messenger shares with the shepherd the calling and the summoning, and they share with the herd in that they understood only the call and the summons. In responding, they are (deaf, dumb, blind). They did not hear what was called to, so it is as if they share with the animal that they listen only to the call and the summons, but the thing called to, the content of the summons, they do not comprehend or understand. And they are dumb, not uttering what the call requires, which is (the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God). They have no intellect directing the movement of the eyes to look at the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that the face of truth in this matter might become clear to them.

So the likeness of those who disbelieved in the Messenger is the likeness of the livestock with the shepherd: they hear only mere calling, just as the animals hear the shepherd and do not understand, with a difference, because animals are not required to respond to those who call them, and they do not hear anything else of what is called to. Therefore the disbelievers are worse than beasts.

The Almighty's words (*summ*, صم) mean afflicted with deafness, which is a defect that prevents the ear from performing its function. (*Bukm*, بكم) means afflicted with a defect that strikes the tongue, preventing it from performing its function. However, the cause of deafness is a positive cause, because something has blocked the opening of hearing so that one does not hear. Because of deafness, they are dumb, and dumbness is the inability of the tongue to speak, because if a person does not hear, he will not speak. That is why, if a person finds himself in an Arabic-speaking environment, he speaks Arabic, and if a person grows up in an English environment, he speaks English. Suppose you grew up in an environment that speaks Arabic, and then you did not hear one word of its words; would you speak them? No. So the tongue speaks what the ear hears; if the ear does not hear, the tongue does not speak. Deafness precedes dumbness, so dumbness is a negative defect, and you find the tongue moving and making sounds with no meaning or understanding. Do we then understand from His saying about them, (deaf), that they are afflicted with deafness? No. The Almighty is saying: We made the ear to hear useful hearing; so it is as if it is idle and hears nothing. Likewise, we created the tongue to speak useful speech, so whoever does not speak with it is as if he were mute, and we created the intellect to think with; if he does not think soundly and logically, it is as if its owner has no intellect. So the deaf person, in truth, is better than one who possesses the sense of hearing but does not understand by it, because the deaf person has his excuse, and the mute person likewise, and the insane person also has his excuse. Would that these disbelievers had been like that! They have stopped their ears from hearing the call, and they are dumb in uttering what would save them, the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and they are blind to looking at the signs of the universe. Had they had sight, they would have looked at the universe as God the Exalted said:

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, are signs for people of understanding.﴾ (3:190)

Had they looked into the creation of the heavens and the earth, they would have been guided by their innate nature to the conclusion that this perfect, well-ordered existence has a maker who made it. But they do not reason, because the process of reason begins after one hears, and after the senses are complete. That is why the human being, in his first formation, is kinetic and sensory: he sees, hears, and tastes, and then rational propositions form in him afterward.

Then the Truth (Allah) says, after that:

﴿O you who have believed, eat from the good things We have provided for you and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship.﴾ [2:172]

This is an address from Allah to those who have believed, that they should eat of the good things. A similar address on the same subject was already given in verse 168, but to all of mankind: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿O mankind, eat from whatever is on earth [that is] lawful and good﴾. We said that when the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, addresses all people, He draws their attention to the matter of faith; but when He addresses the believers, He gives them the rulings of faith. Allah does not impose a ruling except on one who has believed in Him; as for one who has not believed in Him, He does not impose on him any ruling, because faith is a commitment. And since you have committed yourself to Him being a wise God, then take from Him the rulings of your religion.

Allah's justice requires that He imposes obligations only on those who believe, and this is contrary to what is customary among humans, because the obligations that human leaders impose on people apply both to those who accept their leadership and to those who do not. If a human leader has power, he uses it to compel those under his authority to carry out what he says.

Allah's address to the believers here came with His saying: ﴿eat from the good things We have provided for you﴾, because the believer is fully certain that Allah is the Creator and that it is He who provides sustenance. He concludes the noble verse with His saying: ﴿and be grateful to Allah, if it is Him that you worship﴾, for the believing servant's gratitude to the Creator Lord is obligatory, as long as the believing servant devotes worship exclusively to Allah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 173:

Almighty Allah says:

﴿Forbidden to you are only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked. But whoever is compelled [to it], neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [2:173]

We find that the word (al-mawt, death) occurs in various forms: there is (mayyit), (maytah), and (mayyitah). An example of this is what the Truth says:

﴿And We drive it to a dead land﴾ (part of verse 9, surah Fatir).

The (mayyit), with the yā' doubled, is one whose affair is destined for death even if he is alive. Thus each of us may be told, "You are mayyit," meaning his destiny is death. For this reason Allah addresses His Messenger:

﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed, they will die﴾ [39:30] (surah al-Zumar).

So the word (mayyit) means that you will die, although you are now alive. But when we say (mayt), with the yā' unvocalised, it means he has actually died. In Arabic poetry it has come:

"And the mayt is none but one who is carried to the grave."

The Truth, glorified and exalted, says: (Forbidden to you are carrion and blood). Had He said (mayyitah) with the doubled yā', we would have said that everything that will die becomes forbidden. But the speech of Allah here is (maytah) with the unvocalised yā', which is the one that is dead in fact: the one whose soul has departed by natural death. For slaughter is the departure of the soul by cutting, meaning you cut it and it dies. But there are creatures that die a natural death (ḥatf anfihā), and when animals die a natural death, the essence of the foods they have consumed remains retained within them, and it is present in the blood. This blood contains many harmful things. In the blood there are harmful, corrupt substances that the body's organs have extracted while it was alive, and which were on their way out of it. When we slaughter it, all the blood flows out, the corrupt and the sound alike. And because the warding off of harm takes precedence over the securing of benefit, we sacrifice the sound blood along with the corrupt blood. This blood is retained by the body when it dies, and the harmful things remain within it, so the flesh becomes filled with harmful substances that afflict a person with diseases. A simple look at two chickens, one slaughtered whose blood was shed, and the other strangled, so its blood was not shed, will show a clear difference in colour. Even if we cook this one and that one, we will find a difference in taste: the taste of the slaughtered chicken will be acceptable, and the taste of the dead chicken will be unacceptable. Those who do not believe in a god or in a method have been slaughtering animals before eating them. Why? Their experiences have guided them to the conclusion that this process has a benefit, even though they did not know the Islamic method of slaughter.

When Allah forbids (carrion), none of us is obliged to answer the question of why Allah forbade carrion, because it is sufficient for us that Allah said it is forbidden. And if the One who provided for you told you, "Do not eat this," He has removed it from the category of direct utilitarian provision, and even if there were no harm that we knew of, He, glorified is He, has said: do not eat it. So do not eat it, because He is the One who provides, the One who created you, and the One who commands you not to eat it. It is not your right after that to ask: why did He forbid it to me?

Suppose we had not been guided to the wisdom of the prohibition, and had not known the harm that befalls a person from eating carrion. Would people have stopped at the command until its cause became apparent, or would they have carried out Allah's commands without thinking? The believers listened to the commands of the Truth and carried them out without hesitation.

Therefore, since Allah addresses us, by virtue of the basis of faith it is necessary that we accept the ruling from Him, and the reason for accepting the ruling is that it issues from the One who rules. As for knowing the reason for the ruling, that is a process of reassuring the intellect and of assurance that Allah has not charged us with a command except that there is benefit for us in it. The believer should not make his faith dependent on knowing the reason.

The Truth says: (Forbidden to you is carrion). The verse is explicit that every carcass is forbidden. And since it is carrion, there was life and spirit in it, then it departed. Yet we eat fish, which is dead, and this is a specification by the Sunnah of the generality of the Qur'an. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Two carcasses have been made lawful for you: fish and locusts; and two bloods: the liver and the spleen."(1)

Why this exception in permission? Because custom (ʿurf) has a role in determining the terms of the Lawgiver. If you swear that you will not eat meat and then eat fish, do you break your oath? You do not break it, and your oath is truthful, even though Allah described fish as fresh meat (laḥm ṭarī), because when custom uses the word "meat," fish is not included in it.

Thus custom has standing. Therefore al-Zamakhshari, author of al-Kashshaf, says on this matter: "If you swear not to eat meat and you eat fish, there is scholarly consensus that you have not broken your oath." He gave another example, saying: if you swear that you will ride a beast (dābbah), and Allah has called the disbeliever a beast when He said: (Indeed, the worst of beasts in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve), is it permissible to ride a disbeliever? It is not permissible. The implication of the verse would be that it is valid for you to ride him. He commented on this, saying: it is true that the dābbah is everything that crawls on the earth, but custom has restricted it to four-legged creatures.

For this reason custom has a role in matters of permitting and forbidding. If someone says: Allah has forbidden carrion, and fish and locusts are carrion, so why do we eat them? We answer him: custom has established that fish and locusts are not meat, as shown by their saying, "When locusts are plentiful, meat becomes cheap," which means that locusts are not meat.

As for fish, it was not like the carrion that Allah forbade, because the forbidden carrion is everything that is slaughtered and whose blood flows, while fish has no flowing soul, that is, no blood. Locusts too have no blood. So the permission to eat them even when dead is due to the absence of a flowing soul, which would result in the transfer of what is harmful from within to the human being. Likewise the liver and the spleen are not blood, for blood has flow, whereas the liver and spleen are solid, congealed flesh, the essence of blood from which the organs of the liver and spleen were formed.

So the Sunnah has an explanatory role in permitting and forbidding. And the Truth's saying: "Forbidden to you are carrion and blood" means that He, glorified is He, forbade them because of the retention of the blood within the carrion and its not flowing out. And by a fortiori reasoning, the prohibition of blood is a binding matter. Allah forbade (the flesh of swine), and we have said that the cause of accepting the ruling is that Allah commanded it. If time establishes the truth of the faith-based proposition concerning the permission, that is a matter that confirms the process of faith. But if we waited and postponed the implementation of Allah's ruling until we were certain of the cause of the prohibition, we would be believing in scholars and scientific discoveries before believing in Allah. For if we wait until the scholars say their word, we have regarded the scholars as more trustworthy for us than Allah. And is there any creature trustworthy over a creature in the face of the Creator? That is impossible. Therefore the believer is the one who takes every ruling issued by Allah, certain that Allah commands him only with something beneficial for him. In reality, the harmful thing is not harmful in its essence; it may benefit in other respects. We give this example, and to Allah belongs the highest example: when you punish your son for some matter, depriving him of his allowance or of a delicious meal, that punishment is not harmful in itself. Rather, indulging him with what he loves and desires, while he walks on a path you do not approve, is an invitation for the son to continue doing what you do not approve. Failing to raise the son with reward and punishment is a harmful thing.

Therefore we say to those who want to find a cause for every prohibition: you have not perceived the prohibition for the sake of discipline. There is a prohibition of a thing because it is harmful, and there is another prohibition of a thing because you want to forbid it as discipline for him. You should not make the process of discipline in values subordinate to the process of reform in bodily matter. The Truth, glorified and exalted, is more merciful to His creatures than a father to his son, and He forbade some of the good things of life to the Children of Israel as discipline, saying, may He be exalted:

﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We made unlawful for them good things that had been lawful for them﴾ [4:160].

So the Truth forbade them good things as discipline for them because of their wronging themselves. Therefore, whenever you see a prohibition, do not look only at the prohibition of a harmful thing, but also consider that there is a prohibition for the sake of discipline, because permitting some good things to these people while they oppose the method is an enticement for them to keep opposing and wronging themselves.

So the Truth has prohibited what harms a person in his body, and has also prohibited some good things to some who oppose Him as discipline for them. As for the prohibition of swine, the will of Allah, mighty and majestic, decreed that He reveal to His creatures the secret of the prohibition, and the scholars established that there are diseases in swine that were not known before, and their danger became clear to them, such as the tapeworm. If the Truth, glorified and exalted, revealed to them one secret, which is the tapeworm, then perhaps there are other secrets more dangerous than the tapeworm.

The Truth also forbids (that over which other than Allah has been invoked). Ihlāl is the raising of the voice, and for this reason it is said: "hallala," meaning he raised his voice with "there is no god but Allah." The crescent is called hilāl because when we see it we cry out "Allahu akbar, my Lord and your Lord is Allah." And when the child is about to be born and comes out of its mother's belly, it becomes aware of its life and of its own existence after having been joined to its mother's being, so it cries. It begins its life with crying, and for this reason those who await a child's birth are reassured when they hear its cry.

For this reason the poet says:

"When the world announces to him of its vicissitudes,
the crying of the infant at the moment of birth is its cry."

It is as if the newborn turns toward something full of distress, and does not notice the vastness of the world and the abundance of its life. Otherwise, what would make it cry, when the world is wider and more abundant than what it was in? So the newborn's cry is the cry of transition from the mother's womb to facing life.

The child's life in its mother's belly was calm, and its nourishment came through the umbilical cord. But at the moment it separates from its mother, its connection to the nourishment-preparing apparatus in the mother's womb is severed, and it loses the supply of nourishment at the moment it leaves its mother's belly, and the supply of suckling has not yet reached it. For suckling is from the supply of this world, and the child does not take it except after taking the least proportion of air to set the lungs working. For this reason physicians are careful to deliver the newborn head first, because if it came out feet first with its head still inside, its breaths would be confined within its mother's belly and it would nearly die. For this reason they now examine the mother to know the position of the fetus, and the physician performs a caesarean operation out of concern for the newborn's life. The first thing the physician does after the child's birth is to clear the passages of air to its nose, and after that he treats the remaining organs.

It is the cry of instinct, just as when its mother forgets it and the time of its feeding has come, it cries. Thus we know that ihlāl is the raising of the voice, and the Truth's saying, "that over which other than Allah has been invoked," means the raising of the voice at the moment of slaughter. Slaughter is of two kinds: slaughter for your benefit, so that you eat and others eat, and slaughter as an offering to Allah. What is invoked for Allah is a sacrifice offered to Allah, whereas "that over which other than Allah has been invoked" is slaughter for the benefit of the human being alone, and in drawing near to their idols and images and what they worship besides Allah.

Since Allah is the One who gave the animals and subjected them to us so that we may eat them, we must mention the Benefactor, and drawing near to Allah alone must be the primary intention. For this reason believers draw near (to Allah) and eat, whereas unbelievers eat without drawing near to Allah; they slaughter and draw near to their gods.

When the Truth, glorified and exalted, legislates, His legislation takes all possibilities into account, unlike human legislators, whom the events of life after legislation compel to change what they have legislated, because cases arise after applying the legislation that were not in their minds when they legislated, owing to the insufficiency of their knowledge of what happens in the universe of matters that compel them and drive them to amend the law. So amending any human law means the occurrence of cases for which the law has no provision at the time of application; legislators therefore resort to amending the law, to include what can accommodate these cases.

But the Truth, glorified and exalted, when He legislates... He codifies in a way that carries within it everything that may newly arise of cases without need for amendment, and

1 This hadith was narrated by al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, from Ibn 'Umar, both as a marfu' and a mawquf report.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 174:

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book and sell it for a small price—they consume nothing in their bellies but the Fire. Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ (174)

Indeed, Allah, glorified and exalted, sends down through His messengers to His creation a method (manhaj) that governs the movement of people's lives, both for them and upon them. He legislates for the people, meaning for their interests, and He legislates against the people if they forfeit those interests, because whoever forfeits another's interest must expect that another will forfeit an interest of his own.

Therefore, it is part of justice in legislation that you make it both for him and against him. Every obligation upon him is matched by an obligation owed to him, for if he has a right, his right is an obligation upon others; and as his right is an obligation upon others, it follows that the right of others is an obligation upon him. Otherwise, from where would the rights-holder obtain his right?

When Allah, the Exalted, sends down the method, the messengers convey it and the people of knowledge (ulu al-'ilm) bear it, so that they may convey it to the people. Those who conceal what Allah has sent down are therefore opposing the method of heaven. Opposing the method of heaven is not possible except from a person who wishes to benefit from the falsehood of worldly life in order to consume the rights of people. When they conceal what Allah has sent down, they have become obstacles to the method of Allah, which came to govern the movement of life.

And what benefit do they gain from this? There must be a benefit for them. This benefit is the small price, such as bribery (al-rishā), or the things they used to take from their followers so that they would bend the rulings of Allah to the desires of people.

Allah explains to them: a thing is not valued except by the valuation of one who knows its reality, and you are valuing the method of Allah, yet the method of Allah may be valued only by Allah. Therefore the price that Allah has set for applying the method must be a profitable and satisfying price for you. If you take a price for concealing the method of Allah and please the people with legislation that agrees with their whims and desires, then you have lost in the transaction, for that price, however high it rises by human measure, is a small price and its lifespan is short.

Prices customarily begin with the first thing on which human life depends, which is the sustenance of its existence: food and drink. Therefore Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿they consume nothing in their bellies but the Fire﴾. And if they consume Fire in their bellies, how can the Fire accommodate all those bellies?

Because the believer, as the Messenger said, eats in one intestine, while the disbeliever eats in seven intestines; that is, the disbeliever eats only for the pleasure of food, for he wants to enjoy it constantly until his belly is strained by what enters it. But the believer takes from food according to what sustains life. The master of creation, Muhammad son of 'Abdullah (ﷺ), says in the noble hadith:

(It suffices the son of Adam a few morsels that keep his back upright.)¹

Thus, for the believer, eating is for the sustaining of life and as fuel for movement, whereas the disbeliever takes food as though it were a self-indulgent pleasure. Allah says: ﴿they consume nothing in their bellies but the Fire﴾, meaning that whenever they desire to fill their bellies out of lust and pleasure, Allah makes the punishment for them of the same kind as what they did with the small price they took. They took in order to fill their bellies with the foul of what they took, and Allah will fill their bellies with Fire, as a fitting recompense for what they did. This is one form of material punishment, followed by another form: ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾, meaning that the Truth turns away from them on a day when creatures have no intimacy except through the face of the Truth.

When we read the expression "so-and-so does not speak to so-and-so," we sense anger in it, because speech among humans is the means of intimacy; if a person refuses to speak to another, it is as though he hates and detests him. Thus ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾ means that He detests them, and sufficient for you is Allah's turning away from His creation as punishment and torment. He had befriended them with blessings, and afterward He turns away from them. Someone may say: how do we read here that the Truth will not speak to them, when He, glorified be He, says:

﴿They will say, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a misguided people. Our Lord, bring us out of it; then if we return, we will be wrongdoers." He will say, "Remain in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun)

We say: it is true that He, glorified be He, says to them: "Do not speak to Me," but when speech is negated from Allah, what is meant is the speech of tenderness, mercy, friendliness and gentleness; as for the speech of punishment, it is cursing. Thus ﴿Allah will not speak to them﴾ means the Truth does not speak to them in a manner that connects them to intimacy. Therefore, when Allah bestows intimacy upon some of His creatures, He prolongs speech with them. An example of this is when Musa came to the appointed time with his Lord, and what did Allah say to him?

He, Mighty and Majestic, said:

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha)

Does this question mean that Allah is asking Musa about what is in his hand? It is a question of intimacy in speech, so that Musa might be relieved of the whirlpool of awe. We may give an example, and to Allah belongs the highest likeness: when a person goes to his friend's house to visit, and the friend's small child comes with a toy, the guest says to the child: "What do you have there?" The guest sees the toy in the child's hand, but his speech with the child is for the sake of friendliness. When the speech of Allah came to Musa with intimacy, He said:

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha)

It would have sufficed Musa to say, "A staff," and his answer to the question would have ended. Had Musa said only, "A staff," that would have been from him a failure to grasp the measure of Allah's intimacy with him in speech. But our master Musa, peace be upon him, seized the question of Allah to prolong intimacy with Allah, and said:

﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean on it, and I beat down leaves with it for my flock, and I have in it other uses."﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha)

Consider the lengthening in Musa's answer. The word "it is" (hiya) is superfluous; "I lean on it" is superfluous, that is, not needed to convey the meaning; "I beat down leaves with it for my flock" is a further lengthening; and "I have in it other uses" is his desire to prolong the conversation even more.

Thus the speech of Allah and gazing upon Him, glorified be He, are the greatest blessings that Allah bestows upon the believers on the Day of Resurrection.

So if Allah withholds from the disbelievers the means of material honor, so that He does not speak to them, this is a grave matter: ﴿Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾. After depriving them of speech and of companionship in His presence, and not purifying them from the abominations they committed, and not making them worthy of His nearness, He then punishes them with severe punishment, as though there were a prior punishment; then comes the greater punishment, because they must encounter a doubled punishment, since they concealed the method of Allah from the creatures of Allah and so caused the misguidance of people. Upon them is the burden of their own misguidance and burdens upon burdens, because they misled others.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed us of the matter of Allah's speaking to people when he said: (Three whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, nor look at them, and for them is a painful punishment: an old fornicator, a lying king, and a poor arrogant man.)²

What is the secret of depriving these of Allah's speech, His purification, and His looking upon them? The old fornicator commits sin without necessity, since he does not suffer the agitation of youth. The king who lies lies to a people who are his subjects, and lying stems from fear of the Truth; for whom does a king fear when the people are under his rule? As for the head of a household who becomes arrogant while poor, this arrogance will bring him much hardship and narrow his paths to ease and to livelihood, placing him in misery through want; if someone wishes to help him, arrogance and haughtiness toward people will stand as a barrier between him and that help. This is the meaning of ﴿He will not speak to them nor purify them﴾. As for ﴿nor look at them﴾: a look is the snare of tenderness, and therefore the Truth cuts off from them at the root the door of mercy and compassion, which is looking upon them. The Truth concludes the noble verse with His words ﴿and for them is a painful punishment﴾, meaning painful; when you hear the form "fa'il," we take it in the sense of the active or passive participle, so we understand "alim" as "painful."

¹ This hadith was narrated by al-Mundhiri in al-Targhib wa'l-Tarhib, al-Zabidi in Ithaf al-Sada al-Muttaqin, al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, and al-Kahhal in al-Ahkam al-Nabawiyya fi'l-Sina'a al-Tibbiyya.
² Narrated by Imam Muslim in his Sahih, from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him.

Then the Almighty says:

﴿Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. So how patient they are toward the Fire!﴾ (2:175)

God tells us the reason for the judgment against them, why He does not speak to them, why He does not purify them, and why they will have a painful punishment in the Hereafter. They have exchanged misguidance for guidance, and punishment for forgiveness. When you see the monstrousness of the punishment, do not be overawed by it, but look at the monstrousness of the crime. When people separate the crime from the punishment, they feel sympathy for the criminal, because they see the criminal only in his state of punishment and trial, and they forget his crime. Therefore, when you see a punishment and find it appalling, you must bring to mind the crime that required that punishment.

This is why we often find people sympathizing with all the criminals who are put on trial and given harsh sentences, because the crime happened a long time ago, we did not see it, and its effects and consequences have ended. Only the criminal remains, so people sympathize with him. For this reason, it is a mistake for trial proceedings to be prolonged. Rather, the criminal must be tried immediately after the crime is committed, while it is still fresh, so that the public does not sympathize with him, because turning the public's heart toward him makes the punishment harsh.

﴿Those who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance﴾. We know that the particle "ba'" (the preposition ba') enters on what is given up. So misguidance here was taken, and guidance was abandoned; they exchanged punishment for forgiveness. Since they took misguidance in place of guidance, and punishment in place of forgiveness, justice requires that they receive the painful punishment. Then the Almighty says: ﴿So how patient they are with the people﴾. This is a condemnation of the punishment, so that people will be repelled by it. God wants us to marvel: how is it permissible for the one who is astray to abandon guidance and take misguidance, and then the result is that he receives punishment and abandons forgiveness? What gives him the hope of being patient in the Fire? Does he have patience to such a degree that he willingly commits the sin that drives him into the Fire? And what made him able to endure this punishment? Does he have a strength that enables him to bear the Fire? And what is this strength?

It is as if the Almighty is saying: you are not aware of what awaits you of recompense, for otherwise what would make you endure this Fire? You persist in your rebellion and your misguidance, and you forget that the Fire will be your portion. If you are certain that the Fire will be your portion, then how did you take assurance in your patience toward the Fire? The Fire is a thing that no human being could ever bear patiently.

That is, after that, the Truth says:

﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth. And indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension.﴾

"That" refers to what has preceded, and what has preceded is the misguidance they took in place of guidance, and the punishment they took in place of forgiveness, and the Fire in which they are tormented, and they have endured it. These are three things that converge: the punishment, the misguidance, and the Fire.

Misguidance is the original cause of the punishment. So if Allah says, "I punished them with such-and-such because they went astray," that is correct; and if He says, "I did that to them because they deserved the punishment," that is also true. Punishment, as a general ruling, takes the form of the Fire. Therefore, when the Truth says "by the Fire," "by the punishment," or "by the misguidance," their reference is all one, and it is referred to as "That." ("That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth.") Whoever alters the Book and conceals it is only rejecting the truth. ("And indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme dissension.") It is a wide abyss into which they fall. Dissension over the divine methodological values is a great chasm. If the disagreement were over material matters, humans could bear it among themselves, and it would be an easy matter. But disagreement over a matter of values cannot be resolved by humans among themselves; hence the breach of disagreement is wide, and none can close it except Allah. That is why He, glorified is He, said:

﴿Indeed, Allah will judge between them concerning that wherein they differ﴾ (Qur'an 39:3).

[Qur'an 2:177 in full:] ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but righteousness is [in] one who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture, and the prophets, and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing slaves; and establishes prayer and gives zakah; and the fulfillers of their promise when they promise; and the patient in poverty, hardship, and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and those are the righteous.﴾ (177)

When the command came from the Truth, glorified and exalted, to change the qiblah (direction of prayer) to the Ka'bah, and the Muslims turned in their prayers toward it, after they had been praying facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), confusion arose at that moment, and every community of a religion (millah) came to have a specific qiblah of its own. The Muslims face the Ka'bah, the Jews face Bayt al-Maqdis, and the Christians face the east. This verse affirms that the dispute is not over the matter of the direction of prayer. Before the change of qiblah, everyone who prayed was facing a direction, and changing the direction involves no hardship.

God, glorified and exalted, says to them: Do not make the matter of turning toward the Ka'bah the whole of righteousness, because this matter involves no hardship. There is no hardship in the Muslims turning toward the Ka'bah after they had been facing Bayt al-Maqdis. Rather, the matter is submission to the command of the One who commands. Righteousness, therefore, is not in easy matters that involve no hardship, but in abundant and great goodness. It includes faith, it includes piety, it includes truthfulness, it includes obedience, it includes excellence, and all aspects of goodness enter into the word "righteousness" (al-birr). Righteousness means something great and vast, and since its meaning is so broad, every aspect of it requires hardship.

Look at what righteousness demands and what it entails, which require hardship from you, and do not argue over the easy and simple matter in which there is no slightest fatigue, such as the matter of changing the direction of the qiblah. If you think that this is righteousness, we tell you: No. Righteousness has responsibilities that differ. The essence of righteousness is that the truthfulness of faith is tested, and that one prefers what God requires over comfort. It requires the believer to commit himself to obedience even if it is hard for him, and it requires that the Muslim refrain from sins, and know that sins have a swift pleasure but their punishment is great. All of that is among the requirements of righteousness and faith. So do not make the matter of turning toward the Ka'bah, or toward Bayt al-Maqdis, or toward the east, the problem, because your faces will turn toward some direction even if you were not commanded. Righteousness, as we know, is the vast goodness that encompasses every aspect of beauty in the universe. The Truth says: (But righteousness is [in] one who believes).

Why did God make the discussion of righteousness a discussion about an embodied being, although righteousness is a meaning? The Truth embodies the meaning, which is righteousness, in the person of the servant who believes, because when He, glorified, wants to affirm a meaning, He makes the essence embodied in it. For example, and to God belongs the highest likeness, when we say: "So-and-so is just" (ʿadil), we describe him in a way that conveys to the listener that he is a man who knows justice. But when we say: "So-and-so is justice" (ʿadl), it is as if he is justice itself. Likewise, when we say: "So-and-so is truthful" (sadiq), it means that he is a person whose essence is characterized by truthfulness, and it is possible for the essence to someday separate from truthfulness. But when we say: "So-and-so is truth" (sidq), it means that truthfulness has blended with him, so it never separates from him. Or the Truth wants to tell us: The true possessor of righteousness is the one who believes in God, or He says: (But righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in God). Or the informing about the essence ("one who believes") in place of the attribute ("righteousness") is evidence of the blending of the essence into the attribute, a blending from which it never withdraws, as if righteousness has become embodied in them.

All these statements are accommodated by the noble Qur'anic text.

The Truth says: (But righteousness is [in] one who believes in God). This is the beginning of faith, and after it comes the end of faith, which is the necessity of believing in the (Last Day). The beginning of the arc is belief in God, and its final end is belief in the Last Day.

Here we ask: How does belief in the Last Day come about?

We say: Belief in the Last Day comes about by believing in God and then believing in what God informs you of. So do not say: "I have placed them in one row." Rather, belief in God comes first, and after that belief in what God has informed me of. God, glorified, has informed that there is another day, so you affirm what He has informed. Then comes the matter of belief in the angels, and the Truth says: (And the angels). How can we believe in a creation of God that we do not see?

Since we have believed in the summit, which is belief in God, and God has informed us that there are angels, even if the existence of angels is unseen, we believe in them, because the One who informed us of them is God. Likewise we believe in the jinn, although we do not see them. Everything relating to the unseen is information from the One in whom you have believed, and therefore you believe in it.

All matters of faith are unseen. You do not say of a perceptible matter: "I have believed in it." Rather, you say "I believe" concerning an unseen matter, because it is an unseen matter with which the senses and perceptions are not familiar, and you want to make it a creed (ʿaqidah). A creed is something tied (yuʿqad), so it never becomes loose. And because it is unseen, it may slip away from us, for if it were a matter that could be witnessed, a person would never forget it, since its being witnessed would make you remember it. It is an unseen matter, and it is called a creed, meaning a bound matter that is never undone.

The summit of creed is that you believe in God, then you believe in what God informs you of among the unseen matters, for which you have no evidence except that God has spoken of them. If you see perceptible matters among the requirements of faith, know that the direction in faith is separate, because the mention of the angels and the Last Day is coming, and both are unseen. Afterward He will mention the Scripture and the prophets, and these two are perceptible.

It is true that the Scripture is a perceptible matter, and so are the prophets, but we did not perceive that God sent down the Scripture or that God sent the prophets. We were not alive at the time of the Scripture's revelation or at the time of the prophet's mission, and our faith came because we believed that God sent down revelation to Muhammad (ﷺ) to be a conveyor of this revelation. All these are unseen matters that we have not seen. The unseen is the ground of the movement of faith, or the foundation of faith.

After that, the verse shifts from discussing the matter of creed to show us that righteousness is composed of creedal matters that are the basis for practical matters, and practical matters are what every religious commitment intends. God, glorified, is not concerned that anyone believes in Him, nor is He concerned that you believe in His angels, books, and messengers. What God desires is that the movement of life on earth be organized by God's method. Therefore the discussion moves to the material matter, and He says: (And gives wealth in spite of love for it), as if the person already possessed the wealth and then "gave" it. When you say "ātaytu," it means "I gave," which differs from "atayt," which means "I came."

What is wealth? Wealth is everything that is valued (yutamawwal), but we have come to use the term for something that can obtain anything valued, and we call it cash (naqd). It has come to dominate, because we buy everything with cash. But the original meaning of wealth is everything that is valued. And how does wealth come to you or to me or to any person? Has any of us come out of his mother's womb possessing anything? No.

What a person owns comes either from someone who was active in life before you, if he was your father or grandfather, or from your own activity.

Therefore one does not say (gave wealth) unless the person has established his own activity by which he becomes one who possesses value, or inherited from one who possessed value. The one who possesses value is the one who moves in life with a movement that may be for himself, and if his movement expands, it will be for his children, and if it expands further, it will be for his grandchildren.

The Truth says: (And gives wealth in spite of love for it). The word "love" is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and a verbal noun is sometimes attributed to its agent and sometimes to its object. For example, the word "striking" (ḍarb): we say "Zayd's striking ʿAmr," and so we find the striker is Zayd and the one struck is ʿAmr.

If it is said: "The striking of Zayd pleased me," if you add "of ʿAmr," we know the striker and the one struck. But if you stop at your saying "the striking of Zayd pleased me," it may have two meanings: the striking issued from Zayd, or the striking fell upon Zayd. So when you use a verbal noun and attribute it to something, it may be attributed to its agent or to its object. (And gives wealth in spite of love for it) can be understood in more than one sense. We can understand it as: he gives wealth while he loves wealth. It may also be understood as: he gives wealth because he loves to give from what he loves, in accordance with God's saying, (You will never attain righteousness until you spend from that which you love). Both meanings are possible. The meaning can be intensified so that it becomes: (And gives wealth in spite of love for the giving), that is, he loves giving and his soul finds rest in giving. It can be intensified further to include all of what has preceded, so the meaning becomes: and gives wealth in spite of love for God who prescribed that for him. All these meanings are possible.

The Truth says:

﴿And they give food, despite loving it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ (Surat al-Insan).

He, glorified, also says:

﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from that which you love﴾ (verse 92 of Surat Al ʿImran).

All these verses clarify the difference between ownership and love for what is owned. It is possible for you to have many things that you own, but not everything you own is something you love. So when you give wealth, you may have removed it from your ownership while you do not love it. In that case you have removed it only from your ownership. Or you may love the thing you give to another, and in that case you have removed it from your ownership and from your love.

Or the wealth in your hand may be merely a tool for you and for others, and it has no place in your heart. Therefore the poet says:

I do not mind preserving my wealth for my time,
spending it in it, in ease and in hardship.
If it is in my hand and not in my heart,
then it is mine, and it does not possess my soul.

The Truth's saying (And gives wealth in spite of love for it) gives us either the status of removing it from ownership or the status of removing it from the heart that loves it. Therefore the Truth reproaches a group of people who want to work for obedience to God, but they spend for God only from what they dislike. God says about them: (And they attribute to God what they dislike).

But to whom is that wealth to be given, to which the saying "and gives wealth in spite of love for it" applies?

It is for (relatives). Do you not see a person whose movement in life has expanded for himself, while his relatives who cannot move are in need? What then is the state of his soul? It must be a troubled soul, because it is expected of the believing person that he regard all people as his relatives. We mention in this context the story of Muʿawiyah when he was the commander of the Muslims. His chamberlain entered upon him, saying: "O Commander of the Faithful, a man is at the door claiming that he is your brother." Muʿawiyah said: "Has it reached such a point that you do not recognize my brothers? Let him in."

When the man entered, Muʿawiyah said to him: "Which of my brothers are you?"

He said: "Your brother from Adam."

So what did Muʿawiyah say?

He said: "A severed kinship. By God, I will be the first to restore it." And he honored him.

If a person cannot maintain ties with all people, can he not at least maintain ties with his close relatives? How then can the believer enjoy the bliss of life while he finds his relatives in need? Even if we look beyond religion and humanity, is the matter not worthy that a person be generous with what he has toward his family?

Within the sphere of faith, when God makes the movement of life in mutual support into circles, He, glorified, wants to distribute the good of society among society. For when He wanted to preserve the human species, He prescribed for us the pure union between man and woman through a public contract and witnesses. Why? Because the fruit of marriage is children, who will bring a new segment of humanity into the world, and this segment must be attributed to the man before people. If the man does not observe God's right regarding his children, people will blame him for that, because they are his children.

Therefore, when we see a person hiding his marriage, such as entering into a customary marriage (zawāj ʿurfī) for example, we say to him: "You want to bring forth a fruit from yourself and then deny it, so children will come who are not attributed to you." Therefore let us be confident that every displaced [child] ...

Then, after that, the Truth (Allah) says:

﴿O you who have believed, prescribed for you is retribution for those murdered: the free for the free, and the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother [i.e., the victim's heir], then there should be a follow-up with fairness and payment to him with good conduct. That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy. And whoever transgresses after that will have a painful punishment.﴾

When Allah calls out, "O you who have believed," this address is the justification (haythiyya) for the ruling that will follow. The meaning of this statement is: I have not imposed upon you by force, against your will or your choice; rather I have imposed it upon you because you have entered into Me through the gate of faith in Me. And since you have believed in Me, then hear the obligation from Me. Allah does not impose obligation upon one who does not believe in Him, and since Allah imposes obligation only upon those who believe in Him, your faith in Him has made you a partner in the contract. So if something is prescribed for you, you are a partner in the prescription, because had you not believed, it would not have been prescribed. It is as if the transaction has been concluded, and since the transaction has been concluded, you are a partner in the obligation. For this reason Allah says "kutiba" (كُتِبَ) with a ḍamma on the kāf, and not "kutiba" with a fatḥa on the kāf. You notice the difference clearly in matters in which a person has a role, for He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail."﴾ (Surah al-Mujadila, 21).

Here He, glory be to Him, is the One who prescribes, because He has no partner. When you read "kutiba 'alaykum" (it has been prescribed upon you), understand that it contains obligation and hardship, and it is the opposite of "kutiba lakum" (it has been prescribed for you), such as His saying:

﴿Say: "Nothing will strike us except what Allah has prescribed for us."﴾ (Surah al-Tawba, 51).

"Kutiba lana" makes us feel that the matter is for our benefit. On the surface it appears that retribution is prescribed upon you, and when retribution is prescribed upon you as a killer, the heir of the victim has retribution prescribed for him. So every "upon you" (ʿalaykum) corresponds to a "for you" (lakum), and you are liable to be either the killer or the one killed. If you are killed, then Allah has prescribed for you; and if you are the killer, then Allah has prescribed upon you. Because what is "for me" must be "upon" someone else, and what is "upon me" must be "for someone else." Legislation does not legislate for a single individual, but for all people.

When He says, "Retribution is prescribed upon you," and then in the verse that follows, "And for you in retribution is life," He has brought both "for you" and "upon you." "Upon you" is for the killer, and "for you" is for the heir of the victim. Thus the legislation is just, because it does not come for one at the expense of another, and contracts always take account of the interest of both parties. "O you who have believed, retribution is prescribed upon you for the murdered: the free for the free."

And who is the free (ḥurr)? The ḥurr is the opposite of the slave ('abd), and he is one who is not owned as property. The ḥurr of everything is its noblest part; it is said "ḥurr al-māl," meaning the most noble of the wealth. The ḥurr in a human being is one whose neck no one controls. The ḥurr of vegetables (buqūl) is that which is eaten unripe, i.e., not cooked on the fire, like pistachios and almonds.

The Truth, glory be to Him, says: "the free for the free." The apparent wording indicates that a free person is not killed for a slave, because He says: "the free for the free and the slave for the slave and the female for the female." But what happens if a slave kills a free person, or a woman kills a man; shall we kill them or not?

Indeed, the Truth sets controls for the matter of vengeance. He, glory be to Him, did not legislate that a free person is not killed except for a free person; rather the intent of the verse is that a free person is killed if he kills a free person, a slave is killed if he kills a slave, and a female for a female. This is the completion of the equation: the recompense of the killer is of the same kind as what he killed, not that the killing extends to one who is better than him. The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, through this legislation of retribution addresses a matter that existed among the tribes, where there was killing for revenge and vendetta.

In the pre-Islamic era, when a battle arose between two tribes, it was natural that there would be dead and casualties from that fighting. If a slave of one tribe was killed, the tribe that owned that slave would insist on escalating the vengeance by taking a free man in return; and likewise, if a woman was killed in that war, her tribe would escalate the vengeance by taking a male in return.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, wanted to settle the matter of vendetta gradually, so He brought this command: "the free for the free and the slave for the slave and the female for the female." Thus the Truth here addresses a matter of escalation in taking vengeance, and lays down a method that settles this excess in vengeance.

In Upper Egypt, we still suffer from heedlessness in applying the sharia of Allah: when a man of one family is killed, they do not take vengeance upon the killer, but go to the most senior person in the killer's family to kill him. Those who take vengeance want the most severe injury, and they may make the price of the victim ten from the other family, and they may mutilate their bodies to satisfy themselves, and all of that is inconsistent with retribution. In the days of ignorance they used to exaggerate in vengeance, and the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, informs all of humanity that this exaggeration in vengeance makes the fires of enmity never extinguish. Therefore the Truth returns the matter of vengeance to its minimum limit: if a tribe kills a slave, it is not right for the other tribe to escalate the matter by taking a free man for the slave.

Thus the Truth legislates a matter that concerns those ancient collective wars, the mass killing that occurred in them, and the resulting exaggeration in vengeance; this is gradual legislation, and Allah, glory be to Him, decreed that the matter of vengeance be returned to its minimum limit, so that if a tribe kills a slave, it is not right for the other tribe to escalate the vengeance by killing a free man. The Truth then legislates that in ordinary circumstances the killer is subjected to retribution by killing him or by blood-money (diya). Another verse came in which the Truth says:

﴿And We prescribed for them therein: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and for wounds is retribution. But whoever gives it as charity, it is expiation for him. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then they are the wrongdoers.﴾ (Surah al-Ma'ida, 45).

Thus retribution for taking a life becomes a life for a life, without distinction between slave, free, or female, but any soul for any soul. And here the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, through codifying the legislation of retribution, addresses a matter in which He wants to extinguish the rancor of vengeance and the boiling of hatred. When you hear the word "retribution" and "killing," it means that the soul is charged with hatred and animosity, and He wants to purify the grudge and vengeful malice from the souls of the believers. The Truth, glory be to Him, gives the heir of the blood the right either to kill or to pardon; and when Allah gives the heir of the blood the right to kill, the matter of the killer's life comes into the hand of the heir of the blood. If the heir pardons, the pardon is not by legislation but by generosity of soul, and thus the Truth absorbs anger and rage.

After that, Allah softens the heart of the heir of the blood, saying: "But whoever is pardoned by his brother [i.e., the victim's heir], then there should be a follow-up with fairness and payment to him with good conduct."

If we reflect on His saying, "whoever is pardoned by his brother," let us notice the transition from the boiling of blood to pardon, then the emphasis on tenderness, as if He says: do not forget the brotherhood of faith. "Whoever is pardoned by his brother, then there should be a follow-up with fairness."

When the Truth says the word "brother" (akh), look whether this brother shares the same father? As in His saying: "And the brothers of Joseph came." Then He elevates the lineage of faith to the rank of brotherhood in faith, saying: "The believers are but brothers," meaning: beware of making the meeting of material lineage without your meeting in doctrinal values.

The basic meaning of "brother" is that he shares the same father, as in: "And the brothers of Joseph came." If they are brothers from other than the same father, He calls them "ikhwān" (brothers in a looser sense); if they advance in faith, He calls them "ikhwa." When He described them as "ikhwān," He said: "Remember Allah's favour upon you when you were enemies, and He brought your hearts together, so you became by His favour brothers." There had been among them wars, hatred and discord; He did not describe them as "ikhwa" because they were still in rancor, so He described them as "ikhwān," and after faith has matured in their souls they become "ikhwa."

Consider the Battle of Badr. Here is Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, who was the pampered and privileged youth of Quraysh, from whom the scent of perfume wafted and whose clothing was of silk; that was before his Islam. All of that changed when he entered Islam: faith removed him from this luxury to the misery of the first believers, to the extent that he wore animal hide, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him in this hardship and said: "Look how faith has done to your companion."

When the Battle of Badr came, he met his brother Abu 'Aziz, who remained upon the religion of Quraysh; the two met in battle, Mus'ab in the camp of the believers and Abu 'Aziz in the army of the polytheists. During the battle, he saw his brother Abu 'Aziz captive with Abu al-Yusr, who was from the Ansar. Mus'ab turned to Abu al-Yusr and said: "O Abu al-Yusr, tighten your grip on your captive, for his mother is wealthy and will ransom him with much wealth."

Abu 'Aziz turned to him and said: "O my brother, is this your instruction concerning your brother?" Mus'ab said: "No, he is not my brother; my brother is this one," and he pointed to Abu al-Yusr. The lineage of blood had ended and the lineage of faith had become the foundation; Mus'ab became a brother to Abu al-Yusr in faith, and his tie to his full brother in lineage was severed because he remained a polytheist.

His saying, "whoever is pardoned by his brother," is as if He urges the heir of the blood to pardon and not to forget the brotherhood of faith. It is true that he is the heir of the victim, because he is of his flesh and lineage, but Allah wanted to make the brotherhood of faith above the brotherhood of blood. "Whoever is pardoned by his brother, then there should be a follow-up with fairness."

The Truth has mentioned brotherhood here to soften hearts, to alert the people of both the killer and the slain that killing does not mean that the brotherhood of faith has ended, no. The believers must keep in mind that the bond of faith brotherhood may weaken. When the heirs of the blood remember the brotherhood of faith, pardon becomes close to their souls. We may observe that the Truth raises us to levels of elevation, reminding us that the pardon of one of the heirs of the blood necessitates that the matter of pardon prevails, so the killer is not killed.

Then let us look at the precision of the Truth in clearing the anger from hearts when He places blood-money in place of killing as retribution. The blood-money that the heirs of the blood take from the killer may be deferred in payment; the killer or his family may be unable to pay promptly. Therefore, the one bearing the blood-money must pay it, and the family of the victim must accept that with fairness, and the blood-money must be paid by the killer's family or by the killer himself with good conduct.

His saying, the Truth: "pardoned for him from his brother anything," the word "anything" (shay') indicates that if one of the heirs of the victim pardons, it is a pardon for one thing, and he has no right to exact retribution afterward; the matter ends, blood is spared. Allah did not want to place an explicit text prohibiting retribution, but He wanted to give the heir of the blood the right to kill. When he has the right to kill, the matter is in his hand: if he pardons, the killer's life becomes a fruit of his kindness; and if the killer lives, this does not leave hatred in the heart of the owner of the blood, but rather the killer will become fond of him, because he has done him good and granted him his life.

But if the text had remained limited to retribution against the killer by the victim's family only, without extending to pardon, the knot would have remained in the heart.

The vendettas present in contemporary societies are caused by our not enabling the heir of the blood over the killer. The proof is that if a killer surrenders himself and goes to the victim's family, enters their house, and insists on seeking pardon, taking his shroud with him and saying: "I have come to you so that you may take retribution from me; here is my shroud with me, so do with me as you wish," it has never happened that the victim's family betrayed the killer; rather what is familiar and customary is that they pardon him. Why?

Because they have gained power over him and his life is in their hands, and customarily enmity turns into affection. The killer remains indebted to his life to those who pardoned him. Those among the killer's children who know this see their father's life as a gift granted to them by the heirs and relatives of the victim; they see that the pardon of the victim's family is what saved the life of their relative. Thus the circle widens, and the matter turns from enmity to affection.

﴿Repel with that which is better, and thereupon the one between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he were a devoted friend.﴾ (Surah Fussilat, 34).

Had Allah not legislated retribution, the matter would have become chaos. But He legislates it,

Indeed, the Truth (al-Haqq) lifts the punishment and torment from the killer when he accepts retaliation (qisas) and it is carried out upon him, or when the victim's family pardons him in exchange for blood money (diyah) and he pays it. But the Truth accepts only the use of the opportunities that it has given to creation so that they may rise in their relations. The Truth does not accept that the family of the slain should hide behind pardon in order to kill the killer after they have announced their forgiveness of him, for that is a mockery of the method that the Truth intended as a way among the servants.

Therefore the Truth says: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you, O people of understanding, that you may be God-fearing.﴾ [2:179]

Here we notice that the Qur'anic discourse sometimes says: "O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you" [2:183]. Here, however, the Qur'anic discourse says: "And for you in retaliation..."

Precise and firm legislation brings both duties and rights. There is no duty without a right, and no right without a duty. And so that one may know the loftiness of the legislation, every believer is required to look at the obligations that are incumbent upon him and link them with the rights that he has, and the believer will discover that, in the light of God's method, he has attained perfect justice.

The legislator is God, and He is the Lord of all people. Therefore no believer is closer to God than any other believer. The obligation of faith prevents injustice, restores rights, and protects and safeguards for the human being his wealth and his honour. It is the habit of a human being to dispute over his rights, wanting them in full, and to try to diminish his duties. But the believing human being is the one who gives the duty in full and therefore receives his rights in full. For this reason the Truth says: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you, O people of understanding, that you may be God-fearing.﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah).

Retaliation is prescribed upon the killer, the victim, and the victim's guardian. If the killer knows that God has decreed retaliation, this obliges him to surrender himself, and his family must not hide him away from people's eyes, because the killer must bear the responsibility for what he has done. When the killer finds himself surrounded by a believing society that rejects killing, he is restrained and does not kill. So there is life in retaliation, because the one who desires to kill can be deterred when he knows that there is someone who will exact retaliation from him, and that there is someone who will not accept concealment on his behalf.

After that we come to those who speak loudly and say: retaliation is brutality and a waste of human dignity. We ask them: why has zeal taken hold of you because a person is subjected to retaliation justly, after he killed another unjustly? What is it that saddens you on his account?

When God legislated punishment, He did not legislate it so that it would occur; rather He legislated it so that it would prevent. When we exact retaliation from the killer, we protect the rest of the members of society from there being among them a killer who does not respect the lives of others. At the same time we protect this lawless man from himself, because he will think a thousand times before committing a crime.

Thus the retaliation against the killer is a lesson to others and a protection for all members of society. For this reason the Truth, glorified is He, says: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you.﴾ The Truth wants to warn us that we should not be seized by false magnanimity, misplaced humanitarianism, and foolish tenderness, so that we say: "Let us prohibit retaliation."

How can we become angry at punishing a killer justly, yet not stir at the killing of an innocent? When the Truth legislates retaliation, it is as if He says: "Beware lest you kill anyone, for you will be killed if you kill him." In that is protection for people's souls from being killed. In the legislation of retaliation there is preservation of your lives, because when you know that if you kill an innocent person you will be killed as a result of your act, you will refrain from killing, and it is as if you have preserved your own blood. That is the lofty and just legislation.

And in retaliation there is life, because everyone is subject to retaliation and everyone has retaliation due to him. It is the legislation that addresses the people of intellect and understanding (ulu al-albab), who know the essence of the things and the rulings that are intended, whereas those who are not people of understanding are those who dispute matters without knowing their essence. Had there been no retaliation, no one would have been restrained, and had there been no retaliation, humanity would have sunk into savagery. The wisdom in codifying punishment is that the crime should not occur, and by this the crime may recede together with the punishment, and the right may be balanced with the duty.

Whoever contemplates the affairs of the cosmos finds that balance in this world, for example in past years, comes from the existence of two great powers, each of which fears the other and each of which disagrees with the other. In this disagreement there is life for other peoples, because if they had agreed upon falsehood, the pillars of their two states would have collapsed, and in that would have been the destruction of the world and the enslavement of the rest of the peoples. Every system in the world would bear hatred, malice, and enmity toward the other and would wish to dominate with its system, but it fears the strength of the other system. Thus we find in that mutual fear a protection for the lives of others, and an opportunity for believers to take up the causes of scientific advancement so as to present to the world a style fitting for human life on earth in the light of God's method. When one of the two powers, the Soviet Union, disintegrated, the United States now seeks an opposite for itself, because it knows that life without a counterpart of comparable strength may embolden the small against it.

It is the fear of punishment that creates the balance between the camps of the world, and it is the fear of punishment that creates the balance within individuals as well.

The justice of the Most Merciful is what has obliged us to deal with crime by punishing it, and for others to witness this punishment so that they may be deterred.

Behold, the Truth, in the crime of adultery for example, affirms the necessity that a group of people witness the punishment so that they may be deterred. Strictness is required in the careful investigation of the occurrence of adultery, because a lack of precision in the investigation afflicts people with anxiety and causes confusion and doubt about lineages. The strictness has also come in the punishment, in the words of the Truth:

﴿The adulterous woman and the adulterous man, flog each one of them a hundred lashes, and let not compassion for them take hold of you in the religion of God, if you believe in God and the Last Day. And let a group of the believers witness their punishment.﴾ (Surah al-Nur) [24:2]

Whoever dares to violate the rights of people also dares to violate the rights of God. Therefore the requirement of preferring faith is to please God, not to please people. In inflicting punishment upon the transgressor there is submission to God's method, and in witnessing this punishment by others there is the spreading of the idea that the transgressor receives punishment. For this reason the Truth legislated the punishment and its public display, so that balance may be established in the human soul.

Next, the Almighty turns to address another social matter. After dealing with the taking of life, the Truth (al-Haqq) moves us to another of life's matters: natural death. It is as if the Truth, having explained the treatment of death by crime, wishes to clarify some of the matters connected with death that comes to a person without any cause that takes away the soul. In the upcoming verse, the Truth deals with some matters related to death in order to achieve economic balance in society, just as the previous verse achieved penal and criminal balance in society. The Truth says:

﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, that he make bequest to the parents and the near relatives, in a fair manner; a duty upon the God-fearing (al-muttaqun). 180﴾

As I have clarified before, the Truth does not force His will upon the servants, but presents to them the matter of belief in Him. If they believe, this belief requires agreement with His method. Therefore the believer shares, through his creed, in the belief in what Allah has prescribed for him. The believer is one who has accepted Allah as God and Legislator, so when Allah prescribes a matter for the believer, the believer has already taken part in the prescribing of this matter by merely declaring his faith. As for the one who disbelieves in the Truth, Allah has not forced upon him his choice of disbelief, so the Truth has prescribed for him only one thing, which is punishment in the Hereafter.

Allah imposes obligation only upon the one who believes in Him, loves Him, and believes in all the attributes of majesty and perfection that belong to Him. Therefore the obligation of faith is an honor with which Allah distinguishes the loving believers in Him. Had the disbelievers realized that Allah had neglected them because they did not believe in Him, they would have hastened to belief, and they would have seen the pride of every believer in the obligation Allah has placed upon him. The believer sees the obligation as submission to the will of Allah, and submission to the will of Allah means love.
