Since love has been established between the servant and the Lord, the Truth wishes to perpetuate this love; therefore the obligations are a continuation of the love between servant and Lord.

The servant loves the Lord through faith, and the Lord loves the servant through obligation, and obligation is a higher rank than the servant's faith. The servant's faith does not benefit Allah, but Allah's obligations are beneficial to the servant. The believer must realize the dignity of the obligation from Allah; obligation is not a humiliation that the Truth imposes on His believing servants, but rather a dignity that Allah wills for His believing servants. Thus is the saying of the Truth: "It is prescribed for you" (kutiba 'alaykum); it is a matter shared between the servant and the Lord. The writing here is a matter shared between the Truth who revealed the obligation and the servant who believed in the obligation.

The Truth here presents a matter concerning bequest, saying, Glorified is He:

﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, that he make bequest to the parents and the near relatives, in a fair manner; a duty upon the God-fearing. 180﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah).

Here we find two conditions. The first condition begins with (idha), which is used for a matter that is certain to occur, namely the occurrence of the event. Death is a certainty for every servant, so the Truth introduced this matter with a condition, (idha), which is a particle of condition and a time adverb for an event. Death is a certain matter, but no one knows its appointed time.

The second condition begins with (in), a particle of condition which we use for a matter that may be doubtful; a person may leave wealth after death or may leave nothing. Therefore the Truth commands the servant to make a bequest, which is good for him. Why? Because the Truth wishes to legislate for collective circulation (al-istitraq al-jama'i): after the Truth enjoins His servants to travel through life, striving so that their provision expands and overflows beyond their needs, this surplus is the good (khayr), and good in this domain differs from person to person and from time to time.

When in the old times a servant left ten pounds, that sum had value; whereas when another servant leaves a thousand pounds in these days, it may be counted by some as a small amount of good. Thus good is measured in every matter according to its time, and therefore Allah did not tie it to a figure. In Egypt, for example, we used to exchange the paper pound for a pound of gold with two and a half piastres left over; but now the gold pound equals more than two hundred and fifty pounds, because the reserve backing of the Egyptian pound in the old times was high. Now the circulating currency has exceeded the gold reserve, so the gold pound has become far more expensive than the paper pound.

Because the true God desires good for people, He did not specify the measure or value of the good. When death approaches a person who has a surplus of good, he must bequeath from this good. We should note that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade waiting for the moment of death to state one's bequest or to inform one's family of debts owed, because a person at the moment of death may not think of such matters. Therefore we must understand that the Truth alerts us to write down what one owns and owes during one's life. He says, and writes his bequest, which is executed after his life. The believer says: "If death comes to me, then to my father such-and-such, and to the near relatives such-and-such."

That is, the believer is commanded to write his bequest while healthy, and not to wait for the time of death to make this bequest. The Truth enjoins good upon whom? (for the parents and the near relatives in a fair manner, a duty upon the God-fearing). The Truth knows that His servants attend to their children and may neglect their parents, because people regard fathers and mothers as those bidding farewell to life, although the parents are the cause of the children's existence in life. Therefore the Truth enjoins His believing servants to set aside a share of good for fathers and mothers, and also for relatives. He, Glorified is He, wishes to protect two weak groups: the parents and the relatives.

This ruling came before the legislation of inheritance. Before the legislation of inheritance, people gave all they owned to their children, so Allah wished to remove them from giving everything to their children and depriving parents and relatives. Afterwards Allah determined the parents' share in inheritance, while the relatives' matter the Truth left to His servants to determine in the bequest. The parents might be disbelievers, so they do not inherit from the son; but the Truth says:

﴿And We have enjoined upon man (goodness) to his parents: his mother bore him in weakness upon weakness, and his weaning is in two years — "Be grateful to Me and to your parents; to Me is the final destination. 14 But if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them; and accompany them in this world with appropriate kindness and follow the way of those who turn to Me in repentance. Then to Me will be your return, and I will inform you about what you used to do. 15﴾ (Surat Luqman).

The Truth reminds His servants of His favor upon them and also of the favor of the parents; but if the parents are polytheists, there is no obedience to them in this polytheism, yet there remains the command to keep company with them in this life in kindness, and to follow the path of the believers who carry the true method. Therefore the believing person may bequeath some good in his will to his parents even if they are disbelievers, and we know that the limit of bequest is one-third of what a person owns, and the rest is for lawful inheritance. But if they are believers, we follow the noble Prophetic hadith: "There is no bequest to an heir" (1).

Thus the weak relatives who are not heirs are included in the bequest; this is what is meant by social circulation (al-istitraq al-ijtima'i). When the Truth alerts His servants to bequeathing for weak relatives during life, He wishes the servants to realize that they bear responsibility toward these people. It is good for a person to work in life, travel through the earth, seek lawful provision, and leave his heirs wealthy rather than becoming a burden on anyone.

On the authority of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to visit me while I was in Mecca. He said, 'May Allah have mercy on the son of Afra'.' I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, shall I bequeath all my wealth?' He said, 'No.' I said, 'Then half?' He said, 'No.' I said, 'A third?' He said, 'A third, and a third is much; indeed, for you to leave your heirs wealthy is better than to leave them dependent, begging from people'" (2).

When Allah grants a person much good through his work, beware, O human, of restricting this good to those who will inherit from you.

Why? Because if you restrict something to those who inherit from you, you may encounter in your life someone who does not inherit but has the claim of kinship to you, and who is in need of someone to help him in his livelihood; if you do not help him, he will resent you and every blessing Allah has bestowed upon you. But when this relative knows that the blessing Allah has granted you will reach him in some measure, even by bequest and not through statutory inheritance, this relative will be filled with joy at the blessing Allah has given you.

Therefore the Truth said:

﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, that he make bequest to the parents and the near relatives, in a fair manner; a duty upon the God-fearing. 180﴾ (from Surat al-Baqarah).

The Truth wishes to draw the servants' attention to the non-inheriting relatives after having included fathers and mothers in inheritance. When a person is a relative of a deceased who left good, and the deceased singled out this relative with some of the good in his bequest, this relative's own soul is filled with good, so he learns not to withhold good from the weak, and thus love is circulated and bonds of affection are established.

The Truth, who is most knowing of His servants' souls, presumes that the testator may not be right and the heir may be right; therefore legislation took precaution for this case, because the beneficiary, when he takes his share of the bequest, will diminish the heir's portion. Therefore Allah, Glorified and Exalted, wishes to protect all parties: He protects the one who made the bequest, the beneficiary, and the heir. From here the Truth says:

﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it, the sin is only upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing. 181﴾

(1) Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan and al-Daraqutni from Jabir.
(2) Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Ahmad and al-Nasa'i.

We know that at the time the Qur'an was revealed, bequests were made orally, writing was not widespread, and therefore the Truth brought the common element among the testator, the legatee and the heir, which is the element of speech; for speech was the clear instrument in that ancient era. There were no contemporary means such as the real estate registry (al-shahr al-'aqari) to document the bequest. Therefore, altering the bequest of the deceased was a sin upon the one who alters it.

As for the testator, his obligation has been discharged. But the obligation of the legatee and the heir is what deserves to be mindful that Allah knows the secrets of the hearts, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.

He wants to set right the relationship between the heir and the legatee. Therefore, the Truth says:

﴿Whoever fears deviation (janf) or sin from a testator, and makes peace between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (2:182)

The Truth wants justice for everyone. If the bequest deviates from justice and from the straight path, and it contains deprivation of the poor and an increase in the wealth of the rich, or the neglect of the closest relatives, then this is a loss of the continuity (istitrāq) that Allah intended. When someone comes who strives in the way of good to return the bequest to what is correct, there is no sin upon him for the change he makes to the bequest, to alter it into the correct form that Allah approves, because Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.

A person may fear from the testator that there will be deviation (janf). Janf is interpreted as iniquity and injustice. Allah may create a person with janf, meaning in a form where one side of his body is lower than the other. We know from the scholars of anatomy that each half of a human being differs from the other half, and this may be clear in some creatures, while it may not be apparent except to the careful and attentive examiner.

A person may have no choice in being deviated (ajnaf). Sin, however, comes by a person's choice, that is, when a person knows the wrong and commits it anyway. So whoever fears from a testator janf, meaning unintentional deviation and injustice, this is a matter in which the testator has no choice. Therefore, correcting that deviation and injustice is good for the testator. But if the testator has intentionally chosen to be sinful, then correcting that sin is obligatory. This is the precision of the Qur'anic legislation, which sharpens all of a person's faculties so that they receive complete justice.

The Truth addressed the question of legislation for humans in the matter of retaliation (qiṣāṣ) by employing all the faculties of goodness in a person when He said: ﴿Whoever is pardoned by his brother in any part, then pursue it with good conduct.﴾ (2:178) It is not a dry legislation like the legislation of humans. It is legislation from the Creator, the Merciful, the All-Knowing of the hidden depths of human beings. The Truth stirs in humans all the impulses of goodness. He also addresses the matter of altering a bequest which the deceased made himself. Whoever contradicts a bequest that was established on justice, there is a punishment for him.

As for the one who intervenes to correct a matter of a bequest, in a way that achieves deliverance for the deceased from janf (unintended injustice, which nonetheless causes pain), or who corrects a bequest that contains sin, this is something Allah wants, there is no sin in it, and through it Allah achieves forgiveness and mercy. Thus the Truth teaches us that whoever hears or reads a bequest must measure it by the logic of truth and justice and the legislation of Allah. If it contains a violation, then he must refer it back to its author. We should note that the Truth has expressed the human feeling of fear of injustice occurring, whether unintentionally or intentionally, when He said: ﴿Whoever fears deviation or sin from a testator, and makes peace between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The word (khāfa, "fears") when it comes in this context indicates the unity of faith in the souls of Muslims. The believer who takes on the correction of this kind of matter may be neither an heir, nor a legatee, nor the testator; he is merely a witness. This witnessing leads him to strive for mutual faith-based solidarity (takāful). Every matter that touches a believer touches all believers. If deviation occurs, this stirs fear in the believer, because its result may afflict other believers, even unintentionally. Thus we see the unity of faith. Faith blends believers with one another until they become like one body: if one of its members complains, the rest of the members respond with sleeplessness and fever.

Therefore, when a believer who has no direct interest in the matter of inheritance or bequest intervenes to correct this matter, the Truth rewards him with the best reward.

The Truth, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Whoever fears deviation or sin from a testator, and makes peace between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This statement draws our attention to the fact that when a person resolves to make a decision regarding a bequest, he must consult those around him and welcome every counsel from people of knowledge and wisdom. This is so that resentments do not arise after the bequest has been finally concluded, that is, after his death. The Truth has put in place the precautions necessary to correct a bequest if it brings about problems, because the Truth wants believers to unite in faith-based solidarity. Therefore, deviation must be addressed by prevention before it occurs. For this reason, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

(The example of one who upholds the limits of Allah and one who violates them is like a people who cast lots (istahamū) over a ship; some of them obtained the upper deck and some the lower. Those in the lower deck, when they needed water, passed by those above them, and said: "If only we made a hole in our share and did not harm those above us." If they leave them and what they want, they will all perish; but if they take hold of their hands, they will be saved and all will be saved.)(1)

The noble hadith gives an example of the necessity of mutual support and mutual counsel among believers for their protection. These are people who divided a ship by lot, and istihām is a lot that has no desire in it. Some of them settled at the bottom of the ship according to the outcome of the lot, and some settled at the top. But those who settled at the bottom wanted some water, and some of them suggested that they make a hole in the ship to obtain water, justifying that such an act would not harm those who dwell in the upper half of the ship. If they had done so, and those in the upper half had not prevented them, they would all have drowned. But if those in the upper half had intervened, they would have prevented the drowning. Likewise, with the limits of Allah: believers must support one another through mutual counsel in applying them. So let no one say: "What happens by others is no concern of mine," because the affair of the Muslims concerns every Muslim. For this reason, a verse came about which Sayyidunā Abū Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "There is a verse you recite but place it other than its proper place," meaning you understand it other than its meaning. The verse is the statement of the Truth:

﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who have wronged; and know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ (Surah al-Anfal, 8:25)

Our teacher Ḥasanayn Makhlūf, former Grand Mufti of Egypt, says in explaining this verse: That is, beware of Allah's testing through trials that may descend upon you, which encompass the wrongdoer and others, such as calamity, famine, high prices, the domination of tyrants, and other things. What is meant is a warning against sins which are the causes of trials, such as approving of evil and innovations and being content with them, compromising in enjoining what is good, divisions in the word of truth, suspending the prescribed punishments, the spread of disobedience, and the like. And in what al-Bukhārī narrated: when the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near..." he was asked: "Shall we be destroyed while among us are the righteous?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases."(2)

Therefore, no Muslim should believe that he is not responsible for the corruption that spreads in society; rather, he must warn and admonish. For this reason, we find that the wisdom of the Truth imposed blood money (diya) on the ʿāqila, that is, on the relatives of the killer, because they may see this killer practicing corruption from the beginning and none of them restrains him. But if they had struck his hand from the start, they would not have been burdened with paying the blood money. Therefore, when you hear the statement of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever fears deviation from a testator﴾, beware of saying: "This matter is none of my concern." No, the matter concerns you, and you must try to make peace between the legatee and the heirs. The statement of the Truth: ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾ means that he is not included among those who alter the word, which we discussed in the reflections before this verse; rather, there is reward for you for your intervention. You have not changed truth into falsehood; rather, you remove falsehood in order to establish truth. Thereby you soothe the heart of the heir regarding what was lost from him, establish the balance of justice through counsel, and make his soul generous so that he accepts the bequest after amending it in a way that pleases the law of Allah. Allah wants the establishment of the balance of justice and for the continuity of purity (al-istitrāq al-ṣafāʾī) among believers to be secured, so that the bequest does not produce evils.

1. Related by al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī, and Aḥmad in his Musnad, from al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr.
2. Related by al-Bukhārī in his Ṣaḥīḥ, in the chapter on trials.

Al-Sha'rawi, after saying: "And the Truth says afterward:"

﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you that you may become righteous.﴾ (2:183)

The Truth, glorified is He, begins this noble verse by softening the ruling that comes with the duty to follow, which is fasting. It is as though He says: "O you who have believed in Me and loved Me, I have prescribed fasting for you." When the ruling comes from one in whom you have faith, you trust that He singles you out with a duty from which benefit will come to you. Let me give an example, and God's is the highest example: suppose you address your son regarding a matter that involves hardship but whose results are beneficial. You do not say to him, "O son, do such-and-such," but you say, "O my little one, do such-and-such," as if you are saying to him: "O my young one, do not take the task I assign you, with its hardship, by the measure of your immature intellect, but take this duty by the measure of the intellect and experience of your father."

The believers take the Truth's address to them, "O you who have believed," as a measure of love for everything that comes from Him, glorified is He, in the way of duty, even if it involves hardship. By accepting faith, the believers are with the Truth in the covenant of faith, and He, glorified is He, has not prescribed fasting for one who does not believe in Him, because he does not enter the circle of the covenant of faith and will face the Blaze.

Fasting is a form of abstention, because the meaning of *sawm* (ṣawm, fasting) is *imsāk* (abstention). The Truth says:

﴿So if you see any human being, say, "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, so I will not speak today to any human being."﴾ (19:26)

This is abstention from speech. Thus, fasting means abstention; but legislated fasting (ṣawm tashrīʿī) means abstaining from the two appetites of the belly and the private parts from dawn until sunset. The principle of fasting does not differ from one era to another. Fasting as an act of worship existed in the religions before Islam, but it was either total abstention from food, or abstention from certain kinds of food, like the fasting of the Christians. Fasting, then, is a method for the training of the human being in the religions, even if the number of days differs and the manner of fasting differs. The Truth concludes the noble verse with His saying: "that you may become righteous" (*la'allakum tattaqūn*). We know that the meaning of *taqwā* (taqwa, God-consciousness) is that we place between ourselves and the attributes of majesty a shield, and that we guard against the seizing of God and guard against the Fire, which is among the effects of the attributes of majesty. His saying, the Truth: "that you may become righteous" means that we refine and trim our conduct so that we keep away from sins, and sins in the soul arise only from the excessive craving of its materiality for some matter. Fasting, as we know, weakens the intensity of materialism, its heat, and its domination over the body. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to young men and others:

"O assembly of youth, whoever among you is able to marry, let him marry, for it lowers the gaze and guards the private parts; and whoever is not able, let him fast, for it is a shield for him."(1)

It is as though fasting trims the intensity of materialism in the young body. Reducing food means reducing the fuel of matter, so the frenzy that drives a person to commit sins diminishes. Fasting in Ramadan gives a person steadfastness for a month, and a person perceives the sweetness of steadfastness and so continues with it after Ramadan. The Truth does not ask you for steadfastness only in Ramadan; rather, He, glorified is He, has chosen Ramadan as a time in which you train yourself in steadfastness, so that it spreads throughout your whole life afterward. For God's choosing of a time, or God's choosing of a place, or of a person, is not to pamper the time, nor to pamper the place, nor to pamper the person. God intends by His choosing of a messenger that the effect of the messenger's selection spread among all people. For this reason we find the history of the messengers full of hardship and toil, and this is evidence that the burden of the message is borne by the messenger and its toil falls upon him. God did not choose him to pamper him, but chose him to make him an exemplar.

Likewise, God chooses certain days from time, not to set them above the other times, but because He, glorified and exalted is He, wants the selection of this time to spread through all times, as with His choosing of the days of Ramadan. The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, chooses places so that their selection spreads through all places. When we hear someone say, "I visited Mecca and Medina and tasted the sweetness of clarity, radiance and illumination, and I forgot everything," such a person thinks he is praising the place, but forgets that the place rejoices when its selection spreads to the rest of the places. So when you go to Mecca to visit the Sacred House, and when you go to Medina to visit the Messenger of God (ﷺ), why do you not remember in all places that God is present in all existence, and that your performance of the pillars of Islam and your conduct of Islam is a drawing near to God and to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?

It is true that your worship while you are in the vicinity of the House of God is marked by precision and good intention. It is as though, while you are in the vicinity of the House of God and in the presence of the Messenger of God, you are ashamed to commit a sin. And when you hear "Allahu akbar" you rise for prayer and are humble, and you harm no one. So why does this conduct not spread from you at all times and in all places? You can summon the intention of worship in any place, and you will find high inner tranquility.

Thus, when God chooses a time, a place, or a person, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, intends that the selection of the person spread among all people, the selection of the place among all places, and the selection of the time among all times. For this reason I am amazed when I find people greeting Ramadan with glorification and the verses of the Qur'an, and after Ramadan ends they forget all that. I say: Did Ramadan come to guard our religion for us, or does Ramadan come to train us to live with the character of purity at all times?

His saying, the Truth: "fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you" tells us that Muslims are not novel in the matter of fasting; rather, people before them fasted, even though the outward form of fasting differed. When the Truth says: "fasting has been prescribed for you," this is an affirmation of the principle, the principle of fasting.

(1) Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary continues:

The Truth, glory be to Him, then details the principle after that, saying:

﴿Days numbered. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days. And for those who are able to do it, there is a ransom: feeding a poor person. And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him. And that you fast is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

The word (ayyaman) indicates time and comes in a general form (mujmalah). His saying, the Truth, about those days: they are (ma'dudat), meaning they are few and well-known days.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 185:

Then, after that, the Truth clarifies for us the duration of the fast, saying:

﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down, a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the Criterion. So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it. But whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days. Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you, and [wants] you to complete the period and to glorify Allah for having guided you, and perhaps you will be grateful.﴾ [2:185]

So, the duration of the fast is the month of Ramadan. And because He, glory be to Him, is the All-Knowing of the necessities that may arise regarding this obligation, He legislates for these necessities. The legislation of God for the concessions of necessity is an announcement to us that it is in no way valid for any human being to step outside the framework of necessity that God has prescribed. Some of those who philosophize superficially like to beautify for themselves the necessities that permit them to depart from the law of God, and one of them says:

﴿God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (part of 2:286).

We say: you understand and define capacity according to the measure of your mind, and then you measure the obligation by it, even though the One who created you is the One who imposes the obligation and knows that you can bear the obligation. He, glory be to Him, imposes only what is within your capacity; the evidence for this is that the Legislator, glory be to Him, grants the concession when the obligation is not within capacity. Let us look at the mercy of the Truth as He says: (Whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days). The word (ill) is a general word, and you are a proof against yourself; and by the command of a skilled Muslim physician who tells you: (If you fast, you will suffer), and illness, its hardship is in some cases chronic; for this reason, the expiation of feeding a poor person is required.

Likewise, God grants you a concession when you are (on a journey). The word (journey, safar) is derived from a root that conveys appearing and becoming manifest, as in our saying: (the morning has become clear, asfara al-subh). The word (safar) conveys moving from a place where you reside to a new place, as though every time you take a step, new things are revealed to you, and the place to which you move is new for you, even if you have become accustomed to travelling there; because it becomes new each time, owing to the circumstances of instability that arise in it. It is true that some buildings and streets have not changed, but what changes is the circumstances you encounter; and it is true that the conditions of travel in our time have differed from travel in ancient times.

Indeed, the hardship of movement in the past was great, but let us compare the travel of yesterday with the travel of today in terms of residence. You will find that travel now, with residence now, involves hardship. It is strange that those who debate this concession debate it in order to prevent the concession; and we say to them: know that God's legislation of concessions transfers them into a required legal ruling; and in this regard Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, narrates: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on a journey and he saw a crowd and a man over whom shade had been cast, and he said: (What is this?) They said: A fasting man. He said: (It is not righteousness to fast while travelling).(1)

When you read the Qur'anic text, you find it says: (Whoever of you is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days). That is, the mere existence of travel requires breaking the fast and making up in other days. The meaning of that is that God does not accept your fasting. It is true that He, glory be to Him, did not say to you: (Break your fast); but the mere fact that you are ill with a temporary illness or are travelling, you are obligated to fast a number of other days, and you would not legislate that for yourself.

And in the Messenger of Allah we have a good example, for he forbade fasting on the day of Eid al-Fitr, because Eid al-Fitr was so named because it achieves the joy of sharing in the end of the fast and passing the test; so fasting on it is not valid, and fasting on the first days of the Eid is a sin; but fasting on the second day of the Eid is permissible, according to the hadith narrated from Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (forbade fasting two days: the day of Fitr and the day of Adha).(2)

Someone may say: but fasting in Ramadan differs from fasting on other days, because Ramadan is the month in which the Qur'an was revealed. I say: it is the fast that is honoured by its coming in the month of the Qur'an. Moreover, He who sent down the Qur'an and prescribed fasting in Ramadan is the One, glory be to Him, who granted the concession of breaking the fast to the sick or the traveller and transferred it to other days outside Ramadan; and He, glory be to Him, is not incapable of bestowing upon the other days the same divine manifestations of attributes that He bestows upon the fasting servant in Ramadan. When the Truth, glory be to Him, legislated fasting in Ramadan, He only intended to spread the narrow time of Ramadan throughout the broad time, which is the course of the year. We fast Ramadan in summer, we fast it in winter, in autumn and in spring; so Ramadan passes through the whole year.

The Truth says: (And for those who are able to fast [yutiqunahu], a ransom of feeding a poor person). The word tawq means capacity, so (yutiqunahu) means it falls within their capacity and their ability; and the ransom is feeding a poor person.

A person may ask: how can a person love fasting and then be permitted to break it in exchange for a ransom of feeding a poor person? I say: this verse shows that the obligation of fasting came gradually, just as the Truth proceeded gradually in the matter of inheritance, first making it a matter of bequest, then transferring it to what is fixed by inheritance. Likewise God willed to bring the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) out of the circle of not fasting, into fasting in which they are given a choice, because they used not to fast; then after that came the command of fasting in which there is no choice. So fasting was first prescribed as optional, and after the Muslims became accustomed to and familiar with fasting, the true word came: (So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it). In this verse the Truth does not mention the ransom or anything else. Therefore, the obligation of fasting was at first optional by His saying: (And for those who are able to fast, a ransom of feeding a poor person); then came the progressive decision, and fasting became an obligation of a fixed duration, namely the month of Ramadan: (The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down, a guidance for mankind and clear proofs of guidance and the Criterion; so whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it). With that, the matter of the ransom ended for those who are able to fast. As for the one who is not able at all, by being ill or elderly, if Muslim physicians say that this is an illness (from which recovery is not expected), we say to him: you will not fast other days, and you must pay the ransom.

The legislation of fasting came gradually, like many legislations that concern moving the obligated from the familiarity of customs, such as wine, gambling and inheritance for example, and these are matters in which God willed gradualness. Someone says: since the obligation of fasting was optional, why did the Truth say after the discussion of the ransom: (And whoever volunteers good, it is better for him)?

I say: when fasting was optional, it was also necessary to open the door of goodness and striving in it; so whoever fasts and feeds a poor person, this is an accepted matter from him, and whoever fasts and feeds two poor people, that is more acceptable. Whoever comes to God without reckoning, God gives him without reckoning, and whoever comes to God with reckoning, the Truth gives him with reckoning. The word of the Truth: (And that you fast is better for you) is a step on the path toward confirming the obligation of fasting; and that obligation was confirmed by His saying: (So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it). It did not come in this verse as His saying: (And that you fast is better for you), because the matter had moved from choice to obligation.

Thus fasting is a method for the education of the human being, and it existed before God sent our master, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the Messenger (ﷺ) came, fasting was introduced to the Muslims as optional at first, then became an obligation after that. God legislated fasting in Islam at first for a number of specified days, then explained the specified days as the month of Ramadan.

What my heart is content with is that God began the legislation of fasting with specified days: three days of every month, namely the tenth, the twentieth and the thirtieth days of the month; these were the specified days in which God legislated that we fast. In those specified days the person had a choice: if he was able to fast, he could fast or pay the ransom. But when God legislated fasting in Ramadan, fasting became an obligation of worship and a pillar of the pillars of Islam; and after that the exception for the sick and the traveller came to us.

So we may observe that fasting in Islam passed through two stages. The first stage: God, glory be to Him and exalted, legislated the fasting of specified days, and we have explained its rulings. The second stage is the legislation of fasting in a limited period: the month of Ramadan. As for the scholars who held that it is permissible for the sick and the traveller to break the fast, because they did not wish to reject God's wisdom in legislation, I say to them: when the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, grants a concession, there must be a wisdom in it higher than the level of our thinking; and what confirms this is that the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, said: (Whoever of you is ill or on a journey).

The ruling here is fasting a number of other days; He did not say: whoever breaks the fast, then for him a number of other days. That is, the fasting of the sick and the traveller has been transferred to the time of residence after the journey and the recovery from illness. As for those among the scholars who said it is a concession: if a person wishes he may do it, and if he wishes he may leave it, then one must supply in the Qur'anic text (whoever of you is ill or on a journey), and he breaks the fast, (then a number of other days). We say: what does not need interpretation in the text takes priority in understanding over what needs interpretation; and let our manner of expression not be the manner of taste but the manner of obedience, for obedience is above manners.

So those who say this do not notice that God wants to lighten things for us. Then what prevents us from understanding that the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, willed for the sick and the traveller a clear concession, so He made the fasting of either of them a number of other days? So if he fasts in Ramadan while ill or on a journey, he has no fast; that is, his fasting is not counted and is not accepted from him. This is what I am content with; but we must take into account that what is meant by illness and journey here is that which takes the whole of a person's faculties out of their soundness.

And what is the meaning of the word (month, shahr) which came in His saying: (So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it)? The word (shahr) is derived from announcing and making manifest. We still use it in transactions, for example we say: we have registered the sale in the (land registry, al-shahr al-'aqari), that is, we make known the registry that a transaction exists, lest after that another transaction be placed over a transaction. So the word (shahr) means announcing and making manifest; and the time period was called (shahr) why? Because it has a sign that makes it manifest. We know that we cannot know the month through the sun; the sun is a mark for determining the day, for the day is from the sunrise to another sunrise, and it has a night and a day.

But the sun has no superficial, apparent, clear distinguishing sign that determines for us the beginning of the month; rather, the moon is what determines that sign and mark, through the crescent that appears at the beginning of the month and shows itself like the old date-stalk. So the crescent came to distinguish the month, and the sun to distinguish the day, and we need both of them together in determining time.

The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, links the acts of worship to apparent cosmic signs, which is the crescent; and after that we take from the sun the day alone, because the crescent does not give you the day. It is as though the appearance of the crescent in a particular form happens after the dark phase has come and ended. The birth of the crescent is the beginning of announcement, proclamation and making manifest that the month has begun; for this reason acts of worship begin from the first night of Ramadan, because the sign, the crescent, is linked to the night. We look for the crescent at sunset, and if we see it, the month of Ramadan has begun. This matter has not differed, because the day does not precede the night, except in one act of worship, which is standing at Arafat; the night that comes after it is attached to the day of Arafat.

The word (Ramadan) is derived from the root r-m-d, all of whose meanings indicate heat and intense heat. (Ramida al-insan) means the inside of a person became hot from severe thirst; (al-ramda') means hot sand; and when it is said (ramidat al-mashiyah), it means the heat struck its hoof so that it could no longer bear to place its foot on the ground. So Ramadan is derived from heat and intense heat, as though when people wished to give names to the months, the naming came...

1 Narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Fasting.
2 Narrated by Muslim.

And since you have tasted the sweetness of the purifying illuminations that the Truth has bestowed upon you in fasting, you will turn toward thanking Him, glory be to Him. This fits that the Truth should respond to you, saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾. We notice that ( إذا ) (idha, "when") came, and ( إن ) (in, "if") did not. The Truth assures you that after you experience this sweetness, you will give thanks to God, because He, glory be to Him, says in the Hadith Qudsi (a sacred hadith, in which the Prophet relates words of God in his own phrasing): "Three whose supplication is not rejected: the fasting person until he breaks his fast, the just ruler, and the supplication of the wronged one. God raises it above the clouds, the gates of heaven are opened for it, and the Lord says: By My might, I will surely help you, even if after a while."(1)

Since God will answer the supplication, and you may be one of the common people with no leadership role, and you are not wronged, then the supplication of the fasting person remains. When you read the word ( سأل ) (sa'ala, "to ask") in the Book of God, you will find that the root of asking in the Qur'an always comes with ( قل ) (qul, "say") in its answer.

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin﴾ (part of verse 219, Surat al-Baqara).

And His saying:

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: The surplus﴾ (part of verse 219, Surat al-Baqara). And His saying:

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend﴾ (part of verse 215, Surat al-Baqara).

Every ( يسألونك ) (yas'alunaka, "they ask you") is followed in its answer by ( قل ), except one verse in which ( فقل ) (fa-qul, "so say") comes with the fa, and that is the Truth's saying:

﴿And they ask you about the mountains. So say: My Lord will blow them away﴾ (part of verse 105, Surat Ta-Ha).

Observe the precision of expression: the first is ( قل ), and this one is ( فقل ). It is as though ( يسألونك عن الخمر والميسر ) (they ask you about wine and gambling) confirms that the asking has already occurred. But His saying ( يسألونك عن الجبال ) (they ask you about the mountains) concerns a question that is yet to come. So it is as though God answered questions that had already occurred, saying ( قل ), while the question that would come afterward was answered with ( فقل ), meaning He gave an answer in advance. Thus there is a difference between an answer to a question that has happened and an answer to a question that will happen, to show you that no one will ever surprise God with a question.

But now we are facing a verse in which a question came and the answer was direct: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me﴾. He did not say ( فقل ) "so say, indeed I am near," because His saying ( قل ) is a process that lengthens nearness. God wants nearness to be in the answer to the question without an intermediary: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾. He made the answer from Him directly to His servants, even though the one who conveys the answer is His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace. There is a story about this: they asked the Messenger of God, "Is your Lord near so that we may whisper to Him, or far so that we must call out to Him?"

Because the custom of the distant is to call out, while the near is addressed in intimate conversation. In order to show them nearness, the word ( قل ) was omitted, so the Truth's saying came: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾. What is the benefit of that nearness? The Truth says: ﴿I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me﴾. But what are the conditions required for this?

The Truth said: ﴿And when My servants ask you﴾. We know that there is a difference between ( عبيد ) ('abid, "slaves") and ( عباد ) ('ibad, "servants"). It is true that the singular of each is ( عبد ) ('abd), but there are ( عبيد ) and ( عباد ), and everyone on earth is a slave of God, but not everyone on earth is a servant of God. Why?

Because slaves are those who are subdued in existence like everything else by things, and there are those who choose to rebel against the Truth. They took their choice as rebellion. But servants are those who chose to submit to God in all matters. They submit together with everyone in that no one controls when he is born, when he dies, or how he comes into existence. But servants are distinguished by the fact that in the matter where God gave them choice, they say: "True, O Lord, You have given us choice, and we have chosen Your method, and we did not leave our desire to govern us. You, glory be to You, said: 'Do such-and-such' and 'Do not do such-and-such,' and we have accepted the obligation from You, O Lord."

Your Lord does not say to you "Do" unless you are capable of doing and of not doing. And He does not say to you "Do not" unless you are capable of both. Thus the words "Do" and "Do not" enter into matters of choice. The Truth has said "Do" and "Do not," then He left things about which He does not say to you "Do" or "Do not," so you are free to do them or not do them. Its name is (the zone of permissible choice). So there is a choice that is bound by obligation through "Do" and "Do not," and a choice that remains for you to do or not do, with no harm resulting from it. Whoever takes the choice and says: "O Lord, You granted me choice, but I leave to You, O Giver of choice, to direct this choice as You wish. I will relinquish my choice, and whatever You tell me, 'Do,' I will do, and whatever You tell me, 'Do not do it,' I will not do."

So the servants are those who took the zone of choice and handed it over to the One who created choice in them, and they said to God: "Even though You have made me one who chooses, I have entrusted myself to You." The servants are those who returned the matter of choice to the One who granted choice, and the Truth describes them with His saying:

﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace." And those who spend the night before their Lord in prostration and standing﴾ (Surat al-Furqan, 63-64).

These are the servants of the Most Merciful. Therefore the Truth says to Satan concerning them: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ (part of verse 42, Surat al-Hijr).

So Satan has authority over slaves in general, because he enters upon them through the door of choice. The word ( عبادي ) (my servants) was not used for anyone other than these, except when the Hour is established, when the Truth will call to account those who led the servants astray, saying:

﴿Did you lead My servants astray?﴾ (part of verse 17, Surat al-Furqan).

At the moment the Hour is established, choice no longer exists, and all become servants; even the disbelievers no longer have choice. When the Truth says: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me﴾, then the servants who are bound to God by the method of faith will not ask God except for something that does not conflict with faith and its obligations.

And the Truth says: ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾, because supplication seeks an answer. And since you seek the answer to supplication, then show good manners toward your Lord. He, glory be to Him, has called you to His method, so respond to Him if you want God to respond to you (﴿So let them respond to Me﴾). After that, the Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, speaks of the word ( الداع ) (al-da'i, "the caller") and does not leave it unrestricted, so He says: ﴿when he calls Me﴾. It is as though the word ( دعا ) (da'a, "to call") comes and a person calls with it, and perhaps he directs the supplication to one who is not able to answer. An example of this is the Truth's saying:

﴿Indeed, those you invoke besides God are servants like you﴾ (part of verse 194, Surat al-A'raf).

And the Truth's saying:

﴿If you call them, they will not hear your call﴾ (part of verse 14, Surat Fatir).

It is as though the caller may take on a quality by which he calls upon one not qualified to answer. Here the Truth said: ﴿I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me﴾. But if he goes and calls upon one who is unable to fulfill it, then God is not responsible for answering his supplication. The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, wants to teach us that a person calls for good for himself, and you cannot determine that good, because you may look at something as good when it is evil. As long as you are supplicating, you think that this is good. So the essential point in supplication is that you love good, but you may err in the path to understanding good or the means to good. You love good without dispute, so your Lord's answer to your supplication may be to withhold the answer to your call if it does not coincide with good for you. Therefore you should not understand that when your supplication is not answered as you hoped and asked, God has not responded to you, and you say: "Why has God not responded to me?" No, He has responded to you, but He has removed from you the folly of the supplication or what you do not know to be evil for you. The One you call upon is wise, so He says: "I will give you good, and the good that I know is above the good that you know. Therefore it is better for you not to be answered in this request."

Let me give this example, and to God belongs the highest likeness: your young son may ask you to buy him a pistol, and he thinks the matter of the pistol is good. But you delay his request and say: "Later I will buy you the pistol, God willing," and you procrastinate and do not bring him the pistol. Is your not bringing him the pistol, according to what he saw, a withholding of good from him? Your withholding the pistol from him contains benefit, protection, and good for the son.

So good is always in proportion to wisdom in handling matters, and you withhold the pistol from your son because you have judged that he is a child who plays with his companions, who may encounter things that take him beyond himself, who may cause someone harm, and who may harm someone with such a pistol.

Likewise, your share of supplication may be that it is not answered, because answering it might harm you. The Truth, glory be to Him and exalted, says:

﴿And man invokes evil as he invokes good, and man is ever hasty﴾ (verse 11, Surat al-Isra').

Therefore He, glory be to Him, says:

﴿I will show you My signs, so do not seek to hasten them﴾ (verse 37, Surat al-Anbiya').

The scholars say: if you intend by supplication humility and servitude, it is beautiful, but the answer is the will of God, and if you measure your share of supplication by its answer, then you are not appreciating the matter. Your share of supplication is worship and humility before God, because you only supplicate when you believe that your means as a human are not able to achieve this, so you asked the One who is able, and you asked the One who possesses. Therefore God says in a Hadith Qudsi: "Whoever is preoccupied with remembering Me instead of asking Me, I will give him better than what I give to those who ask."(2)

Let us learn what the Messenger of God taught 'A'isha, Mother of the Believers. She asked the Messenger of God: if I happen to encounter the Night of Power, what should I supplicate? She said: "If this night reaches me, what should I supplicate?"

Look at the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace: he taught the Mother of the Believers 'A'isha to supplicate with the broad measure of good, so he said to her: "Say: O God, You love pardon, so pardon me."(3)

There is no beauty finer than pardon, and no good finer than pardon. So I do not say "Give me, give me," because this may apply to the Truth's saying: ﴿And man invokes evil as he invokes good, and man is ever hasty﴾ (verse 11, Surat al-Isra').

So whoever says: "I supplicated my Lord and He did not answer me," we say to him: Do not be lacking in understanding. It is better for you that you are not answered in what you requested, for God gives you good at the time He wills.

After that, the Truth leaves some matters of existence in society to respond to you with something, then the evil in it becomes clear to you, so that you know that withholding its answer from you was the very good. Therefore supplication has conditions. The Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, calls us to good provision. For in the noble hadith from Abu Hurayra there is his saying: "Then he mentioned a man who travels far, disheveled and dusty, who raises his hands to the sky, saying: O Lord, O Lord, while his food is unlawful, his drink is unlawful, his clothing is unlawful, and he is nourished by the unlawful. How could he be answered?"(4) The Messenger reveals before us how the instrument of the one who supplicates becomes corrupted. Therefore, the non-answering of supplication is either because the instrument of supplication is corrupted, or because you supplicated for something you thought was good for you, but God knows that it is not so, and so He takes you by the hand to the sphere of His wisdom and withholds from you the matter that carries evil for you.

And there is another thing: He may withhold the answer from you, because if He gave you what you love, He would have given you the good of the transient world, and He loves you, so He keeps the answer for you until the good of the enduring. These are elevations that only the elect attain. And there are other elevations, represented in that as long as supplication contains humility and submission, God may apply to you what came in the Hadith Qudsi: "God descends to the lowest heaven and says: Who calls upon Me, that I may answer him, or asks Me, that I may give to him? Then He says: Who lends to one who is neither poor nor unjust?"(5)

And because a person is attached to matters he loves, as long as they have not come, he keeps saying "O Lord." This supplication, God loves to hear from such a servant, so He says: "Indeed, among My servants are those whose supplication I love, so I test them so that they will say: O Lord." The believing person does not make his share of supplication that it be answered; rather, his share of supplication is what the Truth said:

﴿Say: My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication﴾ (part of verse 77, Surat al-Furqan).

Indeed, the meaning of lordship and being nurtured is that you always say: "O Lord." And let me give this example, and to God belongs the highest likeness: a father may give his son a monthly allowance, and the son takes the monthly allowance and disappears all month long
