He, glorified is He, wants of you not merely to perform Hajj, but He wants you to complete it and make it complete, fulfilling all the requirements of the Legislator for it. When the Truth says: (And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah), someone may say: Hajj is one thing and 'Umrah is another thing, as evidenced by joining it to it with a conjunction, and conjunction ('atf) requires difference just as it requires sharing. If sharing is found but difference is not found, then the conjunction is not valid; rather there must be both a common element and a distinct element. The sharing between Hajj and 'Umrah is that both are rites (nusuk) and acts of worship, and the difference is that Hajj has a specific time and requires standing at 'Arafah, while 'Umrah has no fixed time and no standing at 'Arafah. But the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says regarding the legislation of Hajj:

﴿And [due] to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House - for whoever is able to find thereto a way﴾ (part of verse 97, surah Al 'Imran).

In that verse there is no mention of 'Umrah, and from this we know that Hajj is one thing and 'Umrah is another thing, and what is obligatory upon us is Hajj. Therefore I always say that we must take the Qur'an as a single whole, and bring together all the verses related to the subject so that we understand the intended meaning completely. When the Truth says in His Qur'an also: (And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah), we know from that that 'Umrah is other than Hajj. And when you read Allah's saying in Surah Bara'ah:

﴿And an announcement from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater Hajj﴾ (part of verse 3, surah al-Tawbah).

we know that there is a greater Hajj and a lesser great Hajj. Therefore the verse (And [due] to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House) came with the Sacred House, which is the common element of Hajj and 'Umrah. We know that the greater Hajj is the Hajj in which the Muslim stands at 'Arafah, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hajj is 'Arafah" (1). And it is the greater Hajj, because the gathering at 'Arafah is great, and it occurs at a specific time and requires standing at 'Arafah.

So the saying of the Exalted: (And [due] to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House): Hajj is the intention to a venerated thing, which is (the House), whereas 'Umrah is the lesser pilgrimage, and its time is common throughout the year, and those who intend the House are spread throughout the whole year. This has been established by the legislation in His saying, glorified is He: (And [due] to Allah from the people is pilgrimage to the House). Since He came with the shared command in His saying "pilgrimage to the House," He intends both the greater Hajj and the lesser great Hajj.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, addresses His servants, and knows that some people will approach acts of worship in a merely formal way, and some may approach worship for purposes other than worship. So it was necessary to clarify the intention behind Hajj and 'Umrah, and that what is required is completing them, and that the intention must be for Allah and not for anything else: not so that it may be said "the pilgrim so-and-so," or so that one may buy cheap goods and sell them for more than their price after returning.

We know that Hajj is the only act of worship whose title remains attached to its doer; for example, one does not say "the one who prays so-and-so" or "the one who gives zakat so-and-so." So if the pilgrim is keen on this title, and it is his motive behind his worship, then he must not depart from the purpose for which the worship was legislated. The Truth says: (And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah). And the word (for Allah) serves us in multiple matters. What are these matters?

When a Muslim wishes to perform Hajj for Allah, it is not valid for him to perform it except with money whose means Allah has legislated. Many people, when they hear the noble hadith:

("Whoever performs Hajj and does not commit obscenity or transgression returns as on the day his mother bore him") (2).

believe that a person may commit whatever sins and wrongs he wishes, then think that one Hajj will remove all his sins. We say to these: First: the Hajj must be for Allah.

Second: it must be from lawful wealth. And since it is for Allah and from lawful wealth, you must know which sins are dropped after Hajj. Not all sins are dropped; rather, the sins related to Allah, the Exalted, are what is dropped, because a sin against Allah is one by which you have not wronged Allah but wronged yourself. But a sin related to people involves harming them or diminishing their rights, and therefore the wronging of servants is not dropped except by restoring the servants' rights.

We know that 'Umrah is the intention to the Sacred House at any time of the year, and Hajj is the intention to the House at a specific time of the year. Some scholars say: this is one obligation and that is another obligation; is it permissible to perform both together, or must each obligation be performed separately?

Some of them addressed the points of merit and excellence. The one who says that performing Hajj alone (ifrad) is better, does so because he dedicated each rite to a separate journey. And the one who says one performs both together, and enters ihram for Hajj and 'Umrah together with a single ihram, goes first and performs the 'Umrah rite, then remains in his ihram until he sets out for Hajj; in this case he has combined the two together (qiran), i.e., performed both with one ihram, and this is what some scholars prefer, because Allah knows that the servant has performed two rites with one ihram. And there is the person who performs tamattu', i.e., performs 'Umrah, then exits from it (tahallul), and afterwards comes before Hajj to enter ihram for Hajj; this is called tamattu', and he is a tamattu' because he has exited from ihram. Some scholars say tamattu' is better because it separates two matters by something that takes it out of the habitual: he entered ihram, then exited, then entered ihram again.

So every scholar has a point of consideration. It is as if Allah does not want to constrict His creation in performing a rite in any of its forms. The Legislator, glorified and exalted is He, has been cautious in imposing obligations, and has respected all circumstances, whether those circumstances may befall without a contender, which are decrees of destiny (qadariyyat), or befall from a contender, which have other causes. So He said: (But if you are prevented, then [offer] whatever sacrifice is feasible).

"Uhsirtum" means you are prevented. There is "hasr," which concerns decrees of destiny, and there is "uhsira," which occurs by the act of an agent, such as the intervention of an enemy, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was besieged in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and it was said to him: do not enter Makkah this year. Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, lightens the burden for us, as if He says to us: I do not waste the preparation of the servants, nor their intention, nor their readiness, nor their ihram; so if they are prevented, then (whatever sacrifice is feasible). The sacrifice (hady) is what is slaughtered seeking nearness to Allah, and an expiation for what has occurred.

Then He says: (And do not shave your heads until the sacrifice has reached its place), i.e., until it reaches the place designated for it. This applies if you are the one driving the sacrifice; but if you are not the one driving the sacrifice, it is not necessary for you to slaughter it, and it suffices that you assign someone to slaughter it for you. And the saying of the Truth: (Then whoever enjoys [the benefit of] 'Umrah until Hajj [must offer] what sacrifice is feasible) means that it is valid for a person to slaughter the sacrifice before 'Arafah, it is valid to delay it until the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), and it is valid to slaughter it after all that.

(What sacrifice is feasible) also means, if obtaining the sacrifice is easy, whether because its price is easy to pay or because it is easy to buy, for the prices may be available while the thing priced is not. (Hady) is what is brought to the Sacred Area (haram), or what guides a person to the path of rectitude. The meaning is derived from hady, which is the goal that leads to the desired end.

And His saying, exalted is He: } And do not shave your heads until the sacrifice has reached its place, and whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head {. The sick person who cannot slaughter the sacrifice and has an ailment of the head is like the Companion who had lice on his head, which caused him pain, and the Messenger of Allah said to him: "Shave your head and fast three days, or feed six poor persons, or sacrifice a sheep" (3).

These are successive legislations, and each legislation has an occasion. Just as there was legislated for one who is prevented what is feasible of the sacrifice, so too was legislated for one who shaves his head due to illness or has an ailment of the head: three things were prescribed: fasting, or charity, or sacrifice.

One who reflects on these three things finds that they are arranged in ascending order. Fasting is an act whose direct benefit does not extend to others; charity is an act of worship whose benefit extends to others, but to a limited degree, since it is feeding six individuals for example; and sacrifice is a slaughtered animal, whose meat benefits a large number of people.

Observe the ascent in benefit: either fasting three days, or feeding six poor persons, or slaughtering an animal, namely a sheep. This is an escalation from the weaker to the stronger, each according to his capacity and ability.

When the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, legislates specific expiations, that is in consideration of the procedures required in Hajj and suitable to the circumstances and condition of the Muslim. So He permitted him, in the case of tamattu' for example, to divide the fasting into two stages: three days during Hajj and seven when you return. It is the ascent in legislations, and a choice of what is easier, which allows the believer to escape the predicament he is in.

(And whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [must compensate] with a ransom of fasting or charity or sacrifice. And when you are safe, whoever enjoys [the benefit of] 'Umrah until Hajj [must offer] what sacrifice is feasible. But whoever does not find [an animal], then fast three days during Hajj and seven when you return.)

The phrase (whoever does not find) means he does not possess it. To this one who does not possess it we say: do not do as many people do before they perform the circumambulation: some of them go to the market and buy the offerings, and then when the obligation of the sacrifice falls upon him he says: I do not have it, so I will fast. Here we say to him: Was not the price of those offerings sufficient to buy the sacrifice?

It is truly strange that you find a pilgrim buying countless gifts, watches and electrical appliances, and filling his suitcases, then says: I cannot find what to buy the sacrifice with. Is that not deception and fraud? Whoever does that deceives himself.

So the saying of the Exalted: (whoever does not find) means he does not find in truth, not one whose wealth is spent on gifts, and then he becomes empty-handed. Therefore those who perform the rite well do not buy their offerings except after completing what is required of the rite, and if money remains with them, they buy according to what they have.

As for those who spend their money on buying gifts and then come at (what sacrifice is feasible) and say: we do not have the price of the sacrifice, so we will fast, the strange thing is that they remember fasting only upon their return. Would it not have been better for one of them to fast from the beginning, from the moment he knows he does not possess the price of the sacrifice and enters ihram for 'Umrah?

It is required that he begin fasting the three days, so that his excuse is in advance and not after the fact. Some scholars permitted fasting the days of tashriq, and the three days of tashriq are those following the day of Eid, because they used to (dry the meat in the sun) (yushriquna al-lahm), that is, spread it out in the sun to dry and become jerky. Then, when he finishes performing the rites, he may either fast the seven days on the road while returning, or when he reaches his dwelling; he may choose what suits him: (whoever does not find, then fast three days during Hajj and seven when you return; that is ten complete). It is known that three and seven equal ten, and [He said "complete"] so that people do not think that what is intended is either three days or seven days, and therefore He said: (ten complete), so that understanding is not confused.

And perhaps the Truth, glorified...

1 Narrated by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.
2 Narrated by al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ahmad from Abu Hurairah.
3 Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

The Almighty then says:

﴿The Hajj is in well-known months. So whoever undertakes the Hajj therein, there shall be no sexual relations, no wickedness, and no disputing during the Hajj. And whatever good you do, Allah knows it. And take provisions, but the best provision is piety. So fear Me, O people of understanding.﴾ [2:197]

We may observe that the Almighty, when speaking of fasting, said: (The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was revealed), and He did not mention the months of the Hajj—Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah—as He mentioned Ramadan. This is because legislation concerning Ramadan is specific to it, so its time must be specified. But the Hajj was known among the Arabs before Islam, and they knew its months and everything about it; so the matter does not need the names of its specific months to be mentioned. The well-known months are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, which end with the Standing at 'Arafat and the days of Mina. The month of the Hajj does not occupy more than ten days of it, yet He included it with Shawwal and Dhu al-Qa'dah, because part of a month is counted as the whole month. The word (ma'lumat, well-known) gives us the wisdom behind not mentioning the names of the months of the Hajj, since they were known to them.

(Fa-man faraḍa fīhinna al-ḥajj). Obligation (farḍ) does not come from the person; rather, the obligation comes from Allah, who prescribed the Hajj as a pillar. If you bind yourself to it by intention and action, and you begin and intend the Hajj in its specific time, you have made the Hajj obligatory upon yourself for this season that you choose, and it becomes binding upon you. His saying, glorified be He: (faraḍa) indicates that you commit yourself to the Hajj, even if it is recommended (mandūb), i.e., not obligatory.

(Fa-man faraḍa fīhinna al-ḥajj, fa-lā rafath wa-lā fusūq wa-lā jidāl fī al-ḥajj). Rafath (sexual talk) pertains to the tongue, to the eye, and to the other limbs. All of them converge on the act of intercourse and its preliminaries: the tongue's rafath during the Hajj is to mention the matter of intercourse, and the eye's rafath is to look at a woman with desire. So rafath is everything that serves as a prelude to intercourse, or is intercourse itself, or what is connected to it, by word, by glance, or by deed.

Although rafath is permitted outside the Hajj, it is forbidden during the Hajj. As for fusūq (wickedness), it is forbidden both during the Hajj and outside it. It is as if Allah is alerting that, although it may be permissible for a Muslim to commit wickedness outside the Hajj, it is not proper for a Muslim to be in the House of Allah and commit such wickedness. Wickedness is forbidden at all times, and the Almighty here alerts the one who has been excessive against himself: he should remember that if he has sinned far from the House of Allah, he should be ashamed to disobey Allah within the House of Allah. For the one who goes to the House of Allah seeks to expiate his sins; so is it reasonable that he commit sins there? You must feel shame, O Muslim, while you are in the House of Allah. And know that this place is the only place where one is held accountable for mere intention.

And Allah, mighty and majestic, says:

﴿And whoever intends therein deviation through wrongdoing—We will make him taste of a painful punishment.﴾ (part of 22:25)

So rafath is permissible in some places, but it is forbidden in the Sacred House; and wickedness is prohibited at all times, and its prohibition is more severe in the Sacred House.

Disputing, although permitted outside the Hajj, is not valid during the Hajj. We should know that the rank of disputing is below the rank of wickedness and below the rank of disobedience. The Messenger said: (Whoever performs the Hajj and does not commit rafath or fusūq returns as on the day his mother bore him) (1). He did not say "and does not dispute." The humanity of the Messenger takes into account the circumstances of the Muslims; it is likely that disputing may arise from a pilgrim as a result of provocation, so the omission of mention of disputing in the hadith is a concession for the believer, but it is not valid to go to excess in it. Disputing is possible outside the Hajj, as evidenced by:

﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ (part of 16:125).

Rather, there is no disputing in the Hajj. Disputing is when each of the two parties twists against the other to encircle him with argument. Then look at the Almighty's consideration of human circumstances and human feelings, and His acknowledgment of them, and His legislating for a reality that is acknowledged: the Hajj takes a person out of his homeland, out of the place of his family, out of his wealth, and out of what he has become accustomed to in life. When a person goes out in this way, people's tempers may become strained, because they all live an unnatural life. There is someone who sleeps in a shared room with people he does not know, and there is a family that sleeps in a shared apartment with only one restroom, and it is possible that someone may want to relieve himself at the time another person wishes to relieve himself. When this matter occurs, a person has no opinion, and for this reason it is said: (No opinion for one who is urgently in need [haqin]), meaning no opinion for one who is confined—that is, for one who wants to relieve himself of urine. The same applies to the haqib, who is the one who holds back his feces, because it is a matter that disturbs a person's balance.

So life during the Hajj is unnatural, and the circumstances of people are unnatural. Therefore the Almighty warns us against entering into disputation, because perhaps the strain from changing one's way of life becomes a cause of mistreating others. The Almighty wants to prevent this strain from affecting our relationships with others. Experience has proven that those who go for the Hajj as a group either return extremely fond of one another, or as bitter enemies.

Therefore the Almighty asks us to be patient with whatever customs of others one sees during the Hajj, and to count his departure from his habits, from the monotony of his affairs, and from his familiarity with his family, counting that before Allah, and to occupy himself with intimacy with Allah, and to bear everything on his side; and it suffices that he is in the House of Allah and in His hospitality.

The Almighty, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it; and take provisions.﴾ Having forbidden us by His saying: ﴿So there shall be no rafath, no fusūq, and no jidāl during the Hajj﴾, which are negative matters—actions from which a person must refrain—here the Almighty follows the negative actions with the command to positive actions, the acts of good that Allah knows. Allah wants us to combine two things in worship: negation and affirmation—negation of what He mentioned concerning rafath, fusūq, and jidāl, and He wants us to affirm and bring into being an action. ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it.﴾ And what is that good? It is the matters opposite to the things prohibited. So if a person does not engage in rafath during the Hajj, it is required of him to be chaste in his speech, in his glance, in his manner, and in his relationship with his wife who is lawful to him; so he refrains from her as long as he is in the state of ihram, and he is asked to do what corresponds to fusūq, of righteousness and goodness.

Regarding disputing, we find that its opposite is speech with gentleness, courtesy, softness, sweetness of expression, and compassion toward people. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it.﴾ And the word "min" in His saying (min khayr, "of good") is for beginning: it is as if Allah, glorified and exalted, wants you to do good, and He sees even the least of good; therefore He said: ﴿Allah knows it.﴾ It is as though it is a good that no one sees; for apparent good is seen by all people, and the expression "Allah knows it" means that whatever good is small, and whatever it is little, Allah knows it. Much good is mere inner intention, and Allah rewards good with the reward that befits it.

The word of the Truth: ﴿And take provisions (wa-tazawwadū)﴾. Zād (provision) is what the traveler takes in order to strengthen himself for his journey. This was a familiar matter among the Arabs of old, because the place they went to had no food. All these conditions have now changed, and the customs of the people who used to go there have changed too. People in the past went to the Hajj with their shrouds, with the salt for their food, with thread and needle; for there was not in Mecca and Medina what would suffice the people. Now people go there to bring the luxuries of life, and you no longer find it strange that so-and-so came back from the Hajj with such-and-such. It is as if the Almighty made all of that a sign that He had foretold long ago, on the day when the valley had no vegetation, when He said:

﴿To which are brought the fruits of every thing…﴾ (28:57).

Look at the precision of the Qur'anic expression in His saying: (yujbā), which means "is taken by force," not by the choice of the one who carries it. It is as if whoever carries fruits of every color there is compelled to carry them, and it is a provision from Allah, not from human hands.

This confirms His saying:

﴿And provide for them of the fruits…﴾ (14:37).

And the Truth's word: (wa-tazawwadū), derived, as we have known, from "increase" (ziyādah). Zād is the food of the traveler, and whoever stores something for a journey has a surplus beyond what his residence consumes, and he takes it so that it spares him the burden of asking, or of looking forward to asking; for the Hajj is a humbling of servitude, and the humility of servitude is what Allah wants for Himself alone. Whoever does not have the means for his journey may humble himself to another person and ask him for food, but Allah does not want the pilgrim to humble himself to anyone; therefore He asks him to take provision in an amount sufficient for his need, so that he suffices himself and his humility remains pure toward his Lord, so that he asks none but his Lord and does not look forward to asking creatures. Whoever asks or looks forward to asking has taken something of that humility which should, at this stage, be purely for Allah, and he directs it toward people, while Allah wants it for Himself, pure.

And if people do not give to the one who asks or looks forward to asking, he may steal or plunder the amount he needs, and his journey turns from seeking righteousness to evil. Some people of Yemen used to set out for the Hajj without provision and say: ("We rely upon God; shall we go to the House of God and it not feed us?"). Then circumstances compel them to steal, and this is the cause of plundering and theft during the Hajj. The pressure of hunger may push a person to plunder and steal to satisfy his need.

From here the Almighty wished to cut off this evil from the human soul, so He said: ﴿And take provisions.﴾ It is a command from Allah to take provision for this journey, in which a person is cut off from his wealth, his family, his loved ones, and his acquaintances. And He, glorified be He, says: ﴿But the best provision is piety.﴾ We know that provision is what protects you from hunger and thirst; and if provision is good for preserving your transient life, then what of the eternal life in which there is no end? Do you not need a greater provision? It is as if provision for the transient journey teaches you to take provision for the lasting journey.

So His saying: ﴿But the best provision is piety﴾ encompasses the provision of this world and the Hereafter. Allah, glorified and exalted, reminds us of tangible matters and moves us from them to matters of meaning; but if you look deeply, sincerely, and truthfully, you will find that matters of meaning are stronger than tangible matters. Therefore we observe in His saying, glorified and exalted:

﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts﴾ (part of 7:26).

This is a tangible matter. And He, glorified be He, adds to us (rīsh), i.e., He does not only cover the nakedness, but extends the matter to the adornments with which one beautifies oneself, and these adornments are the rīsh—that is, what a person adorns himself with. Then the Truth said:

﴿And the garment of piety—that is best﴾ (part of 7:26).

That is, I have favored you with clothing and adornment, but there is something better than them, which is (the garment of piety). If you believe that tangible clothing covers your nakedness and protects you from heat and cold, and you adorn yourself with its finery, understand that this is a tangible matter; but the better matter is the garment of piety. Why? Because the disgrace of the Hereafter is worse than the disgrace of this world.

So His saying: ﴿And take provisions, for the best provision is piety, and fear Me, O people of understanding﴾ means that the Truth wants you to take provision for the journey, a provision that keeps you from asking, from looking forward to asking, from plundering, or from seizing by force; and beware of entering into anything that Allah has forbidden. But your provisioning is within the circle of: (fear Me, O people of understanding), that is, O people of intellects. Allah does not call people's attention to the intellect they possess except that He wants them to make their intellects judge the matter, for He, majestic is His affair, wants you to judge with your intellect; so if you let your intellect judge the matter, the judgment of intellect will be on the side of the command of Allah.

1 Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 198:

Since God, Glorified and Exalted is He, in the vastness of His kindness and mercy, wishes in this sacred rite and blessed journey that people should cooperate, He permitted a group of pilgrims to take on the task of serving others, to facilitate matters for them. It is remarkable that those who serve the pilgrims are granted by God a dispensation in the Hajj to depart before others, because that is a necessary public interest. Suppose that people all refrained from serving one another: who then would attend to the interests of the people? It follows that there must be people whose portion is to work at serving the pilgrims. God, Exalted and Glorified is He, made this clear and explained it in His saying:

﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord. And when you depart from ʿArafat, remember God at the Sacred Monument (al-mashʿar al-ḥarām), and remember Him as He has guided you, though before that you were certainly among the astray.﴾ (2:198)

(There is no blame upon you) means: there is no sin upon you and no hardship. (That you seek bounty from your Lord) means: that you earn a livelihood during the Hajj, which is an act of worship, and the gain that comes through it is a bounty from God. In earlier times they used to say, in this word, (ḥājj) and (dājj), one with a ḥāʾ and one with a dāl. (The dājj) is the one who goes to the holy lands only for trade, and we say to him: there is no objection to your going to perform the Hajj and trading as well, because you will be facilitating a matter, for if we prohibited it, who would then attend to the affairs of the pilgrims?

Why did the Truth say (seek bounty from your Lord) and not say (provision, rizq)? God clarified in the verse before it: do not set out except with your provisions. So you do not, through this action of yours, seek provision; that is, you do not go to the Hajj in order to eat from trade. Rather, you go with your provision, and what you gain is in excess of your need and is a bounty from God, Exalted and Glorified is He. He, may His majesty be exalted, wants that there be no hardship in your permissible work; so He removed blame from it. You have come with your food and drink, and it suffices you to take a reasonable profit, so that there is no trace of injustice in it, such as exploiting the need of the pilgrims. For this reason He called it (bounty), meaning something in excess of need.

All seeking of provision and seeking of bounty must not escape the mind of the one who seeks provision and bounty: all of it is from God. Beware of saying: "the strength of means," and beware of saying: "intelligence or precaution"; none of that at all, for all provision is from God and is a bounty from God. There is no harm to you in seeking bounty from the Lord, for He is the Creator and the Nurturer, and we are His nurtured; so there is no shame in your seeking bounty from God.

Then the Truth says after that: (And when you depart from ʿArafat, remember God at the Sacred Monument). When you fill a cup to its brim, it overflows over its sides with the excess; so the overflowing (ifāḍa) means something that has separated from what is present because of surplus.

His saying (when you depart from ʿArafat) indicates that God has decreed that ʿArafat will be filled to capacity, and everyone who leaves it is as though overflowing beyond the number set for it. This is a decree from God in the Hajj. If you witness the scene that God has written for all Muslims, God willing you will see this matter: it is as though a vessel has filled and so it overflows. You do not know from where the pilgrims come nor to where they go. Whoever looks at those circling the House thinks they are a human mass, and likewise when the pilgrims pour out on the evening of the Day of ʿArafat, it seems to you when you look at them that there is no distinction between them; for this reason it is said: "the ravines of the tribe flowed over him like a torrent."

The poet said:

So the ravines of the tribe flowed over him when he called
his companions, with faces like dinars.

Another said:

When we had fulfilled from Mina every need,
and whoever was to wipe the corners had wiped them,
we took up the ends of conversations among us,
and the valleys flowed with the necks of the mounts.

That is, it was as though it were a rushing torrent; exactly thus is the ifāḍa from ʿArafat. When you contemplate the people heading toward (Muzdalifa), you wonder where all this crowd had been. You see the valleys in which people and vehicles move like a flood, and you cannot distinguish one person from a group; and at the station of the pilgrims there are two outpourings: an outpouring from ʿArafat, and then a second outpouring, which the following verse explains, when He, Glorified is He, says:

﴿Then pour out from where the people pour out, and ask God for forgiveness; indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ (2:199)

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 199:

We pronounce "Arafat" in two forms: sometimes we say ('Arafat) as it occurs in this verse, and sometimes we pronounce it ('Arafah), as in the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) saying: "Hajj is 'Arafah" (1). 'Arafat is plural, and 'Arafah is singular.

This word has become a proper noun for the vast place where the pilgrims gather on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah. Do not think that it is a mountain. When you hear "Mount 'Arafat," as people say, understand that what is meant is the plain attributed to 'Arafat, and not 'Arafat itself. For this reason you will find many people who think that if they do not climb the mountain called Jabal al-Rahmah, which is near the rocks on which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood during the Farewell Pilgrimage, then it is as if such a person has not performed Hajj. We say to them: No. The standing (wuquf) takes place in the valley, and the mountain adjacent to the valley we have named Mount 'Arafat. So the mountain is the one attributed to 'Arafat, and not the valley attributed to the mountain.

There are many opinions regarding the origin of the word 'Arafah. There is a difference between a name that is originally a descriptive term and then becomes a proper noun, and a name that is a proper noun from the very beginning. We have said: if you name something as a proper noun from the outset, it is not necessary that the word carry its literal meaning. You may name a wretched man "Sa'id" (happy), and name a black woman "Qamar" (moon). This is not called a descriptive name but a proper noun. However, when people name, they seek a good omen from the root meaning. It is said: "I name my son Sa'id, hoping he will be happy." When it is a daughter, you may give her a name contrary to her condition; she may be plain, and you name her "Jamilah" (beautiful), hoping for good omen from the name. Here the taking of a proper noun is for good omen. The Arabs, when they named names, sought good omen through them. For example, they would name (a boy) "Sakhr" (rock) so that they would be strong before enemies, and they would name a dog "Kalb" so that no one would dare against him.

It was said to an Arab: "You choose good names for your slaves, calling them 'Sa'id,' 'Sa'd,' and 'Fadl,' but you choose bad names for your sons; you call them 'Murrah' (bitter), 'Kalb' (dog), and 'Sakhr' (rock)." The Arab said: "Yes, because we name our sons for our enemies, so that they may be at their throats, and we name our slaves for ourselves." The word 'Arafah is now a proper noun for a place, but there is disagreement about the reason it was so named. It was said: because Adam descended in one place and Eve descended in another, and each kept searching for the other until they met at this place, so it was named 'Arafah.

Speaking of Adam and Eve requires us to investigate the reason for their separation, which made each of them search for the other. If Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created them to be spouses, why did He separate them? Imagine the state of Adam, created in a strange, vast world alone, looking around and finding no human like himself. By God, would he not long for a human being to dispel his loneliness?

And what would his state be when he sees a human? Without doubt, he would meet them with intense longing. For this reason Allah separated them and made each seek a person who would dispel his loneliness. Had each remained beside the other, the matter might have been ordinary. Thus Allah willed that each of Adam and Eve would long for the other, so He distanced them from each other, then they met after a long separation, and longing led to the meeting. After the meeting come affection, mercy, intimacy and tranquility, which is what is sought in life for a couple. There is another statement regarding the naming of 'Arafat: that the angels said to our master Adam while he was in that place: "Recognize your sin and repent to your Lord," and he said:

﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ (Qur'an 7:23)

Thus he recognized his slip and recognized how to repent. Or, when Allah willed to teach Ibrahim, peace be upon him, who had supplicated his Lord that He make the hearts of people incline and yearn toward this place. Ibrahim saw in a dream that he should slaughter his son. That was a difficult matter in three respects: the first difficulty is that it was a dream and not revelation; the second is that he was his only son; and the third is that he himself would be the one to slaughter him.

These are three harsh difficulties, and it is not reasonable that this matter passed over the father of the prophets easily or smoothly; rather he must have pondered it much within himself, asking whether it was a dream or something else. From here the day before the day of 'Arafah was called the Day of Tarwiyah (reflection/watering). When our master Ibrahim became certain that the dreams of prophets are true, he knew that he must carry out what he had seen. The place where he came to know the reality of the dream was called 'Arafah. Or, when the dream came to him of slaughtering his son, Satan did not let such an opportunity pass, and he had to enter to whisper to Ibrahim. Did he not say: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ (Qur'an 7:16)?

So when Satan appeared to Ibrahim, he stoned him with pebbles seven times the first time; then he came back to him another time and he stoned him seven times; and when he came to him a third time he stoned him seven times. After that he did not come to him again. Ibrahim ran, fearing that he would pursue him; and for this reason the place was called Muzdalifah, and the muzdalif is the one who hastens, and it is called "Dhu al-Majaz," meaning that he passed through Muzdalifah, and he would have understood the matter at 'Arafah.

Or, Jibril used to show him the rites in this place, saying to him: "Have you recognized?" and Ibrahim would reply: "I have recognized" ('araftu). Or, a person recognizes his Lord there at the end of what has been prescribed for him of the pillars: each of us recognized the pillars: this one recognized, that one recognized, a third, a fourth, and so on, so all of us become 'Arafat, and the place becomes servitude to Allah, shared by all the pilgrims.

(﴿So when you hasten from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram.﴾) The Mash'ar al-Haram is in Muzdalifah. "Remember Allah" means that Allah has facilitated for you this arduous journey, and brought you secure and intending the Sacred House of Allah, and then you return forgiven, and this is a matter that deserves that you remember Allah with thanks and gratitude.

(﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾), because His guidance of you and His teaching you is the shortest way to reach goodness, and it is a greeting from Allah to His creation, and a greeting must be returned; so as He guided you, remember Him. (﴿And indeed, before it, you were among the astray﴾), because they had performed Hajj many times in the Jahiliyyah, but you were performing Hajj in error, while now you perform it in guidance. (﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾).

His saying "Then" (thumma) indicates that standing at 'Arafah or spending the night at Muzdalifah is necessary, because "thumma" indicates sequence with slowness and deliberate following.

So His saying "Then depart" is evidence for those who say that spending the night at Muzdalifah is necessary. This verse was revealed because the Quraysh considered themselves the people of the Haram, so they were never subject to what other people were subject to, and therefore they did not go with the people to 'Arafat. Allah intends by Hajj equality among people, and for this the Prophet said in the Farewell Pilgrimage: "All of you are the children of Adam, and Adam was created from dust. Let people cease boasting of their forefathers, or they will be more contemptible before Allah than dung beetles" (2). So Allah had to abrogate the practice of the Quraysh, and He said: "Then depart from where the people depart," meaning there is no distinction or differentiation for you among Muslims.

Some exegetes say that the meaning of "from where the people depart" is intended to be from where Ibrahim departed, meaning that our master Ibrahim, peace be upon him, laid down all the rites of Hajj after Allah had taught them to him. Thus "the people," though plural, the intended meaning of the word "the people" is Ibrahim. We should not be surprised that "the people" means Ibrahim, because Allah described him as an "ummah." The word "people" is applied to a person who combines many qualities; for this reason Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said about our master the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

﴿Or do they envy the people for what Allah has given them of His bounty?﴾ (Qur'an 4:54)

The Truth described the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as "the people." And the man who went to the believers to inform them of the polytheists' preparation to fight them, concerning whom the saying of the Exalted was revealed: "those to whom the people said" (Qur'an 3:173), is one man, yet Allah described him as "the people," as if by his warning the Muslims he gathered all the qualities of good within the people.

﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah; indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ Indeed, the Truth, glorified and exalted, knows that the children of Adam cannot observe His rights as they ought to be observed, so things must slip from them, and He, glorified and exalted, knows that because He is their Creator; so His command, exalted in wisdom, is that they seek His forgiveness, in order to expiate their misdeeds.

1 Narrated by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi.
2 Narrated by al-Bazzar from Hudhayfah. The ja'lan is a lowly insect.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 200:

﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasik), remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance. Among the people is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter.﴾

We know that (qada) comes with many meanings, and the foundation of these meanings is the decisive settling of a matter with wisdom. A matter may be decided with wisdom because it has been completed in performance, as in ﴿fa-idha qadaytum﴾, meaning "when you have finished your rites." This is one meaning. It may also be because you have settled a matter by a certain decree, such as the Truth's saying:

﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ (part of verse 23, surah al-Isra').

It may also be that (qada) means to judge with a binding judgment, as you say: "The judge has qada (ruled)." So all of these revolve around the meaning: to settle with wisdom. ﴿Fa-idha qadaytum manasikakum fa-dhkuru Allah﴾: that is, when you have finished your rites. The manasik are places of worship of a certain kind: 'Arafat is a place of standing (al-mawqif), and Muzdalifah is a place of the sacred landmark (al-mash'ar al-haram) where the pilgrims spend the night. Mina is also a place of rites for spending the night, so every place in which worship occurs is called a (mansak) rite-place.

As for His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿fa-dhkuru Allah﴾, that is, the remembrance of Allah should always remain present in the verses, as though when you are granted success in performing something, beware of being deceived. Rather, remember your Lord who legislated for you, then granted you success and helped you. It is as though the Truth wishes to put an end to what the Arabs were accustomed to in that era. In former times they would perform the pilgrimage, and when the tribes gathered in Mina, each tribe would stand with its poet or its orator to enumerate its glories and the glories of its forefathers, and the pre-Islamic achievements they had, and they would bear blood-money (diyat), bear the burdens (hamalat), feed people with food, and do other customs. So Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, wished to end among them this custom, which was boasting of fathers and their deeds, and He said: ﴿fa-dhkuru Allah kadhikrikum aba'akum﴾ ("remember Allah as you remember your fathers"). Remembrance (dhikr) means directing thought toward something not present at the moment one mentions it, and a person cannot remember events of the past except the event that has a beneficial effect, and the remembrance is in proportion to the beneficial effect.

In earlier times they used to feed people with food, and the one who feeds people performs an important function in such primitive, that is, Bedouin, lands. Among the exaggeration regarding the large bowls (jafanat), some of them, such as al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi for example, had a bowl under which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) related that he would shelter during the midday heat. The jafna is the vessel in which food is placed, so consider how large the jafna could be!

As for "they bear the burdens (hamalat)," it means that when one tribe rose against another and killed many of them, persons of lineage, generosity, nobility and courage would volunteer and bear all these traces from their wealth. The diyat are what the people of nobility among them volunteer to pay when a killer has slain a victim and cannot afford his blood-money. All these deeds were considered glories. The Truth, glory be to Him, wished to return them to Himself in everything, so He said to them: You remember your fathers, because they did such-and-such, and your fathers boast of their fathers. Transfer these and trace them back to the Creator of all fathers and all mankind. Whatever good flows through the hands of fathers returns to Allah. So if you remember your fathers for the good they offered, then remember the One who supplied them with that good.

He wants them to remember Allah as they remembered their fathers, "or with even greater remembrance," because every being deserves remembrance in proportion to the good it has offered, and you will not find all good except with Allah. Therefore we must remember Allah.

Moreover, Islam wished to end boasting of fathers so as to make glory intrinsic within the believer's self, that is, glory arising from a sublime deed that originates from and is accomplished by the person himself. For this reason, of those who boast of their forebears they say that they are "'azamiyyun" (bone-worshippers), that is, those attributed to a glory made by people who have become bones gathered in graves. God wants us to be intrinsic in our glories, that is, to take pride in what we ourselves do, not in what our fathers did, for the fathers have passed on to what they offered, and God wants man to acquire an intrinsic faithful, obligatory selfhood. Whoever wishes to boast should boast of himself, and for this the poet says:

"And do not be 'azamiyyin boasting of a past
whose present is ruined."

"Inherited lineage from the ancients benefits no one
except those of resolve who are jealous of their lineage."

"And a branch from a fruitful tree which bears no fruit
they count, however high its origin, as firewood."

So a plant that has no fruit, people regard as mere firewood, and the Truth wishes to awaken in the believer a selfhood that acts, not a selfhood that boasts that "he was and he was," but rather every person must present what he takes pride in:

"The young man is not the one who says, 'My father was,'
the young man is the one who says, 'Here I am.'"

When the Arabs boasted against one another, one would say to the other: "Brother, what do you boast over me about?"

The second would reply: "I boast over you by my fathers and my grandfathers."

The first would reply: "Remember well that your fathers' glory ends with you, while my fathers' glory begins with me. Why should I not give my fathers the glory of having begotten me?"

On this a man said:

"They said, 'Abu al-Qasr of Shayban,' I said to them:
'No, by my life, but from him is Shaybān.'

And how many a father has risen through a son of noble height,
just as 'Adnan was exalted by the Messenger of Allah."

As long as the people boast of one of their own tribes, they cling to whoever supplies them with support so that they may become something lasting and influential in existence, not that limited thing represented in feeding people, bearing burdens and paying blood-money, but rather by bearing the message of universal humanity.

﴿Fa-dhkuru Allah kadhikrikum aba'akum aw ashadda dhikra﴾. For your remembrance of Allah will connect you to His support, and will give you help so that you may be worthy of leading the movement of life on earth, establishing in it security, peace, mercy and justice. This is what should be the field of glory.

Afterward, the Truth draws our attention in what follows to the fact that when a person has completed the rites, he is fit to humble himself before Allah and to ask Allah for what he loves to ask. Asking Allah varies according to the aspirations of those who ask. They used to ask Allah only by saying: "O Lord, give me camels; O Lord, give me sheep; O Lord, give me cattle; O Lord, give me an orchard (ha'it), that is, a garden; O Lord, give me as You gave my father."

They had in mind nothing but material matters, and Allah wished to make them rise in the matter of asking Allah, and to elevate it to something more enduring, lasting and beneficial. From here comes the faithful excellence, for if you are going to ask Allah for a commodity of the goods of this world, what is the difference between you and the people of the jahiliyyah?

This is what we understand from the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic, at the end of this verse: ﴿Among the people is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share in the Hereafter.﴾ So the servant, when he performs his rites for Allah, finds himself fit to ask Allah, and since you have found yourself fit to ask Allah, then ask Allah for a lasting good, because a person only raises his need to the one asked in proportion to the standing and rank of the one asked. You may go to a person and ask him for ten piasters, and go to another richer than the first and say: "Give me a pound," and to a third: ask him for ten pounds. You ask in proportion to each one's resolve in answering your request.

Relevant part of the commentary on the preceding verse: Therefore, since the servants, after performing the rites, stand in a position of asking Allah, let them raise their request to Allah and seek from Him what is beneficial forever, and let them not lower the request to purely worldly, perishing matters. ﴿Among the people is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share or portion in the Hereafter.﴾ The servant may not desire from his supplication to Allah anything but this world, having no share or portion in the Hereafter, and such a person is weak in resolve, because he has asked for something in the perishing world, whereas Allah wishes us to raise our faithful resolve. Therefore the Truth follows it with: ﴿And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾

This is a fragment of the commentary on the preceding verse. So since the servants, after completing the rites, are in a station of asking of God, let them raise their request to God and seek from Him what is beneficial always, and let them not lower the request to purely worldly, perishing matters. (“And among the people is he who says: Our Lord, give us in this world, and he has no portion in the Hereafter.”) Indeed, the servant may not want from his supplication to God anything but this world, having no share or portion in the Hereafter. Such a person is low in aspiration, because he has sought something of the perishing world, whereas God wants us to elevate our faith-based aspiration. Therefore the Truth follows it with: ﴿And among them is he who says: Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.﴾ (2:201)

Why did we not forget the world here? Because it is the field (farm) for the Hereafter. As for His, glory be to Him, saying: (“Give us good in this world”), the scholars have differed concerning it. Some of them restricted it and said: the good of this world is the righteous wife. And of the good of the Hereafter they said it is Paradise. Others said: the good of this world is knowledge, because action is built upon it; and regarding the good of the Hereafter, they said it is forgiveness, because it is the mother of all aims.

From surveying the statements of the scholars, we find them agreeing that the good of the Hereafter is that which leads to Paradise, namely forgiveness and mercy, but they differ regarding the good of this world. I say: why do we not make the good of this world more general and comprehensive, so we say: O Lord, give us everything that makes this world good in Your sight for Your servant.

The Truth concludes this verse with His saying: ﴿and protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾. When He, glory be to Him and exalted, bestows favour upon His servants, He bestows it upon them by removing them from the Fire and admitting them into Paradise, as if mere removal from the Fire were a blessing. So when one is admitted into Paradise after being removed from the Fire, it is as if He has bestowed upon the person two blessings, because He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ (Qur'an 19:71).

Its meaning is that every person will see the Fire, either while on his way to Paradise, and he will say: "Praise be to God, faith rescued me from this Fire and its punishment." So when he sees the Fire and its dreadful sight, he praises God for the blessing of Islam which saved him from the Fire. Then, when he enters Paradise and sees its bliss, he praises God a second time. Likewise, those of the People of the Heights (al-A'raf), who are neither in the Fire nor in Paradise, will see the Fire, and the Truth says:

﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has indeed triumphed﴾ (Qur'an 3:185).

The Lord then says:

﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ [2:202]

Al-nasib (نصيب) is the portion or lot. As for "مما كسبوا" (mimma kasabu, "of what they have earned"), we know beforehand that it contains kasb (كسب, earning) and also iktisab (اكتساب, acquiring). Iktisab has the form of ifti'al (افتعال), whereas kasb is a routine matter. For this reason you find that iktisab is used only for evil; it is as if the one who does evil exerts effort in it, whereas doing good is something natural for a human being. What is meant by "مما كسبوا" here is the gain from completing their acts that they performed in the Hajj: ihram and talbiyah, tawaf, sa'y, going to Mina, going to Arafat and standing there, proceeding (ifadah) to Muzdalifah, and throwing the pebbles (ramy al-jimar) at Mina, and the tawaf of ifadah. All of this is gain for the person who has attained the honour of Hajj.

When we read "والله سريع الحساب" (wa-llahu sari' al-hisab, "and Allah is swift in reckoning"), let us understand that speed is when the time taken by an event is reduced. Instead of an event taking you an hour, you may complete it in half an hour. Every event has a duration, and when an event has a duration and you want to reduce it, you must hasten in it so that you complete it in the least time. Reducing time requires speed of movement in the action, and this applies to actions that need treatment and labour from a human being. But He, glory be to Him, acts by "كن" (kun, "Be!"), and His work requires no treatment, and therefore requires no time. Hence He is swift in reckoning, because He needs no time, and because no affair preoccupies Him from another affair. This is the difference between the power of the One, glory be to Him, and the power of the created being: when the created being performs a task, that task occupies him from other tasks, so he cannot perform two operations at the same time. But the One, the Unique, is not preoccupied by one act from another, and therefore He does what He wills, whenever He wills, and for whomever He wills.

For this reason, Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib was asked: "How does Allah reckon all creatures in a single moment?" He replied: "As He provides for them in a single hour." He is the One who provides for them, and just as He provides for them, He reckons them.

The Lord then says:

﴿And remember Allah during the appointed days. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for him who fears Allah. And fear Allah, and know that you will be gathered to Him.﴾ (2:203)

We note that the remembrance of Allah is a common matter in all the rites of Hajj. "In appointed days" means in the days of Tashriq (the days of drying meat, the three days after the Day of Sacrifice). On the ninth day we are at 'Arafah, and on the night of the tenth we spend the night at Muzdalifah. Then after that we "pour forth from where the people pour forth" (ifadah), going to throw the Jamrat al-'Aqabah (stoning the major pillar), and some of us go to perform the Tawaf al-Ifadah and complete our rites, or perhaps go to sacrifice and exit the lesser state of ihram (tahallul al-asghar), if one has no wife with him; and if he has performed the Tawaf, he exits the greater state of ihram (tahallul al-akbar). As for the "appointed days", meaning the days of Tashriq, they are the three days after the Day of Sacrifice. They were named so in reference to al-shuruq (sunrise), and shuruq is specific to the sun. In the past, when they slaughtered their animals, they would take the meat and "sharraqu" it, that is, expose it to the rising of the sun as a form of preservation, and from here these days were called the days of Tashriq. When we hear His saying "in appointed days" we understand from it that they exceed two days.

Then the Lord says: "Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for him who fears Allah." The saying of the Lord, glorified and exalted be He, "in appointed days," then His saying "whoever hastens in two days," indicates that the word "days" (ayyam) is used for the plural, which is more than two days, that is, three days. But the Lord, glorified and exalted be He, gave the performance of two days the ruling of performing three days. If you hasten in two days, there is no sin upon you, and whoever completes three days, there is no sin upon him. How can that be?

Because the matter is not one of time, but the presence of an intention of worship. You may sit for three days while not present in the intention of worship. Therefore He, glorified be He, said: "for him who fears Allah." So beware of measuring actions by their duration; rather, they are by the sincerity of intention and the God-consciousness within them.

The Lord concludes the verse with the noble saying: "And fear Allah, and know that you will be gathered to Him." The Lord, glorified and exalted be He, used the word "tuhsharun" (you will be gathered) to suit the crowding of Hajj, because just as He gathers you in this gathering while you have choice, He, glorified be He, is able to gather you while you have no choice. So if you have gone of your own choice to this great human gathering in Hajj, know that the One who obligated you to go of your own choice to join this massive assembly is the One who is able to bring you while your choice has been taken from you.

The Almighty says next:

﴿And among people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents. 204﴾ ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals. And Allah does not like corruption. 205﴾

Allah, glorified and exalted, wishes to place before us an existential matter: that every action has an outward aspect and an inward aspect. It is possible to perfect the outward aspect while deceiving people in the inward one. So people have with one another an outward and an inward. It is in a person's interest, together with all other people, to belong to a world in which every human being knows that there is a Wise God who knows everything about all of us.

If you have something I do not know, and I have something you do not know, how will our interests be managed? For this reason, it is among the necessities of our lives that we all believe together in a God who looks into all our inner selves, and this is what makes us keep to good manners. Hence it has been said: (If you are blinded to the judgement of the earth, you will not be blinded to the judgement of heaven).

Thus the judgement of heaven and God's knowledge of the unseen is a matter for which we must praise Him, for it is He who will protect each one of us from the others. And when God veils our unseen selves, that is a blessing for which we must thank Him, because souls are fickle. If you knew what I hold against you in some moment, it may not please you, and you may never forget it, and your opinion of me would remain bad. But opinions and views pass through me and through you and come to an end. And if each of us were to see the unseen of the other, life would be exhausting. The well-known saying states this: (If you were to reveal to one another what you hide, you would not bury one another).

So it is by God's mercy and one of His greatest blessings upon His creation that He veiled the unseen of His creatures from one another. And the Truth warns us against those of whom He said: (And among people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you), that is, those who show good contrary to what they conceal of evil. For this reason the poet depicted this matter:

We spent the night gathered in censure, while our condition
out of fear was the condition of those gathered in praise.

That is, if we were to reveal ourselves, we would all be speaking in censure; rather, we are all flatterers when one of us meets another, each saying with his tongue what is not in his heart. As for (whose speech pleases you), is it forbidden that speech should please you? No; speech may please me, but not in the worldly life. The speech that pleases is that which relates to the affair of the eternal Hereafter, so as to secure for us good with the One who owns all good.

It suffices for one who hears praise from one who praises him, while the praiser himself harbours dislike for him in his heart, and that suffices as a testimony that the one praised is foolish: he says to himself, "The one praised is stupid, for I praise him and he believes my praise." Allah, glorified and exalted, alerts us to the necessity that the Muslim be wakeful and discerning. Whoever speaks to us words that please us in the worldly life, we suspect that his words are not sound, because the best speech is that which concerns the lasting affair.

For this reason, when the caliph of the Muslims sent to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, saying to him: "Why do you not visit us, as other people visit us?" Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq wrote to the caliph: "As for what follows: I have nothing of the world that I fear for, and you have nothing of the Hereafter that I hope for for you." It is as if he meant to say to him: leave us to our state; you need someone who sits with you and praises you, and you do not know that the first people to hold a bad opinion of you are those who praise you.

(And among people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you). This verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, whose name was Ubayy, and he was given the epithet al-Akhnas because he withdrew (akhanasa) and returned on the day of Badr, and did not fight the Muslims with Quraysh. He excused himself to them by saying that the caravan had escaped from the Muslims and had returned to them. Whenever he met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) he would show his Islam, soften his speech to the Messenger, and claim that he loved him. But after he left the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he passed by a field of crops and donkeys belonging to some Muslims, and he burned the crops and killed the donkeys. Although the verse was revealed concerning al-Akhnas, it encompasses every hypocrite.

(And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents). Do not say, "Allah bears witness," but bring your witnesses to testify to the truth of your words; for the meaning of "Allah bears witness" is your report that Allah bears witness for you. You are lying in this, and you want to lend credibility to your lie by drawing Allah into the matter.

When you hear someone say to you, "I call Allah to witness that I am such-and-such," say to him: "This is a report from you that Allah bears witness, and you may be lying in this report. I prefer that two human beings testify, and we do not drag Allah into this testimony." (And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents). "The most contentious of opponents" is one who is defiantly sinful; it is said: "So-and-so has lados," meaning he has defiance in his disputes and argues falsely. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the most contentious opponent."¹

That is, one who argues with falsehood and has harshness in sin: he is disobedient and, at the same time, harsh in his disobedience. And why is he "the most contentious of opponents"? Because the one who confronts you openly makes you guard against him, whereas the one who meets you with hypocrisy wants to deceive you. This is harshness in dispute: the clear opponent is better, because he confronts you with what is in his inner self; but when you face one who conceals his enmity and displays his love, he is harsh against you in his dispute, because he wants to deceive you and plot against you.

(And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land). "Turns away" (tawalla) means departs; that is, he says to you what pleases you, but when he turns away from you, he transfers the matter to reality by displaying what he was concealing. The meaning may also be that when he takes charge of something else, from wilayah (authority), so that tawalla contains the sense of turning away and withdrawal, and also the sense of assuming authority.

(And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals). The earth, without human intervention, was created in the form of goodness, and corruption is an accident caused by humans. We know that corruption does not befall any matter except that humans have a hand in it.

Why have we complained of a crisis of food, but have not complained of a crisis of air? Because humans have no intervention in the air, and in proportion to human intervention there is corruption. We intervened slightly in water, and corruption came of it: we did not handle its conveyance well in good pipes, so it reached us polluted, or chlorine was added to it or removed from it. In proportion to intervention is the spreading of corruption. In former times a person would go to the direct source of water in the wells and take the natural water that God created without human intervention, and there was no pollution or anything else.

Thus, in proportion to the presence of a human being in the movement of life that is not guided by faith in God, corruption arises. For this reason humanity needed a heavenly method. Creatures other than humans have no method of their own; they are created by instinct and perform their function only. The beast has never refused to be ridden by you, nor refused to bear your burdens, or to be used in ploughing or irrigation; even when you slaughter it, it does not refuse you. Why? Because it is created with the instinct by which it performs beneficial movement without choice on its part. If it resists at some time, that is only because of an accidental matter, such as an illness.

But the one who has choice must have a method that tells him: do this, and do not do that. If he is upright in following the method in "do" and "do not", his life proceeds in balance; but if he is not upright, life is corrupted. This is what we understand from His saying: (And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein), as if corruption is what needs an action. Leave nature and the creatures as they are, and you will find them working in orderly perfection, in good condition.

Thus corruption is an accident caused by the human who lives without a method, for (when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein). It is as if the original state of the earth and what is in it came in the form of goodness; so if you do not add to the good, then do not try to corrupt it. He, the Exalted, said:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers." Unquestionably, it is they who are the corrupters, but they perceive not. 11–12﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah).

From here we understand that they thought the earth needed their movement to reform it, although the earth without their movement is good, because they do not move by the method of God.

So from this verse we understand that when a person "turns away", meaning returns, or takes up authority, and strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein, then corruption in the earth is an accident that results from human striving without a method from God. As long as a human has choice, there must be a higher method than him that preserves that choice; if he has no method and goes after his desires, he is inevitably a corrupter.

Consider the stupidity of one who corrupts the earth: does he think that he alone will benefit from the earth, so that he permits himself to corrupt the earth for others? He forgets the reality: just as he corrupts for others, others corrupt for him. Who, then, is the loser? We will all lose.

﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and animals...﴾ 205 (Surat al-Baqarah).

The word harth (crops/tilth) has two meanings: sometimes it is used for crops, and sometimes for women. The first meaning occurs in His saying:

﴿And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the tilth, when the sheep of the people grazed in it...﴾ 78 (Surat al-Anbiya').

So harth in the verse means crops, and crops result from ploughing and stirring the earth. Your work, O human, is to stir and plough the earth, and bring the seed that God created into the earth that God created, and water it with the water that God created, and grow in the air that God created. For this reason the Truth draws our attention and alerts us, saying:

﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ 63–64 (Surat al-Waqi'ah).

The second meaning: harth is used for woman, in His saying:

﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾ (part of verse 223, Surat al-Baqarah).

Just as the purpose of tilling crops is to produce plants, so too the woman is for bearing children. He, the Exalted, says:

﴿So go to your tilth as you wish﴾ (part of verse 223, Surat al-Baqarah).

Those libertines who wish to permit intercourse with a woman's whole body, we say to them: notice His saying "your tilth", and the tilth is the place of growth; so intercourse is in the place of growth only. Do not understand it as a generalization; it is a specification. The Truth continues describing the one who speaks good words yet strives to corrupt the earth, saying: (and destroy crops and animals). "Nasl" means offspring and descendants.

The Truth concludes the verse: (And Allah does not like corruption), that is, the Truth wants you, if you do not employ the power that God created in you as thought and giving, then at least leave the matter as God created it, because God does not like you to corrupt what He created good in its essence.

What has preceded in this verse is merely one image of the ways the Islamic call was received in its early days by those who were hypocrites toward its strong reality: they bring words that please, and deeds that please those who are hypocritical. We know that hypocrisy was a sign of the strength of the Muslims, and for this reason hypocrisy did not arise in Makkah but arose in Madinah. The Truth said:

﴿And among the people of Madinah are those who have become adept at hypocrisy﴾ (part of verse 101, Surat al-Tawbah).

Someone may ask: how could this phenomenon appear in the strong faith environment of Madinah? We say: because Islam in Makkah was weak, and no one flatters the weak, whereas Islam in Madinah became strong, and it is the strong whom people flatter.

So the existence of hypocrisy in Madinah was a healthy phenomenon indicating that faith had become strong, such that one who had no Islam claimed it. These people would speak fine, beautiful words, and might do, in front of those they flattered, deeds that pleased whoever saw or heard them; but they did not remain firm upon the truth. When they turned away, that is, vanished from the sight of those they flattered, they returned to their original disbelief, or when they were entrusted with something, they strove in the earth in corruption.

This verse touches on something that shows the discernment of the believers: the verse exposed the hypocrite. al-Akhnas was the chief of hypocrisy, and the exposure of the hypocrite in this manner indicates that behind Muhammad (ﷺ), and behind the believers in Muhammad, there is a Lord who informs them of whoever deceives them, and also...

¹ Narrated by al-Bukhari. The meaning of "al-alad al-khasim" is: the most severe in his disputing.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 205:

﴿When he turns away, he strives in the land to cause corruption therein and destroy crops and livestock; and Allah does not love corruption.﴾

Almighty and Exalted Allah wants to set before us an existential matter, and this existential matter is that every deed has an outward aspect and an inward aspect. It is possible for you to perfect the outward aspect while deceiving people in the inward aspect. Thus people have an outward and an inward with one another. It is in a person's interest, together with all other people, to belong to a world in which every human being knows that there is a Wise God who knows everything about all of us.

So if you have something that I do not know, and I have something that you do not know, how will our interests be managed? Therefore it is among the necessities of our lives that we believe together in a God who is aware of all our inner secrets, and this is what makes us keep to good manners. For this reason it was said: (If you are blinded to the decree of the earth, you will not be blinded to the decree of the heavens).

Thus the decree of the heavens and Allah's knowledge of the unseen is a matter for which we must praise Him, because it is He who will protect each one of us from others. When Allah concealed our unseen, that is a blessing for which we must thank Him, because human souls fluctuate. If you knew what is in my soul toward you at a moment, it might not please you... and you might never forget it, and your opinion of me would remain bad. But suspicions and opinions pass through me and through you and then end. If each of us were to be aware of the unseen of the other, life would become exhausting, and the transmitted saying states this: (If you were to disclose to one another what you think, you would not bury one another).

Thus it is from the mercy of Allah, and from His greatest blessings upon His creatures, that He concealed the unseen of His creatures from one another. Allah warns us about those of whom He said: ﴿And among people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you﴾, that is, those who show good contrary to what they conceal of evil. For this reason the poet depicted this matter:

We spent the night agreeing on blame, while our state
out of fear was the state of those agreeing on praise.

That is, if we were to disclose ourselves, we would all be speaking blame, but we are all flatterers when one of us meets another, each saying with his tongue what is not in his heart. As for ﴿whose speech pleases you﴾: is it forbidden that speech should please you? No. Speech may please me, but not in the worldly life. The speech that pleases is that which relates to the matter of the everlasting Hereafter, so as to secure for us good with the One who owns all good.

It is enough for the one who hears praise from one who praises him, while the praiser himself harbours hatred for him in his heart, and that is enough as evidence of the praised person's foolishness: he says to himself, (The praised person is a fool, because I praise him and he believes my praise). Almighty and Exalted Allah alerts us to the necessity that the Muslim be alert and perceptive. Whoever speaks to us with words that please us in the worldly life, we accuse of not speaking well, because the best speech is that which concerns the lasting matter.

For this reason, when the caliph of the Muslims sent to the Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, saying to him: Why do you not visit us, that is, why do you not come to us as people come to us? Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq wrote to the caliph: "To proceed: I have nothing of this world that I fear for it, and you have nothing of the Hereafter that I hope for you." It is as if he wanted to say: leave us and our state. You need someone who sits with you and praises you, and you do not know that the first people who hold a bad opinion of you are those who praise you.

﴿And among people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you﴾. This verse was revealed about al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, whose name was Ubayy, and he was given the epithet al-Akhnas because he withdrew (khanasa) and turned back on the day of Badr. He did not fight the Muslims with Quraysh, and he excused himself to them by saying that the caravan had escaped from the Muslims and returned to them. Whenever he met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) he would show his Islam, speak gently to the Messenger, and claim that he loved him. But after he left the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he passed by a field and donkeys belonging to some Muslims, so he burned the field and killed the donkeys. Although the verse was revealed about al-Akhnas, it includes every hypocrite.

﴿And Allah bears witness to what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents.﴾ Do not say, "Allah bears witness," but bring your witnesses to testify to the truth of your statement, because the meaning of "Allah bears witness" is a report from you that Allah bears witness for you. You are lying in this, and you want to lend credibility to your lie by bringing Allah into the matter.

When you hear someone say to you, "I call Allah to witness that I am such-and-such," tell him: this is a report from you that Allah bears witness, and you may be lying in this report. I prefer that two human beings bear witness, and that we not drag Allah into this testimony. ﴿And Allah bears witness to what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents.﴾ "The most contentious of opponents" is the one who is wicked in his disobedience.
