Habil offered a fat she-camel, for he was a owner of sheep, and Qabil offered a bundle of grain from the worst of his crop. Then a fire descended and consumed the sacrifice of Habil and left the sacrifice of Qabil. He became angry and said, 'I will surely kill you, so that you will not marry my sister.' He said, 'Indeed, Allah only accepts from the righteous.'"

So the birth of the first dispute among mankind came when two people competed to monopolize some benefit, and this was a clear example of what can happen when benefits are narrow in relation to desires.

"Mankind were one community," but they differed at the moment of monopolizing benefits, and every person came to have his own desire. Had Allah willed to make His method for Adam a lasting method until the Hour came, it would have been so. But in His mercy, He, glory be to Him, knows that He created us, and knows that we reason at one time and forget at another, and comply at one time and neglect at another. So Allah willed to continue for His creation the procession of messengers. Therefore the saying of the Truth comes: (Then Allah sent the prophets as bringers of good news and warners). The task of "good news and warning" is that people remember that there is a Paradise and a Fire. Therefore every messenger gives good news to whoever of his people believes, of Paradise, and warns whoever of those people disbelieves, of the Fire. The Almighty reminds us that He made us bear witness against ourselves regarding His oneness, and He says:

﴿And [recall] when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying], "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we have testified." [This] – lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were of this unaware." Or [lest] you say, "It was only our fathers who associated others with Allah before, and we were [merely] descendants after them. So will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ [7:172-173] (Surat al-A'raf).

He, glory be to Him, informs that He brought forth the descendants of Adam from their loins, bearing witness against themselves that Allah is their Lord and Sovereign, and that there is no god but Him, just as He had created them upon that. Then after He brought them out into existence from Adam, He came to the first creation, which was Adam, and gave him the method, and desires did not yet exist, so the method remained applied among the children of Adam. After that the desires multiplied, and the multiplicity of desires arises only from monopolizing benefits, and that is due to fear of the monopolizing of others. Thus self-love arose, and since benefits could not accommodate the greed of people, the love of monopoly and possession spread. We find this matter clear when goods are abundant and fill the markets. You can buy any commodity at any time you like, and you find it available; then there is no crisis. But a crisis arises when the quantities of goods offered fall short of people's need, so people scramble to monopolize them. Thus we know that when benefits exist, but fall short of desires, problems are generated.

By the mercy of the Almighty toward creation, and by the completeness of His knowledge of the weakness of humans before their desires and before their monopolizing of benefits, He sent messengers to mankind to give good news and to warn. (And He sent down with them the Book with truth, to judge between people concerning that over which they differed. And none differed over it except those who were given it, after clear proofs had come to them.) It is as if the Truth did not wish to leave mankind to differ, but heedlessness on the part of people is what produced this difference. (After clear proofs had come to them, out of animosity among themselves.) From this wise saying we know that disagreement arises only from the will to transgress, and transgression is that a person wants to take what is not his right. And as long as each of us wants to take what is not his right, hatred must arise.

(So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they had differed, by His permission.) That is, Allah guides those who believe from every people to the messenger who came as a bringer of good news and warner, and who bore the method of truth to judge between people concerning what they differed over. In this way the method remains dominant until a long period passes in which souls become heedless, and through it desires begin, and forgetfulness of the method of Allah occurs, and desires arise, so Allah sends messengers to restore people to the upright method. This continued until the message of Islam came as the seal, and Allah sent our master Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to all the world. In this way the Almighty Allah guaranteed for us that no disagreement would arise in the foundation, for if we were to differ over the foundation of the creed, there would befall us what befell the earlier nations. They differed, so Allah sent to them messengers as bringers of good news and warners, but for the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Truth willed for it a clear method that protects it from disagreement over the foundation of the creed. And if people of the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, differ, then they must seek guidance from the true method embodied in the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

We know that among his distinctions, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is that he is the Seal of the Prophets in truth, and you will not find in the procession of messengers a messenger to whom Allah entrusted the establishment of a new ruling that was not revealed in the Book of Allah, except our master Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Allah gave His messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the delegated authority to legislate on behalf of Allah, under the protection of Allah's preservation of him, for He, glory be to Him, said:

﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from.﴾ [59:7] (part of verse 7, Surat al-Hashr).

This is a clear command to the believers to comply with the command of the Noble Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because what he commands them contains righteousness and good, and to refrain from what he forbids them, because he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, forbids only matters that contain no good for the community of Muslims. The Almighty commands the congregation of Muslims to obey the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, because it is obedience to Allah, so He, may He be exalted, says:

﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah; and whoever turns away – We have not sent you over them as a guardian.﴾ [4:80] (Surat an-Nisa').

Thus we see that obedience to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is obedience to Allah, and whoever turns away from his obedience will have punishment in the Hereafter. The Almighty further affirms obedience to Him and obedience to His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saying:

﴿Say, "Obey Allah and the Messenger." But if they turn away, then indeed, Allah does not like the disbelievers.﴾ [3:32] (Surat Al 'Imran).

Thus we know that obedience to the Most Merciful necessitates obedience to the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. So Allah delegated to His Messenger the authority to legislate for mankind. And he, peace and blessings be upon him, does not speak from desire.

Another distinction of the community of Muslims is that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, left us the right of ijtihad (independent reasoning) in matters for which no text came in the Qur'an or the Sunnah, or for which a text came but admits more than one meaning. This means that the Almighty has made the community of Muhammad, peace be upon him, secure in that it will reach through ijtihad what settles any disagreement, and that no disagreement will reach the essence. Had Allah known from eternity that we would differ in disagreement over the soundness of the creed, He would have sent us messengers.

We find that all the differences among the sects of Muslims do not go outside the framework of understanding the texts of the Qur'an or the hadiths of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and every Muslim wants to draw his evidence from the Book and the Sunnah. This means that we will not abandon the foundation, but each of us wants to take the correct ruling. Indeed, we find that some Muslims who did not find their evidence in the Qur'an and the Sunnah have tried to fabricate a hadith and attribute it to the Messenger of Allah, in order to build upon it the ruling they want. Such people's abode is the Fire, for they have spoken in the tongue of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, what the Noble Messenger did not say. They have lied about him, and whoever lies about him deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire.

So all of us converge around the Qur'an and the Sunnah and the Prophetic [tradition]. Where, then, is the problem? The problem is that people must be intelligent and knowledgeable so that they know whether what is taken from the Qur'an is acceptable or not, and whether the hadiths relied upon meet the standards of criticism and authentication (jarh wa ta'dil) or not?

So the soundness of ijtihad and opinion among the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, has made them secure in everything of the method. The disagreement among them has not reached what the earlier nations reached. But they must be attentive and advance until they distinguish the matters that are not from the indications of the Qur'an, and then some people want to attribute them to the

Then the Almighty says:

﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come upon you the like of what came upon those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said: "When will the help of Allah come?" Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ [2:214]

That is: did you suppose that you would enter Paradise without trials befalling you? The Almighty negates this supposition and says: the matter is not so; rather, one must bear the consequences of faith. Had faith been merely a matter of speech, it would have been easy, but what makes faith difficult is action, that is, compelling the self to follow the method of faith. Some of those who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) were too proud to say: "There is no god but Allah" (lā ilāha illā Allāh), because they understood what it required. Had it been a mere word spoken without a store of action to support it, it would have been easier for them to say it. But they were people who would only say the word in its true sense, and therefore they were fully certain that if they said "There is no god but Allah," all their former beliefs would come to an end. So they did not say it, because they refused and declined to discharge its right and to fulfil its requirement.

The Almighty says: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come upon you the like of what came upon those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them﴾. What is the connection between this verse and the verses before it? The discussion had been about the Children of Israel, who supposed that they would enter Paradise without being tested, and who came to have desires by which they distorted the method. As for the community of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they must prepare themselves for trial and learn how to bear hardships.

In grammar we know that there are particles of negation and jussive. Among the particles of negation are (lam) (لم) and (lammā) (لما). When we say (لم يحضر زيد) (lam yahḍur Zayd, "Zayd did not attend"), this is a statement about the past, and it is possible that he attends now. But when you say (لما يحضر زيد) (lammā yaḥḍur Zayd), the negation continues until now, meaning that he has not come up to the moment of speaking, but his attendance and arrival are expected. Therefore the Almighty says:

﴿The Bedouins say: "We have believed." Say: "You have not believed, but say: 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts."﴾ [49:14]

When the Bedouins heard this, they said: "Praise be to Allah," for there was still hope that they would believe. Allah willed that the Bedouins be truthful with themselves. Some exegetes say this verse was revealed concerning a group of the tribe of Banu Asad, who came to Medina in a year of drought, declared the testimony of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and said: "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." They were asking for charity and trying to lay claim to favour over the Messenger (ﷺ), saying that they had not fought him as others had done. So this verse came to make clear that faith is a rank higher than the outward display of Islam. But that does not mean they were hypocrites; for this reason the Noble Qur'an makes clear that displaying Islam does not mean faith, because faith is an inward process of the heart.

They had declared submission to Allah and wished to perform the same deeds as the Muslims, but this is not the whole of faith. They said: "We have believed," and the Almighty said to them: "No, you have not believed; be truthful with yourselves. Faith is an inward matter, and one may not say 'you have believed,' because it is a matter in your heart; rather say 'you have submitted,' that is, you have yielded and done as the believers do. Whether you did that out of faith or not is another matter."

Here the verse says: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come upon you the like of what came upon those who passed away before you?﴾ That is, it is impossible for you to enter Paradise unless there comes upon you trials like those of the nations before you; you will surely be tested and purified through adversity and hardship, and whoever remains steadfast after that deserves to enter Paradise. So do not suppose that you are a community distinguished from others in the matter of testing. You will not enter Paradise without trial; on the contrary, your trial will be in proportion to your blessings.

You will attain a high station among the nations, and therefore your trial must be proportionate to your station. If you are people of high standing who will bear the final message and spread through the world, then your trial must be proportionate to the greatness of your responsibility and your mission.

﴿Adversity and hardship touched them, and they were shaken﴾. The word of Allah (ولما) indicates that what befell those before them of trial will befall the believers in the same way.

When we reflect on the Almighty's words ﴿and they were shaken (wa-zulzilū)﴾, you discover a unique feature of the Arabic language: the expression of the sound conveying the reality of the movement. The word (زلزلوا) originally comes from (zalzalah), and this word has two syllables: (zal, zal). (Zal) means to slip or fall from its place, and the second likewise has the same meaning, that is, to fall from its place. So the word gives us the meaning of repeated falling: a first fall and a second fall, and the second fall is not an extension of the first but in the opposite direction. Had it been in one direction, it would have come out monotonous. The second slip comes opposite the first in direction, as if one falls to the right once and to the left another time.

Similarly (al-khalkhalah) (الخلخلة), movement in two opposite directions: (khal) the first to the right, and (khal) the second to the left, and thus the shaking continues.

Thus (al-zalzalah) carries within it a change of direction, which in physics is called inertia (al-quṣūr al-dhātī). An example of this is what happens to a person riding in a car: after that, the driver brakes the car forcefully (the brakes, al-farāmil), and the passenger is thrown forward once, then backward again, and the front windscreen may shatter depending on the force of the impact. What caused this thrust? The cause is that the passenger's body was disposed to move forward; the driver stopped the car while the passenger was still disposed to move forward, so he is jolted and may strike the car's interior parts when it suddenly stops. The process of (zalzalah) is exactly like that: in it a thing is struck with a jolt forward and backward, or to the right and left, or in any two opposite directions.

(Zulzilū) means that the great, overwhelming, repeated calamity has struck them, and it does not recur in a single pattern but in varying repetitions: at one time faith seizes them, then misfortunes and events seize them, and the matter repeats until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those who believed with him say: ﴿When will the help of Allah come?﴾

Then comes the statement: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ Do they ask first, then return to their senses and answer themselves ("Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near"), or is this a clarification that the matter oscillates between "When will the help of Allah come?" and "Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near"?

The situation in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reached the peak of choice and trial, yet the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him continued to hold fast to faith. Adversity and hardship touched them and they were shaken, that is, a violent tremor struck them that shook them, until the matter reached the point that, from the effect of this shaking, ﴿the Messenger and those who believed with him say: "When will the help of Allah come? Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near."﴾

The arrangement of the expression in this form, ﴿When will the help of Allah come?﴾, means first a request for the help to come quickly, then the good news afterward in the Almighty's words: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near.﴾ This was not out of doubt or suspicion concerning it. This impatience and then the good news were part of the great shaking: ideas became mixed up; some people say "When will the help of Allah come?" and then a voice from the battle answers them: "Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near."

The context of the verse requires that those who said "When will the help of Allah come?" were the Companions, and that the one who said "Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near" was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then the Almighty, exalted is He, moves after that to another matter, which has spread in this form: the phenomenon of believers asking about things. It is a healthy faith-based phenomenon. The believers could have refrained from asking about things on which no religious obligation had been given, for fear that the answer might restrict their action. Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Leave me alone as long as I leave you; for those before you were destroyed by their excessive questioning and their disputing with their prophets. So when I command you to do something, do of it what you are able; and when I forbid you from something, leave it."(1)

Nevertheless, they used to ask about the finest details of life, and this phenomenon confirmed that they were devoted to the obligations from Allah; they wanted to build all their conduct on an Islamic basis, and they wanted to ask about the ruling of Islam on every action in order to act upon it.

(1) This hadith was narrated by Imam Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Imam Ahmad in his Musnad, from Abu Hurayrah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 215:

The Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever wealth you spend, let it be for parents and near relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it.﴾

The question was asked by ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh, who was an elderly man. He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have much wealth, so what should I give in charity, and to whom should I give it?" He was not asking only for himself; he was also voicing the feelings of others. For this reason the answer came in general terms, not restricted to the questioner alone, but encompassing all the believers.

The question is "what they should spend" (mādhā yunfiqūn). It is as though the thing spent is what they are asking about. Spending, as we know, requires a agent who spends (al-munfiq), a thing spent (al-munfaq), which is wealth, and a beneficiary (al-munfaq ʿalayh). They asked "what they should spend," as though the act of spending were already accepted, but they wanted to know what exactly to spend. The question comes in this form, and the answer comes bearing the answer to that aspect and to an additional matter.

The Truth says: "They ask you what they should spend" — this is the question, and the answer is: "Say: Whatever wealth you spend, let it be for parents…" The superficial reading thinks the question was only about what to spend, and that the answer concerned only the beneficiaries. We say: No. Why have you forgotten His words, "from good (khayr)"? The wealth spent must be characterised as coming from a good source.

Then He further explained: since you believe that spending is obligatory, you must know what it is that you spend and who deserves to be spent upon. "Say: Whatever wealth you spend…" Good (khayr) is what is fine and beneficial. The beneficiary is the circles closest to the one who spends, because Allah wishes to charge the believer with his own particular circles, so that these circles join together, and the society as a whole is burdened by itself. When He, glory be to Him, charges me with my family, my parents, and my near relatives, this is the protection of the household. Each of us has parents and near relatives, and my circle includes my parents and my relatives, and then it spreads out to another matter: the orphans and the needy.

Take each one of us and count his circles — parents, near relatives, and those around him among the orphans and the needy — and you will find that the interlocking circles have embraced all the needy, and society has borne its members, and there remains none but the one incapable of work. We know that the questioner was ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh, and he had a remarkable story. He was lame, and the lame is excused by Allah from jihad: "There is no blame on the blind, nor on the lame, nor on the sick" (cf. Qur'an 48:17).

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wished to go out on a military expedition, and ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, do not deprive me of jihad. My sons are preventing me from going out because of my lameness." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Allah has excused you among those whom He excused." He said: "But, O Messenger of Allah, I wish to step into Paradise with my lameness."

This is the one who asked what they should spend, and the answer came from the Truth: "Say: Whatever wealth you spend" — that is, whatever wealth you bring out, because spending means bringing out. Good here is wealth, and spending requires bringing wealth out of a person's ownership, by sale, gift, or kindness. The root of the word "infāq" is taken from "nafaqat al-sūq," meaning it became brisk (rā'ija), because the market stands on goods. When you come to the market and find no goods, that means the market is brisk; but when you find goods piled up in the market, that means the market is still stagnant.

So the meaning of "nafaqat al-sūq" is that all the goods have gone, just as life goes from an animal; when we say "nafaqat al-dābba," the animal has died. The aspects of spending He has made clear in His saying: "for parents, and near relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer." Is every orphan needy? Perhaps the orphan has inherited wealth. But we must understand that the matter is not merely meeting the need of the needy, but standing beside the weak in whatever corner of weakness. For when a child is an orphan and has wealth, and then he sees you showing him compassion, he feels that his father has not died, because his fatherhood remains in his believing brothers. Afterwards he will not grow up with envy towards children whose fathers are alive. But when the orphan sees every father occupied with his own children while the orphans whose fathers have died are left aside, then resentment appears in him, and the instinct to object to destiny is nurtured, and he says: "Why should it be me whose father died?" But when he sees all people as his fathers, and they connect with him through smiles, affection, welcome, and help, he will feel that one who has a single father is abandoned by people relying on the presence of his father; but when his father dies, people turn to him with kindness and love. The consequence is that love spreads in the Islamic society, along with harmony and contentment with the decree of Allah, and no one objects to the death of his father. If destiny has taken his father, he has left him many fathers.

Had those who refuse affection and compassion towards the orphan, on the grounds that his father left him enough, known what follows from this compassion of benefit to the spirit, they would have competed in showing compassion to him. The matter is not one of material need, but of spiritual need.

I always say: we must educate the young that Allah does not take anyone from His creation while the earth still has need of him. Observe this matter among those around you, and you will find that a man has died and left young children, and his family and acquaintances grieve because he left his children young; then they forget the matter after a time, and people are surprised that the sons of that man have become the leaders of the neighbourhood, as though their father had been a restraint upon their provision, and when the father ended, Allah opened the taps of provision for the sons, so that a person is not tested through a cause.

After spending on orphans we find spending on the needy and the wayfarer. We have learned that the needy (miskīn) is the one in need, and the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl) is the one cut off from his family and wealth. The Truth concludes this verse with His words: "And whatever good you do, indeed Allah is Knowing of it." Allah wishes to turn human nature to a principle, which is: beware of seeking the reward for the good you do with these people from any of creation, but seek it from Allah; and beware of trying to have people know that you spend on relatives, orphans, and the wayfarer, because those whom you wish to know cannot grant you any recompense, and their knowledge will not add anything to you. It is enough for you that Allah knows, the One who gave you, and what you have been given from that of which He has made you a successor, seeking His pleasure. When people spend to seek the pleasure of people, they afterwards meet ingratitude and denial, so that the giver has lost what he spent, and has left evil in those upon whom he spent.

If a Muslim intends by spending and doing good the pleasure of the Supreme Creator, may He be exalted, He will preserve what he spent as good deeds and reward for the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will subject to him the hearts of those to whom he gives charity, with love and fidelity in kindness. This is a justice from Allah that is manifest in that He treats the show-offs in this way, for they give while their minds are on having given to people; but if they gave to Allah, the recipient would not deny the beauty of the gift. You gave it for His pleasure, so it is as though Allah says to you: I will leave you to him so that he may reward you. For this reason the one who gives charity in secret is among the seven whom Allah shades under His shade on the day when there is no shade but His, among them:

"…a man who gave charity and concealed it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends" (1). This is the better course in voluntary charity. As for obligatory zakat, declaring it is better; likewise with prayer, the obligatory prayer is better performed openly, and the voluntary prayer is better performed in private.

But if you act with Allah in your mind, you will find the effect of giving and the fidelity of the one who receives. So beware, even in a subtle way, of trying to let people know that you are doing good.

(1) Narrated by Muslim from Abu Hurayrah.

This is the commentary of al-Sha'rawi (*Tafsir al-Sha'rawi*, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 216:

Then, after that, the discussion returns (al-Haqq, "the Truth," i.e. God) to a matter it had already addressed in His saying: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there﴾. The discussion returns to fighting, and speaks of the general principle concerning fighting, saying:

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ (216)

The dislike of fighting is a natural matter, stated by the One who created man. He, glorified is He, does not treat the matter with sophistic treatment, meaning by saying: "And what is in fighting?" No. Rather, the Creator says: I know that fighting is disliked. And even if what you dislike befalls you in it, you know that the One who legislated it has decreed that. Had the Truth not said that fighting is hateful, people would have understood that God depicts the difficult matter as easy.

Almighty and Majestic God says to those who believe: Know that you are facing hardships, troubles, and the need to leave your wealth and to leave your pleasures and enjoyments. For this reason we find that the great statesmen who excelled in politics and succeeded in leading their societies did not like their peoples to plunge into battles except under compulsion. When they are compelled, they explain to their soldiers that they are warding off, through fighting, something worse than fighting. This means that they mobilize the human soul until it confronts the situation with all its strength, all its faculties, and all its will.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you﴾. He, glorified is He, says to us: I know that fighting is hateful to you, but I wanted to spread among you a principle. This principle is that you should not judge great matters within the limits of your own knowledge, because your knowledge is always deficient. Rather, take matters through My knowledge, for I may prescribe something hateful, yet good comes from it. And you may see a thing you love from which evil comes. For this reason the Truth alerts us that many matters we love may bring evil, so one of us says: "I expected good from this matter, but evil is what came to me from it."

There are other matters that we think evil will come from, but they bring good. For this reason the Truth leaves some anomalies in society so that people become certain that Allah, glorified and exalted is He, does not run the affairs of good according to the requirements and measures of the knowledge of servants; rather, He runs judgment according to the requirements and measures and knowledge of the Lord of the servants. Let us look at what the Truth related as an example for people of this:

﴿And [mention] when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease [traveling] until I reach the junction of the two seas, or I will continue for years." And when they reached the junction between them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, a passage. And when they had passed beyond, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have certainly suffered fatigue from this journey of ours." He said, "Did you see when we retreated to the rock? Indeed I forgot the fish, and none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it; and it took its way into the sea in an amazing manner." He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they returned, retracing their footsteps.﴾ (Surat al-Kahf)

Moses, peace be upon him, was traveling with his servant to the junction of the two seas. It is said that it is the meeting place of two seas in the east. With them was food: a salted fish which they ate from. But the travel and hardship made them forget the fish, and the fish went off by a sign from Allah into the sea. When Moses reached the junction of the two seas, he asked his servant to bring the food after long exhaustion. But the youth told Moses that he had forgotten the fish, and that none had caused him to forget it except Satan. The fish took its path into the sea. Moses said: This is what we were seeking, as a sign of our arrival at our goal, which is the junction of the two seas. That is, the matter of the fish and its loss is what we were seeking, for the man we came for is there in this place. Moses and the youth then retraced their footsteps once again.

So what happens? Moses, peace be upon him, meets the righteous servant, al-Khidr, who is one of Allah's friends. Allah taught him the divine knowledge (al-'ilm al-rabbani) which Allah bestows on His pious servants as a fruit of sincerity and piety. Moses, peace be upon him, asks the divine servant, our master al-Khidr, peace be upon him, to teach him some of the right guidance. But the divine servant, to whom Allah gave knowledge exceeding the capacity of human comprehension, says to Moses, peace be upon him:

﴿He said, "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me. And how can you have patience over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?"﴾ (Surat al-Kahf)

Moses had earlier known that the loss of the fish was a matter that outwardly appeared evil but inwardly contained good, because that was the path and the sign by which Moses would know how to meet the righteous servant. The same context continues in the story of Moses and the righteous servant, a story whose outward appearance is evil and whose inward reality is good, whether in the matter of the ship that he damaged, or the boy whom he killed, or the wall that he built.

The knowledge of the righteous servant was divine knowledge, so Moses wished to learn some of this knowledge. But the righteous servant alerted Moses, peace be upon him, that what he might see was beyond the endurance of patience, because what Moses might see of actions might appear to him to be outward evil, but in its inward reality there is all good.

Moses, peace be upon him, accepted to take the position of a student, with courtesy, before the scholar whom Allah had granted divine knowledge. The divine servant stipulated on Moses that he should not ask except after the divine servant had told him about the reasons. Moses and the divine servant came upon a ship; they boarded it, and the divine servant damaged the ship. Moses said:

﴿"Have you damaged it to drown its people? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 71)

The righteous servant replied:

﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ (72)

Moses remembered that he had promised the righteous servant to be patient. But what should Moses do, now that he found the righteous servant damaging a ship that was carrying them on the sea? It is a matter difficult for the soul. For this reason Moses said:

﴿"Do not blame me for what I forgot, and do not impose upon me difficulty in my affair."﴾ (73)

Moses returns to his promise to the righteous servant, and asks him only not to burden him with matters beyond his capacity. The righteous servant and Moses, peace be upon him, set out, and the righteous servant found a boy and killed him. Moses said:

﴿"Have you killed a pure soul without it having killed someone? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾ (from verse 74, Surat al-Kahf)

The righteous servant reminds Moses that he would not be able to have patience with him, and Moses apologizes for what he did not know. The righteous servant and Moses passed by a village and asked its people for hospitality, but the people of the village refused hospitality. The righteous servant found a wall leaning, about to fall, and began to rebuild it. Moses said:

﴿"If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ (from verse 77, Surat al-Kahf)

Then came the separation between the righteous servant and Moses. The righteous servant informed Moses of what he had not known and had not been patient with. As for the damaging of the ship, it was to save its owners from its being seized by them, because there was a king who would take every good ship by force. So he wanted to make it defective, so that the king would leave it to these poor people. The killing of the boy was a mercy to his believing parents; this son would have brought them tyranny and disbelief, and Allah wanted to replace him with someone better than him. As for the wall he built, it was over a treasure, and it belonged to two orphans of this village. Their father had been righteous, so it was necessary to rebuild the wall until the two boys reached maturity and extracted their treasure. The righteous servant says about all these actions:

And recite the saying of Allah, glorified and exalted:

﴿"And I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of that over which you could not have patience."﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 82)

The righteous servant does not attribute this divine action to himself, but attributes it to the Creator who taught him. Thus the Truth releases some matters of the cosmos so that man does not think that good is always in what he loves and that evil is always in what he hates. For this reason He, glorified is He, says: ﴿And perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾. So if fighting is hateful to you, perhaps there is good for you in it. And in connection with the mention of disliking, we clarify that there are *karaha* (كَره) and *kurha* (كُره). *Al-karaha* (الكَره), with an open kaf, is the hateful thing that you are compelled and forced to do; whereas *al-kurha* (الكُره), with a kaf pronounced with a damma, is the difficult thing.

It may be that a thing is hateful and yet not difficult, and it may be difficult but not hateful. The Truth says: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is kurh for you﴾. Let us note that the Truth, whenever He legislates, says *kutiba* (كُتب) and does not say *katabtu* (كَتبت). This is so that we understand that Allah will not legislate except for the one who believes in Him. He, glorified is He, has not prescribed any obligations on the disbeliever. Would it be logical that Allah obligates the one who believed in Him and leaves the disbeliever without obligation?

Yes, it is a logical matter, because obligation is good. Some people may view obligation as restrictive. We say to them: If faithful obligation were restrictive, Allah would have obligated the disbeliever with it. But Allah obligates only the one He loves. He, glorified is He, commands only good. Moreover, Allah obligates only the one who believes in Him, because the believing servant is in a covenant of faith with his Lord.

So when Allah says *kutiba* (كُتب), this means that He, glorified and exalted is He, intends that He has not intruded upon anyone's freedom of choice which He granted to him. Allah, glorified and exalted, has left people free to choose whether to believe or not to believe. Whoever believes by choice and willingly has entered into a covenant of faith with Allah, and according to this covenant Allah has prescribed obligations upon him. Among these obligations is fighting, so He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾.

His saying ﴿for you (ʿalaykum)﴾ means that fighting, at the moment it is prescribed, appears outwardly to be nothing but hardship, so ʿalaykum came to suit the matter. After the end of fighting, if we are victorious, we take the spoils, and if we are defeated and martyred, we have Paradise.

The Truth expresses the outward appearance of the matter of fighting, saying about it: ﴿And it is hateful to you, and perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾. This is a general principle, as we have said. Therefore we must refer the matter to the One who knows it, ﴿And Allah knows, while you know not﴾. So every matter we must refer to the wisdom of Allah who ordained it, because He is the One who knows.

There is a story from human heritage recounting the case of a man from China. The man owned a large plot with many horses, and among the horses was a stallion he loved. It happened that the stallion wandered off into the pastures and did not return, so he grieved over him. The people came to console him for the loss of the horse, but he smiled and said to them: "And who told you that this is an evil for you to console me about?"

After some time, the man was surprised by the stallion, with a herd of mares being driven behind it. When the people saw this, they came to congratulate him, but he said to them: "And what do you know that this is good?" So the people fell silent from congratulating him. After that his son came to ride the stallion, and it bolted with him, and the boy fell from the horse and broke his leg. The people came again to console the man, and he said to them: "And who told you that this is evil?" After that a war broke out, and the government gathered all the young men of the town to fight the enemy, but they left this son because his leg was broken. So they came to congratulate him, and he said to them: "And who told you that this is good?" So we should not take every matter by its outward appearance, whether it is good or evil. Rather, we should take every matter of life in light of the saying of the Truth:

﴿So that you do not despair over what has escaped you, nor exult over what He has given you.﴾ (from verse 23, Surat al-Hadid)

And the Truth is the One who says: ﴿And Allah knows, while you know not﴾. And to Allah belongs the highest likeness. We have previously given the example of the compassionate father who loves his only son and hopes for his remaining in this world. So when the son falls ill, the father gives him the bitter medicine, and when he gives him the dose, the son dislikes the medicine, but it is good for him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 217:

After that, the Almighty, glorified and exalted is He, speaks of another question, in which He says:

﴿They ask you about fighting in the Sacred Month. Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin), but barring from the way of Allah, disbelief in Him, (barring from) al-Masjid al-Haram, and driving out its people from it, are greater in the sight of Allah; and fitnah (persecution/disbelief) is worse than killing. And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ [2:217]

The question here is not about the Sacred Month, because it was well known to them from the days of Jahiliyyah; rather the question is about fighting in the Sacred Month. So what is the benefit of the question then? It is a provocative question, and the matter has a story. We know that the year has twelve months, and Allah has made in it four sacred months: one single month, which is Rajab, and three consecutive ones, which are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram. The meaning of "sacred months" is that fighting is forbidden in them.

Allah knows the pride of the creation over the creation, so He has made for His creatures a screen that protects their pride. Among these sunan (laws/customs) that Allah has established is the inviolability of fighting in the sacred months and the sacred places. It may be that war harms the combatant, but his pride before his enemy prevents him from halting the fighting, so he continues the war whatever the cost. Then the Almighty comes and says to the warring parties: Lay down your hands in these months, for I have forbidden fighting in them. Perhaps the combatants themselves wish from their depths that someone would intervene to stop the war, but their pride prevents them from retreating; and when the judgment of heaven intervenes, each of the two parties will find an argument to withdraw while preserving its face. Likewise Allah made sacred places, where fighting is forbidden, so that people say that it is Allah who has forbidden them, and they serve as a screen protecting their pride.

Thus the Almighty, who created man, wished to protect man so as to spare blood. If people remain for three months without war, then another month, and they enjoy in this period peace, rest and calm, they may come to love peace and not think of war again. But if war continued without pause, the frenzy of war would remain in their souls. This is the distinctive feature of the sacred months.

The sacred months are sacred in time and in place, because time and place are the container of events; every event needs a time and a place. When time is made sacred and place is made sacred, each of the two sides of the fighting gets an opportunity to calm down.

Here the Almighty presents an issue that the adversaries of Islam among the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Jews wanted to raise. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to send some sariyyas for reconnaissance, and a sariyyah is a limited number of fighters. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a sariyyah headed by Abdullah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi, the son of the aunt of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and sent with him eight men, and appointed him as their leader, and gave him a letter and ordered him not to open it until after two days' march, so that no one would know where the sariyyah was going; in this there was precaution in concealing the news.

When the sariyyah had travelled two nights, Abdullah opened the letter and read it, and behold: "Go to (Batn Nakhlah), which is a place between Makkah and al-Ta'if, and gather intelligence about the caravan of Quraysh, and do not compel anyone among those with you to march unwillingly." This meant that each member of the sariyyah had freedom of movement; whoever prefers not to march with the sariyyah has this right.

While they were on the way, a camel belonging to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and 'Utbah ibn Ghazwan strayed, and the two went searching for the camel, and six fighters remained with Abdullah. The six went to (Batn Nakhlah) and found (Amr ibn al-Hadrami) with three others, on a caravan of Quraysh, so they engaged them in battle. This day, in their assumption, was the last day of Jumada al-Akhirah, but it became clear to them afterwards that it was the first of Rajab, that is, one of the days of a sacred month.

The Muslims killed Ibn al-Hadrami, he was killed by Waqid ibn Abdullah, one of the companions of Abdullah ibn Jahsh, and they captured two of those with him, and one fled. When this happened, and it became clear to them that they had done it on the first of Rajab, then they regarded their fighting and their booty as a violation of the sanctity of the month of Rajab.

The matter was debated among the Muslims before Quraysh talked about it, for they said: Muhammad claims that he respects the sanctities and respects the sacred months, yet he fought in the sacred months, shed our blood, seized our property, and took men captive. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refrained from the booty and the captives until Allah decided the matter, and then the judgment of heaven descended in this wise word:

﴿They ask you about fighting in the Sacred Month. Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin), but barring from the way of Allah, disbelief in Him, (barring from) al-Masjid al-Haram, and driving out its people from it, are greater in the sight of Allah; and fitnah is worse than killing. And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever - those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah).

We affirm that fighting in the Sacred Month is a great matter, but look, O disbelievers of Quraysh, at what you have done to Our servants, and compare the greatness of this with the greatness of that. You say: fighting in the Sacred Month is a great matter, but your barring from the way of Allah, your disbelief, your preventing the Muslims from al-Masjid al-Haram, and your driving out the people of Makkah from it, are greater in the sight of Allah than fighting in the Sacred Month. So do not do what is greater than fighting in the Sacred Month, and then be seized by zeal for the sanctities.

It seems that Allah wanted to set out a clear principle: do not take from the particulars of religion things and shelter behind them with a word of truth while you intend falsehood. Reality presents things as they are, and we say: Yes, fighting in the Sacred Month is great. But O disbelievers of Quraysh, know that the persecution of the believers in their religion, your barring them from the path of Allah, your disbelief in Him, glory be to Him, and your violation of the sanctity of the Sacred House through what you do in it of worshipping other than Allah, and your driving out its people from it, these sinful matters are, in the sight of Allah, greater in crime and more grievous in sin than fighting in the Sacred Months to recover for the Muslims some of their rights from you.

Hence the Almighty returns the arrows of the polytheists upon their own breasts: (And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able). That is, beware lest you think that they will respect the Sacred Month or the Sacred Place; rather (they will not cease fighting you), that is, they will persist and continue fighting you (until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able).

Consider His saying: (if they are able). Its meaning is a challenge to them that they will never be able; for "in" (إن) always comes with a doubtful matter. Then the Almighty continues: (And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally). They will continue fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. Then the Almighty concludes the verse with a matter in which He says: (And whoever of you reverts from his religion). This verse is matched by another verse in which the Almighty says:

﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void, and he, in the Hereafter, is among the losers.﴾ (Part of verse 5, Surat al-Ma'idah).

If we compare the two verses, we find that the verse we are contemplating contains His saying: (and dies while he is a disbeliever), whereas in Surat al-Ma'idah this does not occur; instead there occurs His saying: (whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void). The scholars have differed on this matter in beautiful differences. But they agreed first that any person who apostatizes from Islam and then dies an apostate, his deeds have become void. Their disagreement focused on the case where he returns and believes a second time, that is, he did not die a disbeliever, but returned to faith after his apostasy: has his deed become void or not?

Imam al-Shafi'i held an opinion: the one who apostatizes from religion has his deeds voided if he dies in disbelief; but if he returns and embraces Islam again, then the deeds he performed before the apostasy are counted for him. Imam Abu Hanifah has a different opinion; he says: No, the verse of Surat al-Ma'idah does not include (and dies while he is a disbeliever), and therefore we carry it over to the verse of Surat al-Baqarah in which that is mentioned, by way of carrying the absolute upon the qualified. Accordingly, whoever disbelieves after his faith, his deed is voided whether he returns to faith afterwards or not, so no deed is credited to him.

Where then is the point of disagreement? It is this: a person believed and performed the Hajj, then, may Allah forbid, disbelieved and apostatized, then returned and believed. Does the Hajj he performed before the disbelief remain credited to him, or is it voided and he must perform a new Hajj? This is the point of disagreement. Al-Shafi'i holds that his deed is not voided since he has returned to faith, because Allah said: (and dies while he is a disbeliever), meaning that if he does not die in disbelief, his deed is not voided. But he does not receive reward for that Hajj which he had already performed. Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, turned his attention to something that many people may overlook: that Hajj is a pillar of Islam; whoever does not perform Hajj while able to, Allah punishes him for his neglect, and whoever performs it is not punished and receives the reward of his act.

So the deeds which the Almighty has demanded: if you do not perform them while you are able, you are punished; and if you perform them, your deed passes through two stages: the first stage is that you are not punished, and the second stage is that you are rewarded for the act. Al-Shafi'i said: if a person performs an act for which he would be rewarded, then apostatizes, then returns to Islam, he is not punished, but he is not rewarded. As for Imam Abu Hanifah, he said: there is no account of his deed that preceded the apostasy, in conformity with the saying of the Exalted: (their deeds have become void), meaning they were annulled and passed away, as though they had never been.

The Qur'an here uses the word (habita), which is used to express a concrete matter: one says (the livestock has become void), meaning it contracted an illness called al-Hubat, because it eats a kind of food by which it swells, and when it swells it may die. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, among what grows in spring is that which kills by hubat or causes illness (yalimm)."(1)

He, peace and blessings be upon him, warns us that good may be mixed with evil, just as happens in spring, when among the plants that grow there is that which pleases the livestock, so they eat it and the illness of hubat comes upon them, so they swell and then die, or (yalimm), that is, they are about to die. Likewise the deeds performed by the disbelievers become apparent like the swelling of the belly, and all these false operations will become void, just as the livestock that ate this kind of greenery become void and then swelled, so that the observer thinks it is fatness; then afterwards he is surprised to find that it is a disease. Allah has given us from this saying the concrete meaning through the similarity of the two images: when livestock become void, they appear as though they have grown and fattened, but it is an abnormal growth; it is not fat or flesh, but a swelling. Likewise the deeds of those who disbelieved: a void deed, even if it appears in its outward form to be great works that are good and fine.

Some people say: Is it conceivable that the disbelievers who produced achievements from which humanity has benefited will end up in this fate? They discovered cures for incurable diseases, relieved people's pains, and made comfortable and useful machines. We say to the holders of such an opinion: Wait, there is an issue on which we must agree, namely that whoever does a deed seeks a reward from the one for whom he did it. Were these people working with Allah in mind, or with humanity, fame and glory in mind? Humanity gave them glory and fame, and since they have received this reward in this world, they have no right to await a reward in the Hereafter. Therefore the Almighty says:

﴿And those who disbelieve, their deeds are like a mirage in a level plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water, until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing, and finds Allah with him, and He pays him his account in full. And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ (Surat al-Nur, 24:39).

The disbeliever thinks that his deeds are righteous and beneficial, but in the Hereafter they are like the mirage that a person sees in the desert and takes for water, and finds himself in the Hereafter before a moment of the

1 Narrated by al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 218:

And Allah, the Truth, says after that:

﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and struggled in the way of Allah — those hope for the mercy of Allah. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

The verse has enumerated three categories. The first category is those who believed; the second category is those who emigrated; and the third category is those who struggled. Those who believed, believing with sincerity for the sake of Allah's countenance, and who emigrated to support the religion, and who struggled so that the word of Islam might be exalted: these have done all of that while they hope for the mercy of Allah. And someone may say: Is not mercy a certainty for them?

We say: No servant has a certainty with Allah, because you may not notice some of your sins from which you did not repent well, nor repented from. You must keep this in mind always, and be certain of bringing to mind the intention of sincerity to Allah in every deed you undertake; for your own self may tell you something that could spoil your deed. Likewise the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is the master of creation and the master of those connected to their Lord, says: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from knowledge that does not benefit, from a deed that is not raised, and from a supplication that is not heard." (1)

The noble Messenger, who is the master of those who seek reward in all his deeds, teaches us that the self may mix with its owner something that spoils obedience. The Muslim must remain in the station of hope. The believer who trusts in his Lord does not say: "Upon Allah is an obligation to do such-and-such for me," because the price of your worship to Allah has already been paid in advance, and what you receive after that is a bounty from Allah upon you; its price is paid to you by bringing you into existence from non-existence and supplying you from nothingness, and its price is paid by Allah providing you with all these things. So if you compare what Allah has demanded of you, supposing you do not benefit from it, you have already benefited from what He gave you first, and every good that comes to you after that is from the bounty of Allah upon you, and bounty is hoped for and not certain.

The greatness of the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, lies in that you call upon Him in fear and in hope. And this example, and to Allah belongs the highest example: among the greatness of your father is that you find a father whom you fear, and whom you desire to fulfil some of your dreams; and if one of these two were to be lost, fatherhood and sonship would be disrupted.

Likewise the greatness of the Lord is both sought and feared: if you desire Him and do not fear Him, you are deficient in faith, and if you fear Him and do not desire Him, your faith is also deficient. Therefore the two must accompany each other: fear and desire. And if a person reflected on what Allah has imposed upon him of faith-based obligations, he would find that he benefits from these obligations many times over. Everything with which Allah rewards His servants is bounty, which is increase. Every provision for a person is pure bounty. And pure bounty is hoped for and not certain. Behold, the Truth says:

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly; indeed, He does not like transgressors. And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation, and call upon Him in fear and in hope; indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.﴾ (Surah al-A'raf).

The whole world is subjected under the compulsion, will and subjugation of the All-Merciful, and He has complete disposition over all created beings, and He is the Originator, the Incomparable. Therefore let the person call upon Allah with humility and submission, in private and in public, and the Truth does not love those who transgress, whether by speech, by showing off, or by harm.

Faith must be sincere to Allah, so a person must not corrupt the earth by associating partners with Allah or by disobedience; for the Truth has laid down the right method for the wellbeing of the world, which is the Qur'an, and the message of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the mercy of Allah is near to those who obey the Truth, majestic and exalted is He.

The greatness of the Lord lies in that He is sought and feared: if you desire Him and do not fear Him, your deed is not accepted, and if you fear Him and do not desire Him, your deed is not accepted. Desire and fear are both required together; therefore the believer who strives in the way of Allah hopes for the mercy of Allah.

And the Truth says: (Those hope for the mercy of Allah). What is mercy? Mercy is that you are not afflicted with pain from the very beginning. And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, says:

﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is healing and mercy for the believers.﴾ (Part of verse 82, Surah al-Isra').

Healing is that you are afflicted with an illness and Allah cures you of it; but mercy is that the illness does not come at all (and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful).

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows about His servants that none of them may be free from having some sin. So if we were to reckon by perfectly precise measures, a person among us would surely be exhausted; and therefore I always like to say with my brothers this supplication: "O Allah, by bounty and not by justice, by kindness and not by the scale, and by compensation and not by reckoning." That is, deal with us by bounty not by justice, and by Your kindness not by the scale, because the scale exhausts us.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught us that entry into Paradise is not by deeds alone, but by the bounty, mercy and forgiveness of Allah. The noble Messenger says:

("None of you will enter Paradise by his deed." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even I, until Allah covers me with His mercy.") (2)

So the believer hopes in Allah and does not make conditions upon Allah. The believer directs his deed purely to Allah, hoping for acceptance, forgiveness and mercy, and all of that is from the bounty of Allah.

1 Narrated by Ahmad, al-Hakim and Ibn Hibban from Anas.
2 Narrated by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Bayhaqi.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 219:

The discussion now turns to another question:

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: "In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." And they ask you what they should spend. Say: "The excess." Thus does Allah make clear to you the verses, that you might give thought.﴾ (2:219)

As we know, *al-khamr* (wine) is derived from *al-satr* (covering). It is said: "So-and-so entered a *khamrah*," meaning a thicket of densely interlaced trees, where he hid. *Al-khimar* is the veil a Muslim woman wears to cover her head, and it too comes from the same root. *Khamarahu al-amr* means the matter mixed with him and confused him. All these meanings derive from the act of covering. *Al-maysir* (gambling) is derived from *al-yusr* (ease), because it appears to people as easy gains without effort.

Wine and gambling were among the things well known in the *Jahiliyya* (the pre-Islamic age of ignorance). When Islam came to confront the Jahili systems, it confronted the belief without leniency. It did not confront and oppose them in stages; rather, it removed them from the outset and raised the banner of "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." Then Islam came to the matters that count as customs and began to ease them, because people were attached to them. For this reason it dealt with them with some gentleness and forbearance. This was part of the wisdom of the Shari'ah. It did not make the rulings, at the beginning, a coercive practice, which could bring about disorder in society and in the whole of existence. Rather, it handled matters with forbearance.

If wine is derived from covering, then what does it cover? It covers the intellect, as is evident from the fact that whoever consumes it loses consciousness. Allah, glorified and exalted, does not want the human being, whom He honored with intellect, to come to the very thing with which He honored him, the thing by which he manages the affairs of the vicegerency on earth, and to cover it and make it absent. For whoever does this is, as it were, returning to Allah the blessing with which He honored him, and this is foolishness.

Moreover, all those who indulge in wine justify their act by saying that they want to forget the worries of this world. We ask these people: does forgetting worries remove their sources? No. Therefore Islam asks you to live your worries so that you may confront them with the full capacity of your mind. If there are worries and problems, Islam does not want you to forget them. No, rather you must employ your intellect in facing them. Since what is required of you is to confront problems with your intellect, do not come to the center that manages life's affairs, which is the intellect, and subdue it by making it absent from its work.

Does forgetting prevent calamities? What prevents calamities is that you strive with the full power of your thought to find the way out of them. If the matter is not within your ability, then it is foolishness to think about it, because Allah wants you to rest your mind regarding such matters. If the matter has a solution and is within your power to resolve, then you need your intellect in its full strength.

Allah, the Exalted, guides us in this issue with the wisdom of the All-Wise, and He gives us the means to judge the matter ourselves before He demands it of us. He, subhanahu wa ta'ala, bestows His favor upon us and says:

﴿And from the fruits of the date palm and grapes you take intoxicant and good provision.﴾ (16:67)

When Allah mentioned *sakaran* (intoxicant), He passed over it without comment. When He said *rizqan* (provision), He described it as *hasanan* (good). We should therefore notice that Allah is paving the way for the position of Islam on wine: He did not attach any description to *sakar* (intoxicant), while He gave *rizq* the description of being good. When people extract an intoxicant from these fruits, they have taken them out of the category of good provision, because there is a difference between taking nourishment from grapes and fermenting them so that they corrupt and become something that covers the intellect.

Furthermore, there is a difference between legislation and advice. When you advise a person, you say: "I will guide you to the path of good, and you are free to follow it or not." When you legislate and establish a ruling, you command this person or that to do the matter, and nothing else.

When Allah, the Exalted, said: "They ask you about wine and gambling," He mentioned the harms to us and left us to pass judgment on them. He, glorified be He, said, addressing His Messenger (ﷺ): "Say: In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people." Had He not said "and [some] benefit for people," people would have been surprised and said: "We take benefits from wine, we earn from it, and through it we forget our worries." These were the benefits for them. But the Truth clarifies that their sin is greater than their benefit, meaning that the return from indulging in them is less than the harm that results from them. This is a just assessment. The matter had not yet entered the domain of prohibition, because it was still in the sphere of counsel and guidance.

His statement, exalted is He: "And their sin is greater than their benefit," places in them a kind of sin. Gradualness in the ruling was necessary, because He, glorified be He, is treating a matter that has become habitual, so He prepares the way to remove it from habit. Habit leads to addiction, so that when a period passes without what your nature and blood have become accustomed to, you become disturbed. Since the matter leads to habituation, it is best to close the door from the beginning and prevent habituation. The beginning of the ruling on wine was that one of the Muslims drank wine before it was finally prohibited, and then came to pray, and [the Prophet's recitation] was: "Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship." Afterward, the discipline of the Truth descended in His words:

﴿O you who have believed, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you are saying...﴾ (4:43)

In this there is training for the one accustomed to wine not to approach it. The person who prays is subject to the ruling that he should not approach prayer while intoxicated. So when does he abstain? He wakes from his sleep and does not approach wine until he has prayed the dawn prayer; then noon approaches and he prepares for prayer, then the afternoon, then after it the sunset and then the night prayer. In other words, he will no longer have a time to drink during the periods in which he awaits prayer. Thus he will have no opportunity except at the end of the night, and when night comes he drinks a cup and then sleeps deeply. The time in which he abstains from wine becomes longer than the time in which he consumes it.

When their habit of wine began to waver, some disputes and problems arose that prompted them to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to clarify a decisive ruling about wine. Then there descended His words, exalted is He:

(O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful. Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred to occur among you through intoxicants and gambling and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?) (5:90–91)

They said: "We have desisted, O Lord."

Thus, by prohibiting wine, Allah, the Exalted, wanted to preserve the human intellect for him, because the intellect is the basis of moral responsibility for the human being, and it is the basis of choosing between alternatives. So the Truth willed to safeguard that blessing for the human being. The primary aim of religion is the preservation of the five essential necessities (*al-darurat al-khams*) that man cannot do without: the preservation of life, the preservation of honor, the preservation of property, the preservation of intellect, and the preservation of religion. All legislation revolves around preserving these five necessities. If you look at these necessities, you will find that their preservation begins with the soundness of the intellect. The soundness of the intellect makes a person think about his religion. The soundness of the intellect makes him think about the movement of life. The soundness of the intellect makes him take precautions to protect honor.

Therefore the intellect is the foundation of the process of moral responsibility around which this matter revolves, and the Truth, glorified and exalted, wants a person not to cover his intellect with anything intoxicating, so that no aggression occurs against these five necessities.

In this verse, which is the subject of our reflections here, Allah has combined wine and gambling. He, exalted be His majesty, wants to protect people from heedlessness. The game of gambling, in its simple form, takes place between two people sitting opposite each other, each of them eager to take what is in the other's pocket. What brotherhood can remain between these two? Each of them is keen to send the other home with empty pockets. What brotherhood can exist between the two?

What is strange is that you see those who play gambling as companions, and each of them is eager to meet the other. What a disappointment in this friendship!

What is also strange is that each of the two parties accepts his companion's act, taking his money while remaining on friendly terms. The greatest oddity is deceit and theft among those who become accustomed to playing gambling. If you observe the lives of those who play gambling, you will find them spending and squandering without caution, never benefiting from what reaches their hands of money, however much it may be. Why? Because money that is acquired with ease is spent without caution. This is the condition of the one who wins. As for the loser, you find him living in regret and pain over what he has lost, you find him in constant poverty, and perhaps he is compelled to sacrifice his honor and dignity, if he does not sell his clothing and his most precious possessions. All of this happens through false security and deceptive hopes that Satan adorns for both parties: the winner, who wishes to have more and more money, and the loser, who hopes to recover what he has lost and to win.

When a person becomes accustomed to gaining without effort, everything becomes cheap to him, and he gets used to living on easy, cheap gain. When he finds no one to deceive into playing with him, he may steal or embezzle. This is the condition of those who play gambling: they are the people of vices in society. They are the ones who take bribes, steal, and riot, have no morals, have no true friend or companion, their homes are ruined, their families broken, and the curse is upon them even in their appearance and their dress.

For this reason the Truth said: "They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and [some] benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." Since the sin is greater than the benefit, the side of sin has been given preference. This is the case regarding the individual process. As for the temporal process, He, glorified be He, said:

﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ (4:43)

After that, He, glorified be He, ended the matter completely with His true words:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, [sacrificing on] stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ (5:90)

Then the verse proceeds to another question: "And they ask you what they should spend. Say: The excess." It is the same question from 'Amr ibn al-Jamuh, and the answer to it had previously been: "Say: Whatever wealth you spend is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler." Here is an answer in another form and image: "Say: The excess." *Al-'afw* means the surplus, and about this the Truth, glorified and exalted, says:

﴿And We never sent into a city a prophet except that We seized its people with poverty and hardship that they might humble themselves. Then We exchanged for the bad condition the good until they grew numerous and said: "Harm and ease have touched our forefathers as well," so We seized them suddenly while they were unaware.﴾ (7:94–95)

Exalted is Allah in His might. He warns and admonishes so that people may remember and take heed. He, glorified be He, never sent a prophet to a people who met him with denial and rejection without seizing them and afflicting them with poverty, misery, sickness, and harm, so that perhaps they would repent to their Lord and humble themselves before Him, that He might lift from them what He had afflicted them with. Then, when they did not return and did not desist from their disbelief and obstinacy, He tested and examined them with blessings: with abundance, wealth, health, and comfort, until they multiplied and their wealth and good things increased. They said, while in the shade of those blessings: "What befalls us of ease and hardship, good and evil, is only the custom of the world and the habit of time. Our predecessors and forefathers likewise experienced what we experience." When they persisted in their disbelief, Allah seized them with punishment and sent down a sudden torment upon them. He turned them about between hardship and ease, and treated them with harm and ease, so that they would have no argument against Allah. When the baseness of their nature became evident and they persisted in their falsehood, Allah seized them with the seizure of the Mighty, the Omnipotent. Let us reflect on His words, exalted is He, on this:

{And We had already sent to nations before you, and We seized them with poverty and hardship that they might humble themselves. Then why, when Our punishment came to them, did they not humble themselves? But their hearts became hard, and Satan made attractive to them what they were doing. So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We opened to them the gates of all things until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly.}

Al-Sha'rawi, *Tafsir al-Sha'rawi* (surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66), on surah 2, verse 220:

Al-Haqq (the Truth) begins this verse with His words: *"in this world and the Hereafter."* It is as if He is saying to us: beware of believing that every obligation from God is rewarded only in the Hereafter. No, the reward will reach you in this world too.

Consider the lives of those who are upright and committed to the method of their religion and to the method of good character. You will find that they have received their reward in this world: contentment, happiness, and security. So much so that people ask: how did so-and-so raise his children, and how did he educate them, despite his modest salary?

They do not realize that God's hand is with him, bringing blessing into every movement of his life. So do not think that reward is confined to the Hereafter. Rather, God hastens reward in this world, while the Hereafter is an addition, and we take the provision of the Hereafter by God's bounty. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: *"None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God covers me with His mercy."*¹

I would like each of us to reflect on the condition of upright people in the way of life, to see how they live and how they provide for their children, and to consider the cheerfulness and contentment they enjoy, and how their lives are free of problems and psychological complexes.

It is as if the All-Glorified and Exalted is drawing our attention to the fact that everything that came in the straight method was sent to organize the movement of life for us and to free us from the desires of the soul.

After Al-Haqq finished speaking about the pilgrimage, the fifth pillar of Islam, He showed us two categories within society. The first category is the hypocrite, whose speech does not match the reality of his heart and soul:

﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you, and he calls God to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents.
