The beginning of marriage was a serious matter, which we entered by offer and acceptance and witnesses, and you enter the matter while studying its consequences and circumstances. But the matter in the process of divorce differs: a man does not control his own anger (aghmar nafsihi), for the cause of it may be trivial or something that could have passed without divorce. So God, the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, willed to give people deliberation and reflection in untying the knot, and He said: "Divorce is twice," meaning once and then once. Someone may say: how can it be twice when we say three? A man once asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), saying: "O Messenger of God, God the Exalted said: 'Divorce is twice,' so why has it become three?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, smiling: "Then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment." So the meaning of "Divorce is twice" is that within your range of choice you have two pronouncements of divorce for the woman; the third is not yours, and why? Because after it there will be a great separation (baynunah kubra), and her returning to you will no longer be your right; rather this woman has become the right of another man.

﴿Until she marries another husband﴾ [2:230].

As for a man saying to his wife, "You are divorced thrice" (anti talaqun thalathan), is it counted as three pronouncements or not? We say: time is a fundamental condition in the occurrence of divorce. A man divorces his wife once, then a period of time passes, and he divorces her again, and it becomes a second pronouncement, and again a period of time passes, and after that we reach His saying: "then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment." Therefore the text of the verse is clear and explicit that divorce by three in a single utterance does not take effect as three pronouncements, but is one pronouncement. It is true that our master 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) made it three pronouncements, because people had made the matter easy, so he saw fit to be strict with them so that they would desist; but they did not desist, and thus we return to the original legislation as it came in the Qur'an, which is "Divorce is twice."

The wisdom of distributing divorce over three occasions and not in a single phrase is that the Truth, glorified is He, gives an opportunity for reversal. Giving the opportunity does not come in one breath and in one sitting. The man who says to his wife, "You are divorced thrice," has not taken the opportunity to reconsider himself, and if we counted his saying as three pronouncements, married life would be destroyed by a single word. But the greatness of the legislation is that the Truth, glorified is He, distributed divorce over occasions so that a person may reconsider himself; perhaps he erred the first time, so he retains her the second time and repents. Whenever you find the legislation distributing a matter that may or may not happen, there must be a time interval between each occasion. Some who pretend eloquence want to justify to people their assault on the method of God, and they say: God ruled that polygamy cannot be achieved, and He said:

﴿And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive to do so﴾ [4:129].

They say: God made justice a condition of plural marriage, then ruled that we will never be able to be equitable between wives however much we strive; so it is as if He went back on the legislation. This is their logic. We say to them: complete the reading of the verse and you will understand the meaning. The Truth says: "And you will never be able to be equitable between wives, even if you should strive to do so," and then He branched upon the negation, saying:

﴿So do not incline completely [away from one]﴾ [4:129].

Since the negation has been made the basis of a further ruling, it has been cancelled out; the matter, as they say, is that the negation of a negation is an affirmation. The ability is established and remains, and His saying, "So do not incline completely," was an indication of it. Likewise here: "Divorce is twice; then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment." Since He said, "then either retention in kindness or release with good treatment," and He said, "Divorce is twice," it means that every act has its time, and that accords with the stages of discipline and refinement. Otherwise, divorce by three in a single word at a single time is one compulsory act, with no discipline, reform or refinement in it. On this matter the Truth says: "It is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them" (4:20), because it is expected of the husband to pay the dowry in return for his enjoyment of the woman; so when divorce occurs, it is not lawful for the divorcer to take anything of her dowry. But the Truth made an exception in the matter, saying: "unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them for what she gives up to be released."

It is as if the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, wanted to give the woman a way out if harm is intended for her and she does not accept that harm. So the Truth comes and legislates: since they fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, He has permitted her, if she ransoms herself, O woman, with some property; and it is disliked to exceed the dowry, unless that excess arises from her disobedience (nushuz) and opposition to the husband, in which case there is then no reprehensibility in exceeding the dowry.

Reality came to match what God legislated when the incident of Jamilah, the sister of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, occurred, when she was the wife of 'Abd Allah ibn Qays. She went to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "I do not blame him in his religion or his character, but I do not love disbelief in Islam." She meant that she lived with him while hating him, so she would not render his right, and that is kufr al-'ashir, that is, denying the husband's right and abandoning obedience to him.

She said that she does not blame him either in his religion or in his character, in order to express other emotional meanings by that. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) wanted to learn that from her, and she said: "I lifted the tent and found him among a group of men, and I saw him as the blackest of them, the shortest in stature, and the ugliest in face." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to her: "Will you return his garden (hadiqah) to him?" She said: "Yes, and if he wishes I will add to it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "We have no need of the addition, but return his garden to him."

This matter is called khul', that is, a woman releases herself from her husband whom she fears she cannot render some right of the marital bond; she releases herself from him with property, so that no harm befalls him, for he may want to marry another and need what he gave as dowry to the one from whom she wants to release herself. The Truth, glorified is He, continues: "It is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them," and this thing is what God mentioned elsewhere:

﴿And you have given one of them a talent (qintar)﴾ [4:20].

The Truth continues the verse with His saying: "unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah," and what is meant here is the two spouses. After that comes the responsibility of the guardians of the spouses and of the society that cares about their affair, in His saying: "But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon either of them for what she gives up. These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah – it is those who are the wrongdoers." The limits of Allah are what Allah legislated for His servants as a barrier separating the lawful from the forbidden. The limits of Allah either come after prohibitions or come after commands. If they come after commands, He says: "These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them," meaning: this is your ultimate aim here, so do not exceed the boundary. But if they come after prohibitions, He says: "These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them," because the Truth wants to prevent the soul from being affected by the forbidden things, for they insistently urge it to act; so if you are far from them, it is better that you remain far.

And consider carefully what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "What is lawful is clear and what is unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters. Whoever guards against doubtful matters has cleared himself regarding his religion and his honour, and whoever falls into doubtful matters falls into the unlawful, like the shepherd who grazes around the sanctuary (hima), about to fall into it. Surely every king has a sanctuary, and the sanctuary of God on earth is His prohibitions."(1) Since the limits include God's prohibitions and God's commands, everything commanded and everything forbidden must remain within its domain of action in "do" and of prohibition in "do not do." When the system of "do" passes into the realm of "do not do," and what belongs to the realm of "do not do" passes into the realm of "do," the order of the universe is disrupted; and since the order of the universe has been struck by disorder, injustice occurs. Injustice is that you transfer a person's right and give it to another person, and the legislation of divorce is one of the limits of Allah; so if you try to bring a matter that does not suit what Allah commanded in social organisation, you have transferred the commanded into the sphere of the forbidden, and thereby you cause injustice.

When the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, addresses the issues of society, He treats them with a treatment that prevents society from falling into diseases and afflictions. If we think well of people, that they legislate for good and for public interest, they legislate according to the extent of their knowledge of things; but we are not safe from their being ignorant of something that happens and that they do not know. They legislated for what they knew, and if they legislate for what they know and are then confronted with things they did not know, what is the position? If they are sincere, they truly trample the pride of their legislative conceit and say: we amend what we legislated; but if they persist in their obstinacy, who is it that suffers? Society is what suffers from their stubbornness.

The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, does not accuse people collectively of there being among them those who do not want good; but there is a difference between wanting good and not being able to achieve it. You legislated according to your capacity and knowledge. We all know that the suffering from experiments in theoretical social laws falls upon society.

We also know well that there is a difference between experimental laboratory science and speculative, passion-driven talk. Experimental science is suffered by the one who conducts the experiment: the scientist toils and exhausts himself in his laboratory, and he is the one who suffers, sacrificing his time, his wealth and his health, living in oblivion of everything except the experiment he is engaged in. When he arrives at a discovery, however, it is society that rejoices in his discovery. But the matter differs in theoretical things, because it is society that suffers from the errors of human legislators, until a legislator comes who has compassion for society and corrects the error of his predecessor.

As for the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, He has brought us legislation that protects humankind from suffering. God, glorified is He, leaves us free in the material, experimental world. Enter the laboratory and you will arrive at things on which you may agree, but beware of the disputes of passions; therefore God, mighty and majestic is He, has undertaken to legislate for what passions dispute over, so as to guarantee that society does not suffer from the error of legislators, for a period of time until another legislator comes and corrects for people what someone else erred in.

Therefore in our contemporary world we find many matters rooted in desire, around which people cling to their passions, until events press upon them with a pressure that leaves them unable thereafter to bury their heads in the sand; they must confront them, and when they confront them they find no solution to them except what Islam has legislated, and they find that they have come together with the legislation of Islam.

Some of those who hate Islam say: you say about your religion that it came to prevail over all religions; once the Qur'an says:

﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion, and sufficient is Allah as witness﴾ [48:28].

(1) Related by al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 230:

Then the Truth (al-Haqq) says:

﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband. And if he divorces her, there is no blame upon them both for returning to one another, if they think that they can keep within the limits of Allah. And these are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear to a people who know.﴾

The Truth had already said: "Divorce is twice" (al-Talaq marratan), and after that He said: "then either retain her in kindness or release her with good treatment." Here the Truth speaks of release (al-tasrih) in His words: "And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband." This is so that He may make clear to us that if matters between the spouses reach the stage of no return, then a harsh lesson is necessary, and neither of them can return to the other easily. God gave them respite by legislating the minor separation (al-bayniyyah al-sughra), which is followed by a new dowry and a new contract, but they did not desist. So the major separation (al-bayniyyah al-kubra) became necessary, namely that the woman marry another husband and experience another marital life. In this way the lesson is harsh.

Some men may take the matter in a merely formal way: they marry a woman divorced three times with a marriage complete in its conditions, of contract, witnesses and dowry, but no sexual intercourse follows from the marriage between them. This is the (muhallil) that we hear about, and it is what Islam has not approved.

Whoever marries on the basis that he is a muhallil, and whoever agrees to that muhallil, let both know that this is forbidden to both of them. There is no muhallil in Islam. Whoever enters into marriage with the intention of muhallil, the wife is not lawful to him, and he has no rights over her. At the same time, if that man divorces her, it is not lawful for her to return to her former husband, because the muhallil was not a husband but a mere imitation of a husband, and imitation establishes nothing in reality. Therefore the Truth said: "she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband."

What is meant here is the natural marriage to which circumstances lead without contrivance and without any intention of making her lawful again. When that man divorces her due to circumstances beyond his will, namely the impossibility of living together, and not for reasons agreed upon, then the former husband may marry the woman who was in his marriage and whom he had divorced three times previously.

(﻿"And if he divorces her, there is no blame upon them both for returning to one another, if they think that they can keep within the limits of Allah. And these are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear to a people who know.") That is, it must be strongly presumed that the matters which were a source of dispute in the past have ended, and that the two have reached a degree of good sense and mutual respect, and have taken a lesson from experience that makes each of them content with the other.

And after that, the Truth says:

﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, then either keep them with kindness or release them with kindness. And do not keep them, harming them, so that you transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself. And do not take the verses of Allah in jest. And remember Allah's favour upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He instructs you. And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ [2:231]

Let us note His saying: ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾, and ask: when the term has been reached and the 'iddah has ended, is there still any keeping with kindness or release with goodness? Is there anything except release? Indeed, there is another verse after it which says: ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands if they agree among themselves in a reasonable manner﴾ (part of 2:232).

So we are before two verses, each of which begins with His saying: ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾. But the continuation of the first verse is: ﴿then keep them with kindness or release them with kindness﴾, and the continuation of the second verse is: ﴿do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾. What is the secret of this difference? We say: "reaching" (bulugh) comes with two meanings. The first meaning: it comes in the sense of approaching, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾. That is, when you are about to rise for prayer, then do that. The second meaning: "bulugh" is applied to actual and factual arrival. When a person is traveling by airplane and lands in the destination country, he notices that the pilot announces that he has arrived at such-and-such a country. So sometimes "bulugh" is applied to nearness, and sometimes to real attainment.

In the first verse, ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, then keep them with kindness or release them with kindness﴾: here the man has divorced his wife, but her 'iddah has not ended; rather, it is nearing its end. So he may release her or keep her with goodness, and the husband has a portion of the 'iddah period that permits him to keep or release, but it is a short time. The Truth wants the husband to hold on to retaining her until the very last moment, and to preserve the causes of reunion and of not separating until the last moment. This is the reason for the expression ﴿they reach their term﴾, that is, they approach reaching the term. The Truth wants us to hold on to preserving married life until the last opportunity that allows keeping, for it is a moment in which the man may utter a word upon which either divorce follows or the return of married life.

As for the second verse, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾, Allah, glory be to Him, wants to confine the discussion of the causes of separation or continuation between husband and wife to the two of them only, and not extend it to anyone other than husband and wife; for between the two there are causes that may make each of them soften towards the other.

But if a third party enters who does not have this, the enmity will grow in his soul and he will not have the need, so the companionship of the spouses will not endure. If a father, a brother or a mother enters the dispute, the hostility will ignite, and each of them does not feel the feeling each spouse has for the other, nor the gentleness of the husband toward his wife, nor the conciliation of the wife toward her husband. These are emotional and psychological matters that exist only between husband and wife, whereas external parties are bound to the husband and wife only by kinship. Hence the eagerness of those external parties to preserve the companionship of the spouses is not like the eagerness of each spouse to hold on to the other.

Therefore we must understand that every problem that occurs between a husband and his wife, and in which no one intervenes, ends quickly without a mother, a father or a brother, because the intervention of an external party is not one who possesses the emotional and psychological motives that exist between the spouses. As for the spouses themselves, a single glance from one to the other may suffice to restore matters to their course. A man may be impressed by a woman's beauty and long for her, and so forget everything. A woman may see in the man something she does not want to lose from him, and so forget what happened between them, and so on. But what of that compared with her mother and his mother, or her father and his father? Between these and the spouses there are no secrets, feelings, intimacy and the like.

For this reason I always advise that disagreement remain confined between husband and wife, because Allah has placed between them an emotional flow. The emotional flow may flow into a yearning and desire for something, and perhaps this desire is what reconciles and makes each of the two parties give up the enmity and divorce. Therefore the will of Allah, mighty and majestic, decreed that a man should not divorce his wife while she is menstruating. Why?

Because during the menstrual period a husband has no desire for her, and perhaps he recoils from her. But the Truth, mighty and majestic, wants a man not to divorce his wife except in a purity period in which he has not had marital relations with her, and after she has washed from the menses, so that he divorces her only when he is at the most intense time of desire for her.

Thus Allah, glory be to Him, wants the disputes between husband and wife to take place within the framework of married life, so that a fence of love, affection and mercy may protect them. But the intervention of other parties breaks this fence, whoever the party may be: a mother, a father or a brother.

The Truth says: ﴿And do not keep them, harming them, so that you transgress﴾. That is, do not, O man, maintain married life for the purpose of harming the woman and humiliating her. The meaning of "harm" (ḍirār) is that you do something which outwardly appears to seek good, while inwardly you intend evil. Therefore the term was applied to the "Mosque of Harm": its outward construction was that of a mosque built for prayer in it, but inwardly its purpose was disbelief and dividing the believers. Likewise harm in marriage: a man says, "I do not want to divorce her, and I will take her back to her home," and he says this while concealing in himself that he will take her back in order to humiliate her and take revenge on her. Islam does not approve of that; rather, it forbids it.

The Almighty warns against such conduct, saying: ﴿And do not keep them, harming them, so that you transgress; and whoever does that has wronged himself﴾. So beware lest you think that when you transgress against your wife after taking her back, you have wronged her. No, you are only wronging yourself, for when you transgress against a person, you have made his Lord his adversary. If he calls down a curse upon you, Allah accepts his supplication, and thereby you deprive yourself of Allah's pleasure with you. Is there any wrong greater than the wrong that brings Allah's displeasure upon you?

The Truth, glory be to Him, continues: ﴿Whoever does that has wronged himself, and do not take the verses of Allah in jest﴾. That is, take Allah's system as a system that came to govern the movement of life with decisiveness, without evasion and without soaring in false imagination; rather it is a realistic matter. It is not proper for anyone to mock what Allah has sent down of regulations that preserve the life and dignity of the human being, man or woman. ﴿And remember Allah's favour upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He instructs you﴾. The favour of Allah upon them, which He reminds them of in the context of speaking about divorce, is that He, glory be to Him, draws their attention to what they were before He legislated for them: where was the woman's share in matters of marriage and divorce in the Jahiliyyah, and what did she become after the Qur'an was revealed? Her rights became protected by the Qur'an.

The Almighty bestows favour upon the believers to draw their attention to their condition before Islam. A man would divorce his wife and take her back, then divorce her and take her back, even a thousand times, without restraint or bond. He would withhold marital intimacy from her for months, leaving her to be tormented by the anguish of separation from him, and she could not speak.

When her husband died, a woman would be banished from society, never appearing and never leaving her house, as if she were a contagion. And before all of that, she was a source of shame for her father, so he would kill her before she reached the age of puberty, under the pretext of guarding his honour and reputation.

In short, marriage was closer to mockery than to seriousness. Then Islam came and settled matters so that there would be no chaos without controls and without laws. So remember, O believers, Allah's favour upon you through Islam, and look at the family system with which He has blessed you, which the world, East and West, pants to reach the like of.

You were a nation without civilization and without culture, worshipping idols, waging war and igniting it among yourselves over the most trivial and base causes, ignorant of reading and writing. Then Allah sent down upon you this refined, mature legislation to which no civilization has yet attained. Do you not remember this favour in which you are by a grace from Allah? Therefore He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And remember Allah's favour upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He instructs you﴾. The Book is the Qur'an, and the wisdom is the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Truth concludes that noble verse with His saying: "And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things."

So beware of accusing your religion of having lacked any legislation for you, for every legislation is ready in Islam, because Allah is Knowing of what the conditions of people will be, so nothing is missed by Allah from what is actually the case, in accordance with what Allah has legislated in His Book, for He, glory be to Him, is the Creator of the universe and the Sender of legislation.

Then the Truth (Allah) says:

﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their (former) husbands, if they agree among themselves in a proper manner. This is admonished to whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day. That is more purifying for you and more pure. And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾

(فبلغن أجلهن) here means: the waiting period (ʿiddah) has ended, and the husband has not used up the divorces, and the husband has no right to take her back except after a new contract and a new dowry. Suppose the husband wants to restore his wife to his marital bond again. Here, the people of obstinacy and enmity among the relatives interfere and stand in the way of completing the marriage. The spouses may each be inclined toward the other, with an emotional and psychological bond between them that no one knows, but those relatives who have entered into the dispute stand in the way of returning matters to their proper course, fearing the repetition of what happened or for other reasons. To them it is said: since the spouses have agreed to return, it is not right for anyone to stand in the way of returning matters to what they were.

His words, the Truth: (فلا تعضلوهن) From it we know that ʿadl (ʿaḍl, prevention) is restraint, and the address is to the family, the relatives, and everyone who cares for the interest of both parties, from among the people of good counsel. And (أن ينكحن أزواجهن) means: those who had divorced them first.

The meaning: do not prevent the husbands from restoring to their marital bond the wives whom they had divorced before. Let the family members who insist on preventing their daughters from returning to their husbands know that by persisting in the dispute they are blocking the benefit of the gradualness in divorce that God's wisdom intended.

The wisdom of legislating that divorce be once or twice is that one who did not reform the first time may reform the second time. Since God, who knows the souls of human beings, has prescribed for them to divorce once or twice, and has given a space of time to the one who erred the first time so that he does not err the second time, therefore it is not right for anyone to stand as an obstacle before the renewal of married life.

His words, the Truth: (أن ينكحن أزواجهن) We note here that the Truth, glory be to Him, attributes the marriage to the women, saying (ينكحن). This requires the woman's consent to returning to the husband, so it is not possible that he divorces her first and then she has no say in returning to him.

(إذا تراضوا بينهم بالمعروف) And since they have agreed and seen that each one's return to the other is better, let the people of evil who stand against the consent of both parties keep away, and let them leave the lawful to return to its course. (ذلك يوعظ به من كان منكم يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر ذلكم أزكى لكم وأطهر) This is the legislation of your Lord, and it is an admonition for you, O you who believe in Allah as a wise Lord, a legislator, and one who knows the impulses of goodness in human souls.

The word (وأطهر) draws our attention to the prohibition of standing in the way of a woman who wants to return to her husband who divorced her after the waiting period has ended, and he wants to marry her again. The Truth conveys to us: do not stand against their desire to return for any reason whatsoever. Why, O Lord?

The answer comes in His words, the Truth: (والله يعلم وأنتم لا تعلمون) Consider the beauty of the Qur'anic context and how His words (والله يعلم وأنتم لا تعلمون) served the meaning that the verses intend. Allah knows, and you do not know, that in the return of matters between the spouses to their proper course there is more purity and more cleanness.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 233:

And then Allah, the Truth, says:

﴿And the mothers shall suckle their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the suckling. And upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and their clothing according to what is reasonable. No soul is burdened except according to its capacity. No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child. And upon the heir is the like of that. And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them. And if you wish to seek a wet-nurse for your children, there is no blame upon you, provided you hand over what you agreed upon, according to what is reasonable. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ [2:233]

Behold the greatness of Islam. Here is Allah, glorified is He, speaking about mothers suckling their children after divorce. Divorce breeds discord between man and woman, and Allah, with the mercy and knowledge of One who knows His servants, looks at the matter and wishes to protect the fruit that resulted from the marriage before discord arises between the parents. So He informs us: do not make your discord, your disagreement and your divorce a source of misery for the innocent, nursing child.

This speech concerns divorced women who have left their husbands' houses, because Allah says afterwards: ﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and their clothing according to what is reasonable.﴾ Since the verse speaks of ﴿their provision and their clothing﴾, this means the woman and her infant are apart from the man, for if she were with him the infant's provision and clothing would be a settled matter. Here Allah imposes a right for the infant, which the mother would not be entitled to were it not for the nursing. Some people have mistakenly understood that provision and clothing are owed to wives in general, and we say to them: No. The provision and clothing here are for divorced women who nurse only.

Allah, the Truth, wishes to make this right a settled matter, so He legislated the infant's right that his father should provide for him with provision and clothing, so that the matter is known to him at the time of divorce.

As for His saying, ﴿The mothers shall suckle their children for two complete years﴾, we note that it does not come in the form of a command. He did not say, "O mothers, suckle!", because a command is liable to be obeyed or disobeyed. Rather, Allah presented the matter in a declarative form, as a natural and necessary fact that does not contradict itself.

Allah says: ﴿And upon the one to whom the child belongs is their provision and their clothing.﴾ Let us reflect on the greatness of the Qur'anic expression in His saying: ﴿upon the one to whom the child belongs﴾. He did not say "upon the father", but used "the one to whom the child belongs" in order to assign him the burdens of provision and clothing, because the responsibility for supporting the child belongs to the father and not to the mother, though she has carried, given birth and suckled, and the child is ultimately attributed to the father. The poet says:

Indeed the mothers of people are but vessels,
Repositories, while the fathers have the children.

Since the child is ascribed to the man, the father, provision and clothing for him are upon the father, and upon him also is the provision and clothing of his mother who nurses him, according to what is customary and recognized, without causing injustice or oppression to the father through excessive spending. Allah says: ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity.﴾ Here the discourse concerns the mother and the father. It is not proper that the divorced woman burden the father of the infant with what is beyond his ability; she should be content with reasonable maintenance.

Allah continues: ﴿No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child.﴾ Allah still reminds the father that he is the one to whom the child belongs, and he must not harm the child's mother by withholding spending on his son, nor leave her begging people for his provision and clothing. At the same time He reminds the mother: do not make your nursling a source of harm to his father by excessive insistence in seeking provision and clothing.

He, mighty and majestic, sets for us the precise framework that secures the child's rights. There is a difference between an infant who enjoys the warmth of life between parents who live together, and one who exists between parents who do not live together.

Allah, glorified is He, gives us another point: the father of the child may die. If the father dies, who then spends on the infant who is in the care of his divorced mother? Here comes the swift answer of the Truth: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that.﴾

The Truth establishes the responsibility of spending upon the one who inherits from the infant's father. True, the infant will inherit from his father, but the care of the orphaned infant is the responsibility of the one who inherits guardianship and has authority over the father's wealth if he dies. Thus Allah, mighty and majestic, guarantees the infant's right from the one to whom he belongs, his father, while the father is alive, and from the father's heir if he has died.

In this way Allah, mighty and majestic, has legislated for the preservation of the child's way of life when both parents are present, and He legislated for him in the case of his parents' divorce while his father is alive, and He legislated for him in the case of his parents' divorce and his father's death. Allah continues: ﴿And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them.﴾ Behold the mercy in Islam: a man's divorcing his wife does not mean that what was between them has ended, such that the children are lost and suffer because of the divorce. His saying, ﴿by mutual consent and consultation﴾, is evidence that there is a common matter still existing between the two parties, namely what concerns the raising of the children. This common matter must take into account the children's right to the tenderness of motherhood and their right to the tenderness of fatherhood, so that the child grows up not deprived of the compassion of either mother or father, even if they have disagreed to the point of divorce.

Both of them must meet through consultation and mutual consent regarding the raising of the children, so that the children feel the affection of both parents, grow up without psychological wounds, and understand that their mother appreciates their circumstances, and likewise their father; and despite the discord and disagreement between them, they have agreed, for the children's benefit, by mutual consent and consultation.

What happens in many cases of divorce, namely neglect of the children after divorce, is a grave matter, because it leaves deep residues and negative effects in the children's souls, and results in their misery and perhaps their being scattered in life. And what fault is it of children whose parents were the direct cause of their coming into life? Is it not better that fathers provide them with the psychological and living conditions that secure a noble upbringing? The method of Allah is before us, so why do we not apply it so that we may be happy by it and future generations may be happy by it? Allah, the Truth, said at the beginning of the verse: ﴿The mothers shall suckle their children for two complete years﴾, but what is the situation if circumstances arise that reduce the period of suckling below two years, or special circumstances arise that make the suckling period longer than two years? Here the Truth says: ﴿And if they both desire weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them.﴾

He, exalted is He, shows us that weaning (al-fisal, i.e., weaning) must be by mutual consent and consultation between the two parents, and there is no blame upon them in that. The Truth says: ﴿And if you wish to seek a wet-nurse for your children, there is no blame upon you, provided you hand over what you agreed upon, according to what is reasonable.﴾ And "to seek a wet-nurse for your children" means to bring a nurse for the infant; so if you wish that, there is no blame upon you for it.

When the divorcing man entrusts the mother with suckling her infant, the child takes from the mother's tenderness that is present in her by nature. But suppose the mother lacks the ability to nurse, or her circumstances do not allow her to nurse him because of weakness in her health or strength. In that case the father is obliged to bring his son a wet-nurse, and this wet-nurse who suckles the infant needs to be given by the father what makes her willing to nurse the child faithfully and to supervise him sincerely.

The Truth concludes this noble verse with His saying: ﴿And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ The Truth warns against someone who takes His rulings and claims to apply them in outward appearance, while he is not concerned with the spirit of these rulings. An example of that is the father who wishes to deceive society: when he sees his son's wet-nurse in front of people, he claims that he spends on her and gives her full wages, and treats her with warmth and honour, while the reality contradicts that.

Allah warns the one who does this: you are not dealing with society but with Allah. ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 2, verse 234:

Then the Truth (Allah) says:

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait for themselves four months and ten days. And when they have reached their term, there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves in an honorable way. And Allah is Aware of what you do.﴾

As we have known, the 'iddah (the prescribed waiting period) is the span of time that Allah has legislated after a marriage that has ended either by divorce or by the death of the husband. The 'iddah is either after a divorce or after the death of a husband. If the 'iddah is after a divorce, its duration is three qur' (the plural of qur', which we have known to mean either the menstrual period or the purity between periods). If the divorced woman is a young girl who has not yet menstruated, or an older woman who has passed the age of menstruation, then the 'iddah changes from qur' to months and becomes (three months).

We have also known that the husband has the right to take back his wife (raj'ah) privately, between himself and her, without the intervention of the wife or her guardian. He may do so during the 'iddah period in a revocable divorce (talaq raj'i). If her 'iddah has ended, his right to take her back himself has lapsed, and he may still remarry her, but with a new dowry (mahr) and a new contract, as long as he still has a right, that is, as long as he has not used up the divorces.

We have said that if the divorces have reached two and there is a third divorce, then she must marry another husband in the natural manner, not with the intention of making her lawful for the first husband (tahlil). As for the 'iddah of a woman whose husband has died, we have known that the Qur'an stipulates that she waits for herself four months and ten days. This applies if she is not pregnant. If she is pregnant, her 'iddah is the later of the two terms. If the later term is four months and ten days, then that is her 'iddah. If the later term is the pregnancy, then her 'iddah is until the pregnancy ends. But is it not possible that her husband dies while she is in the ninth month of pregnancy, and she gives birth before he is buried? Does that mean her 'iddah has ended? No. It ends with the later of the two terms, which in this case is the passing of four months and ten days. Although some jurists (fuqaha') say that the 'iddah of a pregnant woman ends with the birth.

However, if her husband has not died, her 'iddah is that she gives birth to her child. If she wishes to marry after that, she may do so, even after a moment.

Some people explain the wisdom behind making the 'iddah of a widow four months and ten days, saying: if she is pregnant with a boy, her pregnancy will become apparent when the child moves after three months, and if she is pregnant with a girl, it will move after four months, and so we give her a grace period of ten nights.

We say to them: may Allah reward you well for your explanation, but the 'iddah here is not for ascertaining the womb's emptiness (istibra' al-rahm), because if it were for that purpose, a woman's 'iddah would end simply upon her giving birth. And if the matter were only to confirm whether or not there is a pregnancy, her 'iddah would be three menstrual periods if she is one who menstruates, and if she is one who does not menstruate, due to youth or old age, her 'iddah would be three months. But Allah singled her out with four months and ten days, in fulfilment of her husband's right over her and in honour of their married life.

Thus Allah, mighty and majestic, made the widow wait the longest period a woman can endure. So, for as long as she is a widow, she does not leave her house, does not adorn herself, and meets no one, out of loyalty to her husband. When her 'iddah ends, that is, when the four months and ten days have passed over her, (there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves), which means that she may adorn herself in her house and go out without displaying adornment, and that whoever wishes to propose to her may approach her. His saying, may He be exalted: (four months and ten), the intended meaning of this period is four months and ten nights.

Here is an educational point of faith that shows that every legal ruling applies to all those who are responsible (mukallaf), even if the ruling does not directly concern them. The widow waited four months and ten days and reached the end of the 'iddah period. Among Allah's rulings for her was that she should not adorn herself, not apply kohl, and not leave her house, out of loyalty to her husband. When she reaches the term and it ends, He says: (there is no blame on you for what they do with themselves), and He did not say: "there is no blame on them."

The address here is directed to men, because every believer has authority (wilayah) over every believing woman. If he sees in her conduct, or in the way she takes care of herself, something that contradicts the 'iddah, he may intervene. For example, if he sees her adorning herself, he may say to her, or send someone to say to her: "Why are you adorning yourself?" The saying of Allah: (there is no blame on you) gives men a guardianship (qawamah) over the widow, so they cannot say: "It is none of our business," because the rule of faith applies to every believer and is incumbent on every believer. Allah, the Truth, Glorified and Exalted, says:

﴿And they enjoin one another to truth and enjoin one another to patience﴾ (part of verse 3, Surah al-'Asr).

His saying, the Truth: (they enjoin one another) does not mean that some people are singled out as those who advise, and others are those who are advised. Rather, each of us is an advisor at one time and advised by others at another time. This is the meaning of (they enjoin one another).

So if you see weakness in another person in any aspect of Allah's rulings, you may advise him. Likewise, if another sees weakness in you in any aspect, he may advise you. When we all advise one another, no obvious error will remain among us.

Thus the verse does not restrict advising to one group rather than another; rather, everyone advises one another, because human circumstances alternate among all people. You, in your time of weakness, are a watcher over me, so you advise me. And I, in your time of weakness, am a watcher over you, so I advise you. That is why the Truth's saying came: (there is no blame on you). He, glorified be He, did not address the women, but addressed the believers, and He did not restrict the address to the guardians of women alone. Rather, He left the ruling for everyone, so that no one would say: "I have no connection with the woman whose husband has died; let her do whatever she likes." For her, it is permissible to adorn herself in what is known in Islam as adornment, and to beautify herself within the limits that Allah has permitted her.

The Truth concludes this verse with His saying: (And Allah is Aware of what you do), that is, Allah knows what is in her soul and in her intention. Suppose she did some act out of the sight of anyone. Do not think that because society did not witness it, the matter has ended. No, Allah knows what she does, even if no one among people has become aware of it.

Through all the previous legislation, Allah, glorified and exalted, has protected the husband's right until the 'iddah ends, and the right of the widow during her 'iddah. He has also protected, through all these legislations, the dignity of the woman. He made the woman a sanctuary (haram) that no one may approach or violate her veil. During this period she is observing an 'iddah that is reckoned for another man, so no one has the right to approach her.

Why? Because a woman, especially a divorced one, may be seized by a desire to avenge herself and her dignity, and she may hasten to remarry. Perhaps the separation or dispute arose from the insinuation of someone's desire for her. And as soon as her divorce is completed and she lives through the 'iddah period, those who desire her may hover around her, or she may herself look toward someone she sees as a suitable husband. That is why the Truth imposes a barrier of time and makes the 'iddah like a forbidden zone, to protect the woman with a substantive protection, not merely a formal one.

The legislation is that of a merciful God, who does not disregard the emotions of the human soul, neither on the side of the man who wishes to marry nor on the side of the woman who looks forward to marriage. He treats this matter with precision, firmness, and decisiveness together, saying, may He be exalted:

﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply of proposal to women or what you conceal within yourselves. Allah knows that you will remember them, but do not promise them secretly, except that you say a known word. And do not determine the tie of marriage until the decreed term reaches its end. And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ [2:235]

"Arradtum" (عرّضتم) is derived from *ta'rid* (التعريض), which is to indicate something not by what it expresses explicitly, but to allude to it by hint.

Allah, glorified and exalted, wishes to give emotions an outlet from this side. The outlet is not merely an expression of the emotion, but a safeguarding of interest. For if allusion were absolutely forbidden, the woman might lose the opportunity of marriage, or the prohibition might cause the man to lose the opportunity of one who seeks her. Therefore the Truth establishes rules that impose upon both man and woman together the etiquette of caution, as if He were saying to us: "I forbid you to propose or to speak explicitly and plainly during the waiting period ('iddah), but there is no harm in allusion from a distance."

For example, a man may praise a woman and enumerate her good qualities in words that are not considered a departure from the etiquette of Islam. Such speech is hinting and allusion. Its benefit is that it expresses what is in the speaker's heart toward the divorced woman, so she knows his opinion of her. Had he not said it, someone else might have preceded him to her and cut off his path to fulfilling what was in his heart, and it might also prevent him from proposing after the end of the waiting period. It may also push him to think in another way, to express himself in a mistaken manner and form.

Thus, allusion has the benefit that it lets the divorced woman know the opinion of so-and-so about her, so that if someone else comes to her, she does not immediately consent to him. Thus we see a ray of the mercy of Allah, the Exalted, toward us, in that He made the waiting period like a forbidden zone that protects the woman, and made allusion an opportunity to express an emotion that lays the foundation of an interest afterward.

The Truth says: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply of proposal to women﴾. The word *khitbah* (الخطبة, proposal of marriage) is derived from the root kha-ta-ba (خ ط ب), and it denotes matters that share several features. Among them is *khutbah* with a dammah on the kha (خُطبة), meaning a sermon. Among them is *khatb* (خطب), meaning a great matter. And among them is the meaning we are concerned with here, *khitbah* with a kasrah on the kha (خِطبة). All these features indicate that there is a great matter being addressed. A *khatb* is a great matter that shakes the whole being, and likewise the sermon is not delivered by the preacher except on a matter of importance, so he admonishes the community about a necessary matter.

The proposal is also a great matter, because it is a decisive matter separating two lives: the life of freedom and the life bound by a family and a system. All these meanings share in being a matter of importance and gravity.

He, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you imply of proposal to women or what you conceal within yourselves﴾. That is, there is no blame upon you if you have placed within yourselves a matter that is hidden from the woman. A Muslim may conceal and hide in himself whatever he wishes. But what informs and makes the divorced woman know that she is in your mind, O you who have kept her matter secret within yourself? You will surely have to hint and allude in a manner befitting respect for the woman.

The Truth says: ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾. He who created you knows that as long as she is in your mind, and her husband has died or divorced her, she has become a hope for you. Had He restricted you, it would have hindered your emotions and the opportunity would have been lost to you to take her as a wife afterward. For this reason, the Truth permitted allusion, so that none of you falls into what is forbidden, which is ﴿do not promise them secretly﴾, by taking from them a pledge that they will not marry anyone other than you, or by saying to her, "Marry me." Rather, he must allude, not disclose or state explicitly. Secret promising is forbidden, but what is permitted is allusion with good manners. ﴿Except that you say a known word﴾, such as saying, "O blessed is the one who will have a wife like you." Similar to this is praise that delights a woman. We all know that a woman in the situation of a divorced woman or a widow possesses a sensitivity and acuity by which she grasps the meaning of speech and its intent.

The Truth continues: ﴿And do not determine the tie of marriage until the decreed term reaches its end﴾. Thus we see that mere firm resolve is forbidden. Resolve precedes action, so when it is forbidden, the prohibition of the act is stronger, more severe, and more restrictive. You may intend to marry her and put your trust in Allah, but do not make it a settled matter until her waiting period is complete. When the decreed term reaches its end and the waiting period has expired, then resolve the marriage contract. Thus the tie of marriage passes through three stages:

The first stage: allusion or hinting.

The second stage: resolve, which is not valid or proper to complete until after the end of the waiting period.

The third stage: the contract.

The purpose of these stages is that each party takes its opportunity for deep reflection on this serious matter. If reflection has led to resolve, then a person may contract the marriage after the waiting period ends. If reflection has led to withdrawal and turning away from such a matter, then the person has what he wishes.

The Truth intends through these stages to give the opportunity to retract if one of the two parties discovers in the other something that does not please him. All these steps show that the contract is not concluded except with resolve. There is no contract without resolve. The Truth wants the Muslim not to proceed to the tie of marriage except after resolve. Resolve means determination that you want marriage in its true sense and with all its responsibilities, its dower, its legitimacy, and its chastity. Marriage without the foundation of resolve will end in failure.

The meaning of resolve is that you reflect on the matter deeply and patiently within yourself until you settle on a firm opinion. Then you may proceed toward marriage as something with permanence and continuity, not a passing lust without any foundation of the soul's determination upon it.

For this reason, marriage founded on lack of deliberation, and dependent on temporary causes such as the satisfaction of desire, does not last and does not succeed. Similar to this is temporary marriage (zawaj al-mut'ah). The reason for forbidding temporary marriage is that the one who enters into it does not intend continuation of married life, and as long as he does not intend permanence, it means he has made it a target for fleeting pleasure.

Those who permit temporary marriage are afflicted in their thinking, because they overlook the element of entering marriage with permanence. What is the reason for restricting your marriage to a term? True marriage is not restricted by such a term. Consider the foolishness of these people, so you know that the matter is not a matter of marriage; rather, the matter is the justification of fornication. Otherwise, why is it stipulated in temporary marriage that he marry her for a month or more?

When a person stipulates restricting marriage to a term, that is evidence of the foolishness of his thinking and the badness of his intention, because true marriage is one entered into with permanence, though he may end it after an hour if he finds that the matter deserves that, and no one will object to such conduct. So why do you restrict yourself to a term? The one who marries for pleasure uses intelligence in the wrong place. He may be clever in one respect but lacking in discernment in another.

A person must enter marriage with resolve, after deep reflection and deliberation, and then carry out the resolve by contract. Beware of placing in your soul a marriage tied to greeds and aims within you, such as lack of permanence or purely for the sake of pleasure. Everything some people think of as carnal and worldly greed is fleeting greed. Dismiss all these thoughts from yourself, for if you desire anything in marriage other than permanence and the desire for chastity, then Allah, glorified, knows it, and your thinking will return as a curse upon you, so beware of Him.

Allah, glorified, warns a person only against what angers Him, glorified. Therefore the Truth concludes this noble verse with His words: ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing﴾. He, glorified, knows the weakness of the human soul and that it may weaken at times. So if something has happened from it, Allah gives it the opportunity to repent, for He, glorified and exalted, is the Forgiving, the Forbearing.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 2, verse 236:

And after that, the Truth, glory be to Him, says:

﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation. But provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means, a provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the doers of good.﴾ [2:236]

We observe that the discussion before this was about divorce of a woman who has been consummated with, or about a woman whose husband consummated the marriage and then died leaving her. But some matters may necessitate the divorce of a woman who has not been consummated with. This verse comes to speak about the woman who has not been consummated with, and in her case the husband either has not specified a dowry (mahr) for her, or he has specified one for her.

Divorce before consummation (talaq qabl al-dukhul) has two rulings: an obligation (farida) was set in the contract, or no obligation was set in it. So the non-specification of the dowry is not a condition of the marriage; rather, if you marry her and no dowry was specified in this marriage, she is entitled to the dowry of her equals (mahr al-mithl) and the contract is valid. The evidence for this is that God, glory be to Him and exalted, says: (There is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them or specified for them an obligation). This means that she was a wife and the husband had not consummated the marriage with her.

We may ask: what is al-mass (touching)? We say: there is mass, and there is lams, and there is mulamasa. A person may touch a thing, but the toucher is not affected by the touched, meaning he does not perceive its nature or condition: is it rough or smooth, warm or cold, and so on.

As for lams, there must be a sensing of the touched thing; as for mulamasa, it is the occurrence of interpenetration between two things. Thus we have three stages: the first is mass, the second is lams, and the third is mulamasa. The word (mass) here indicates entry and intercourse, and it is lighter than lams, and gentler than saying lamastum or baashartum. We take this meaning because there is a Qur'anic context elsewhere that has come to be explicit in a meaning, and therefore from its context we can understand the intended meaning of the word (mass) here. The Lady Mary said:

﴿How can I have a boy when no man has touched me and I have not been unchaste?﴾ [19:20]

The Qur'an clarifies, on the tongue of our lady Mary, that no human had made the contact with her that results in a boy. The expression is at the utmost precision, and because the matter involves exposure of intimate matters and secrets, the Qur'an used the lightest word to describe that matter, which is mass. It is as if God, glory be to Him, wants to affirm her chastity even in wording: He negated mere touching by a human, not mulamasa or mubashara, although the intended meaning of the word is intercourse, because the verse is concerned with establishing Mary's chastity.

Let us reflect on the Qur'an's courtesy in treating the matter in the verse we are discussing; it is as if the Truth, glory be to Him, expresses the word with the final limit of its meaning and with the lightest expression.

The Truth says: (or specified for them an obligation). You know that when "or" (aw) comes in speech between two things, it means "either this or that." So is an obligation specified for them in exchange for the touching? The corresponding opposite of (as long as you have not touched them) is that you touch them, and the corresponding opposite of (specified for them an obligation) is that you do not specify for them an obligation. It is as if the Mighty and Majestic Truth says: there is no blame upon you if you divorce women as long as you have not touched them, whether you specified for them an obligation or did not specify for them an obligation. Thus the Qur'anic style is keen to alert the mind to noticing meanings.

We may note that the Truth used the word (in) for the possibility of the occurrence of divorce, and (in), as we know, is used for doubt. It is as if God, the Mighty, does not want divorce to be something taken lightly and realized; so He did not use (idha), but placed it in the position of doubt, so that the verse reinforces the saying of the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace: "The most detested of lawful things to God is divorce."(1)

Then the Mighty Truth says after that: (But provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means). That is, if you divorce a woman before consummation and you did not specify an obligation for her, then give her a provision (mut'a). The scholars said regarding the amount of the provision: it is what equals half the dowry of women like her, because she would have been entitled to half the dowry, and since no dowry was specified for her, she is entitled to the like of half the dowry of women like her. The Truth says: (the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means), meaning the provision should be within limits that suit the husband's condition: the wealthy man must give what befits God's bounty to him, and the poor man must give within the limits of his capacity.

The Qur'anic word (al-muwassi') is derived from (awsaʿa), and the active participle is (muwassi'), and the passive participle is (muwassa' 'alayhi). So which of these names applies to the husband? If you consider that provision comes from the Truth, then he is (muwassa' 'alayhi); and if you consider that the Truth asks you to widen the movement of your life so that your provision comes to you, and in proportion to your widening of it is God's widening for you, then he is (muwassi').

So the muwassi' is the one who has widened for himself by widening the movement of his means in life. And al-iqtar is poverty, being reduced; in proportion to the abundance and in proportion to the straitness is the provision. When the Truth, glory be to Him, requires a legal ruling, He does not intend merely the enforcement of the ruling upon the one addressed, but He distributes the responsibility in the general right of faith. His saying (provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means) means: if one is found who does not carry out God's ruling, then you must unite in enforcing God's command that every man who divorces his wife before consummation provide for her. The plural in the command, His saying (provide for them), is evidence of the community's solidarity in enforcing God's ruling.

1. Narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Bayhaqi and al-Hakim from Ibn 'Umar.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 2, verse 237:

And after that he said:

﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already specified a dowry for them, then half of what you specified (is due), unless they forgo it, or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes it. And that you forgo is nearer to piety. And do not forget graciousness between yourselves. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

That is: as long as he has not consummated the marriage with her and has not enjoyed her, you do not take the whole dowry; rather, she is entitled to half the dowry. And let us know that there is a difference between a ruling being established by the law of justice, and looking at a ruling from the aspect of grace (fadl). Let me relate this incident so that we may learn from it:

Two men went to a man to judge between them, and they said: "Judge between us with justice." He said: "Do you want me to judge between you with justice, or with what is better than justice?" They said: "Is there anything better than justice?" He said: "Yes: grace (fadl)."

Justice gives every owner of a right his right, but grace makes the rights-holder relinquish his right or some of it. So legislation, when it sets the scales of justice, does not wish to deprive the fountain of faith of the generosity of grace; He gives you justice, but then He, glory be to Him, says: (And do not forget graciousness between yourselves). Justice alone may be burdensome and resentment remains in souls, but the process of grace ends contention, enmity and hatred.

Contention arises when I think I am the one who has the right, and you think you are the one who has the right; and it is possible that circumstances adorn my understanding for me, and circumstances adorn your understanding for you. So when we cling to the case of justice we will not reach the degree of contentment in human souls. But when we turn to grace, we are satisfied and it ends.

And the Almighty, exalted is He, says: (And if you divorce them before you have touched them), that is, before you have entered upon them, (and you have already specified a dowry for them), meaning you have named the dowry, (then half of what you specified), (unless they forgo it), and what is meant by (they forgo) is the divorced wife.

Some ignorant people say, may God protect us: "The Qur'an contains a grammatical error (laḥn)." They thought that the correct form in the language would be "illā an ya'fū" instead of "illā an ya'fūna." This kind of ignorance does not distinguish between the waw of the verb and the waw of the plural. Here it is the waw of the verb: the word of the Truth (illā an ya'fūna) derives from the verb ('afā) and (ya'fū).

Thus we understand that the wife may forgo half her dowry and relinquish it to her husband. The Truth continues: (or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes it), and what is meant by him is the husband and not the guardian, because the context of the verse indicates that the intended person is the husband, although some exegetes have said that it is the wife's guardian. We should know that the guardian has no right to forgo anything in the matter of a woman's dowry, because the dowry is the right of the wife; it is a principal property and a principal livelihood in the life of the woman, since it is the counterpart for enjoying her body.

For this reason you find some people who do nothing with a woman's dowry, and save it for her, so that if one of them falls ill, they buy for him from this dowry even a tablet of aspirin, for it is treatment from lawful sustenance, and God may place healing in it. So the woman keeps her lawful dowry for such occasions, so that she may do with it something in which God places goodness, because it is from lawful sustenance without deceit or fraud.

And to those exegetes who proclaimed that the guardian of the wife is the one who forgoes, I say: Why would the Truth ordain a ruling in which the woman relinquishes her right and forgoes half, while the man is not generous enough to forgo half? Why does heaven place the whole burden on the woman? Is it logical that women forgo, or that he in whose hand is the marriage contract, meaning the wife's guardians, forgo, so that forgiveness comes from the wife and from her guardians, that is, from one side only?

We must understand well the context of grace in which God said: (And do not forget graciousness between yourselves). Reciprocity in forgoing is between the two, between the man and the woman, and by it we understand the meaning of His words, exalted is He: (or he in whose hand is the marriage tie forgoes it), that it is the husband. Just as the woman may forgo the half that is due to her, so the husband may also forgo the half that is due to him.

The Truth says: (And that you forgo is nearer to piety), because it is very possible that one of the two parties thinks he is wronged even if he takes the half he deserves. But if he takes nothing, that is nearer to piety and safer for souls. And let us always remember in such situations the words of the Truth: (And do not forget graciousness between yourselves). Even in a situation of disagreement that leads to a man separating from a woman he has not consummated with, God says: (And do not forget graciousness between yourselves), that is, do not make it into enmity, vengeance and grudges; and know that the Almighty makes some things into determined causes for a decree we do not know. This matter makes a person not believe that his own causes are the sole agent.

An example of this: we may find a man who was taken with a woman he saw and married her, or another woman whom a young man saw and did not like, and then another man came to her and was taken with her. That means that God, mighty and majestic, decreed acceptance for her at the moment she saw the young man as suitable for her and he saw her as suitable for him. For this reason the peasants of old used to say: "Do not grieve when a man comes to propose to your daughter and does not like her, for it is written on the forehead of every girl: 'O men, pardon (ʿafwan, with a kasra on the ʿayn and a shadda on the fāʾ) the women of men'; so she is not his, and therefore this man is not her portion." We must not neglect the causes of destiny in these matters, for this is more conducive to protecting human souls from grudges and rancor.

The Truth concludes the verse with His words: (Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do). He, glory be to Him, knows what is in the breasts and what lies behind every behavior. After that comes a verse to establish a matter of faith: this matter of faith is that the obligations of Islam are all collective obligations, so you cannot separate one obligation from another. Do not say: "This is a devotional obligation," and "this is a principle of public interest," and "this is a criminal matter." No. Every matter the Truth commands is a matter of faith that, together with the others, forms a complete method.

﴿Guard over the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before God in devotion.﴾ 238

Then he returns to the family and to the woman whose husband has died, saying:

﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, [let them make] a bequest for their wives: provision for a year without eviction. But if they leave, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves of reasonable [conduct]. And God is Mighty and Wise.﴾ 240 (Surat al-Baqarah).

So God, exalted is He, has separated one single matter, the matter of the separation between spouses, into two parts with one verse, ﴿Guard over the prayers…﴾, and placed between them the discussion of prayer. This is to alert us to the unity of the obligations of faith. Since the Almighty speaks of matters whose manifestations are either a voluntary breach through divorce or a predestined parting through death, God, glorified and exalted, wished to bring the human being into the act of worship that connects him to God, who legislated divorce and prayer and decreed death.

Why did God choose prayer over the other acts of worship to interrupt the context of the discussion of the legislation of divorce and separation? Because prayer is what grants believers tranquility, when matters of marriage and divorce distress and worry them, whether through the breach of choice in the divorces that have occurred or the hardship of separation through death. Their hearts will only be steadied by standing before their Lord to perform the prayer. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the first to do this: whenever a matter distressed him, he would stand to pray.

The believer goes to the Creator, who arranged for him the causes of marriage, divorce and separation, to ask Him to relieve his anxiety and sorrow. Since the believer has chosen to go to the One who directs destinies, he should know that God, who directed those destinies upon him, did not leave them without rulings; rather, He set for every matter a fitting judgment. The believer's only task is to accept predestined matters with contentment and then go to God devoutly, humbly and as one who prays. For the matter, whether it is divorce or death, contains fear and separation, whether by choice or by the predestined separation of death.

As for His words, ﴿Guard over the prayers and the middle prayer﴾, we understand that what is meant in the verse is the five daily prayers. But what is meant by the middle prayer?

Sometimes a particular and a general appear together, as in His words:

﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house as a believer, and the believing men and believing women, and do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction.﴾ 28 (Surat Nuh).

How many times do the father and parents appear here? They are included in His words, ﴿forgive me and my parents﴾, and in His words, ﴿whoever enters my house﴾, and in His words, ﴿the believing men and believing women﴾. That is, they are included three times.

So the placing of the general after the particular means that the particular is included within the general, so the command regarding the particular is repeated in a way that suits its particularity.

His words, ﴿Guard over the prayers and the middle prayer﴾, convey this meaning. If we ask, what is the meaning of "guard" (ḥāfiẓū)? The answer requires us to understand that there is "memorizing" (ḥifẓ), which is opposed to "forgetting" (nisyān), and "preserving" (ḥifẓ) which is opposed to "wasting" (taḍyīʿ). The two meet, for whoever has kept something and forgotten it has wasted it. Whoever has kept money and then squandered it has also wasted it. So all these meanings meet in the loss of a thing. Thus "preserving" means that you ensure the continuation of something you possessed. If you memorize a verse of the Qur'an, you must keep it in your self; and if God has blessed you with wealth, you must safeguard it.

His words, ﴿Guard over the prayers﴾, mean: do not waste them. It may also carry another meaning, namely that you have tasted the sweetness of prayer in the nearness of the companionship of your Lord, and that is more fitting and more deserving that you hold to it more firmly. This statement applies to the five prayers that we know.

His words, ﴿and the middle prayer﴾, are a mention of the particular after the general, as if God commanded the preservation of that particular twice: once within the sphere of the general, and once singled out by God for its specificity. What is the reason for singling out the middle prayer? The word "middle" (wusṭā) is the feminine of "middlemost" (awsaṭ), and the "middlemost" and the "middle" refer to a matter standing between two things in balance, meaning the two sides are equal. The two sides can only be equal in number, in the case of the five prayers, if the prayers are odd (witr), that is, single; for if they were even, we would not know which is the middle among them. Since the intended meaning is the middle of the five, it is the third prayer, preceded by two prayers and followed by two prayers, if you count according to the order of the first, second, third, fourth and fifth.

If the reckoning is by the obligation of prayer, the first prayer God, mighty and majestic, made obligatory is the noon prayer (ẓuhr). This is the first obligation, then the afternoon (ʿaṣr), then the sunset (maghrib), then the night (ʿishāʾ), then the dawn (fajr). If the middle is taken by legislation, it is the sunset prayer, and this is an opinion held by many scholars.

If the middle is taken according to the number of rak'ahs in the prayer, you will find that there is a prayer consisting of two rak'ahs, which is the dawn prayer; a prayer of four rak'ahs, which is the noon, afternoon and night prayers; and a prayer of three rak'ahs, which is the sunset prayer. The middle among them is the three-rak'ah prayer, which is between the even and the four-fold, and so it is the sunset prayer too. If you take it in relation to the day, the dawn is the beginning of the day, then noon after it, then afternoon, sunset and night, so the middle is the afternoon.

If you take it as the middle between the audible and the silent prayers, it may be the dawn prayer or the sunset prayer, because the silent prayers are noon and afternoon, and the audible ones are sunset, night and dawn. Between night and noon comes the dawn prayer, or the sunset prayer considering that it comes between noon and afternoon on one side, and night and dawn on the other.

If you take it because the angels gather in it, since they are at the two ends of the day and the night, this means the afternoon prayer or the dawn prayer. Thus the "middle" comes from the consideration by which it is reckoned, whether it is by number or by legislation, or by number of rak'ahs, or whether audible or silent, or according to the descent of the angels of day and night. Each of these considerations has its own ruling.

Why did God hide its identity from us? We say: He concealed it so that each of us would be alert and know that there is a difference between a thing in itself and a thing that is left ambiguous in relation to others, so that every prayer becomes "the" prayer, which leads to the preservation of all the prayers.

Since the middle prayer may be the dawn, the noon, the afternoon, the sunset or the night prayer, that is more conducive to preserving all the prayers. Thus the ambiguity of the thing serves to spread its explanation. For this same reason and cause, God concealed the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr): instead of being one night of power, it became nights of power.

Likewise, His words, ﴿Guard over the prayers and the middle prayer﴾, mean the five prayers in general, and each prayer has a particular characteristic. The Almighty wants us to stand for every prayer as devoutly obedient people. The clear command is ﴿and stand before God in devotion﴾. The original meaning of qunūt in the language is persistence in a thing. The noble Qur'an has urged and encouraged the perpetuation of obedience to God and the constancy of humility and submission, as we see in the words of the Noble Lord:
